The post nDiligence Releases Four-Year Study Identifying a Critical Supply-Chain Vulnerability Across 50 Platform Types appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
San Francisco, California, USA, November 12th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Four-year cybersecurity study finds all 50 types of software and devices examined vulnerable, with 46 rated Critical or High risk.

nDiligence, Inc. today announced the release of Attack the Glass (ATG) research to the general public.

The four-year study examines a cybersecurity vulnerability in how applications use people’s own devices to build what appears on screen, load data and run code while the application is in use.

An attacker who exploits it can change what people see and what their software does, after every security check has passed. The research is free at https://atg.nDiligence.com.

Much of the software people rely on, from web browsers and mobile apps to vehicle displays, medical devices and industrial control screens, builds its user interface on the device while it is running, a process called runtime client-side rendering.

The code, data and media it assembles come from dozens or hundreds of suppliers: the organization’s own systems, its vendors and their vendors.

An attacker who gains control of any one supplier gains placement and access inside the running application. Sign-in, encryption, Zero Trust, firewalls and code review all function before the code is loaded onto the device.

Once loaded, the code is trusted, and nothing checks what it does. The attacker can change what appears on screen, capture what the person types and act with that person’s authority.

In February 2024 the domain behind Polyfill.io, a code library loaded by more than 100,000 websites, was sold to a company the U.S. Treasury later sanctioned.

The altered code ran for months on visitors’ devices, and no automated security tool detected it; researchers found it that June. The underlying vulnerability was never fixed.

The ATG research documents how the same technique could deliver disinformation inside genuine news and election sites, show commanders and infrastructure operators a false picture, or hide safety alerts from selected users.

Due to security concerns from this type of threat, the team behind nDiligence spent more than two years privately briefing governments before publishing.

“People trust what they see with their own eyes. In the modern world we are constantly looking at screens, and we have grown to trust applications, websites, devices and companies, assuming they have 100% control over what is shown to us,” said Robert Beckett, Founder and CEO of nDiligence, who led the four-year research into the ATG vulnerability.

“ATG demonstrates how an attacker can hijack that trust without detection or attribution. A commander, a grid operator, a voter or a reporter can be looking at a screen that every security system says is safe, and what it shows can be manipulated. Whoever controls the screen can influence what people believe, decide and do, with sophisticated targeting. And right now, nobody can tell when or where it is happening. The cybersecurity community needs to understand this vulnerability so we can protect the integrity of software systems across industries, governments and critical infrastructure.”

Across the 10 categories examined, the research classifies five effects an attacker can achieve: deceive, disrupt, degrade, deny and destroy. All materials are free to share under Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) CLEAR, including a sixteen-chapter whitepaper, twenty online demonstrations and remediation playbooks.

“ATG was discovered during our research into digital supply-chain threats,” said Beckett. “Our team has spent more than 15 years working in online threat intelligence and countering influence operations, which is why we recognized how the ATG vulnerability could be exploited. Since 2024, we have been working with researchers, vendors and governments to find ways to close this gap. Anyone who builds, operates or defends systems that people use to make critical decisions needs to understand and mitigate the ATG vulnerability.”

About nDiligence

nDiligence, Inc. is a supply-chain intelligence company that builds trusted provider networks and keeps the supply chains beneath them under continuous watch.

Its founders bring decades of experience in internet supply chains and in national security and intelligence systems. The ATG research was self-funded. Learn more at https://www.ndiligence.com/.

Contact

Chief Product Officer

Anna Patterson

nDiligence, Inc.

press@ndiligence.com

articles.description:

According to Microsoft’s security advisory, an attacker can send a specially crafted message file and persuade a victim to open it in Outlook. The application may then connect to an attacker-controlled […]

The post CISA Confirms Active Exploitation of Outlook User Interaction 0-Day Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has confirmed active exploitation of a Microsoft Outlook zero-day vulnerability CVE-2026-124194 that can expose user authentication data.

According to Microsoft’s security advisory, an attacker can send a specially crafted message file and persuade a victim to open it in Outlook. The application may then connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing its usual warning about external content.

That connection can disclose the victim’s NTLMv2 hash, authentication data that an attacker could use to impersonate the user. Microsoft classifies the issue as spoofing rather than remote code execution. Its assessment identifies a high impact on confidentiality, but no direct impact on data integrity or service availability.

Microsoft released security updates for an actively exploited Outlook network-spoofing flaw (CVSS 6.5), allowing unauthenticated attackers to spoof networks.

The weakness falls under CWE-356, which covers software that fails to obtain proper user approval before a potentially unsafe action. Here, the missing warning removes a safety check before Outlook reaches an outside network location.

Active Exploitation of Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability

However, “missing user interaction” does not mean this is a zero-click attack. Microsoft explicitly states that the victim must open a malicious file. The Outlook Preview Pane is not an attack vector for this vulnerability. That detail helps defenders avoid confusing it with earlier Outlook flaws that required no user action.

Cyber Security News previously covered Russian hackers exploiting Outlook through CVE-2023-23397 and CISA’s warning about the MonikerLink vulnerability. Those reports provide background on Outlook exploitation, but their attack methods should not be treated as evidence of how this new flaw works.

Microsoft lists affected 32-bit and 64-bit editions of Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2021, and Office LTSC 2024. Fixed builds include 16.0.14334.21048 for LTSC 2021 and 16.0.17932.21140 for LTSC 2024. Microsoft 365 administrators should use the Office security release guidance linked in the advisory to identify the correct update for their deployment.

CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on November 10, 2026, setting a November 24 remediation deadline and requiring organizations to apply vendor mitigations, assess internet exposure, and discontinue affected products if fixes are unavailable.

Administrators should identify affected Office installations, deploy the relevant fixes, and verify installed build numbers rather than relying only on update deployment reports. The moderate severity label should not outweigh the confirmed exploitation evidence when teams set their patching order.

Microsoft marks exploitation as detected, although the reviewed advisory does not identify attackers, victims, campaign scale, or indicators of compromise. Those gaps should remain explicit rather than being filled with details from older Outlook attacks.

articles.title: Critical Red Hat Quay Vulnerability Allows Unauthenticated Attackers to Hijack Container Registries
articles.description:
A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay lets anyone who can reach a registry’s key server take over its token signing. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 and carries a CVSS score of 9.8, according to Red Hat’s advisory and the National Vulnerability Database. Red Hat published it on November 11, 2026. Quay is an […]

The post Critical Red Hat Quay Vulnerability Allows Unauthenticated Attackers to Hijack Container Registries appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical flaw in Red Hat Quay lets anyone who can reach a registry’s key server take over its token signing. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-123710 and carries a CVSS score of 9.8, according to Red Hat’s advisory and the National Vulnerability Database. Red Hat published it on November 11, 2026.

Quay is an enterprise container registry that stores and serves images. The weakness sits in its service key server. When a caller asks to rotate a signing key, the server only checks that the JWT is signed by an approved key and has the right audience and issuer. It never checks whether the token was meant for key rotation.

Red Hat Quay Vulnerability

An anonymous token from the /v2/auth endpoint passes that check. Red Hat’s Bugzilla report says the audience comes straight from a client-supplied service parameter, so the attacker controls it. This applies when FEATURE_ANONYMOUS_ACCESS is on.

With that token, the attacker sends their own key to the /keys endpoint. The new key copies the approval of the key that signed the request and can be saved with no expiry date. Quay then trusts it right away.

From there, the attacker can sign registry tokens that work on any repository. That gives read and write access to private images and lets them swap repository tags. Private images often hold secrets, so a leak can reach well beyond the registry.

Replaced tags are just as risky, because build systems may pull the poisoned image later. The same pattern has hit other registries, such as the Gitea container registry flaw that exposed private images.

Red Hat lists Quay 3 and Quay 5 images as affected, and the NVD entry shows the same products. Only deployments where /keys is reachable by untrusted clients are exposed. The Bugzilla note says the logic has been present since the first public commit.

Red Hat’s first step is to limit /keys at the proxy or load balancer so only trusted internal components can reach it. Next, check audit logs for service_key_rotate and service_key_delete events with a null expiration_date. Remove any approved service keys you don’t recognize.

Deleting a rogue key will not fix the problem for long. The anonymous request can simply install a new one until a fixed build is running. Teams should keep the /keys block in place and watch Red Hat’s advisory for a patched release. The advisory names no fixed version yet.

Registries sit at the center of software delivery, so a stolen signing key puts every image at risk. Teams that rely on Quay can also read our guide to the best container registry security tools for more ideas on protection.

Red Hat credits its own researcher, Dave O’Connor, with finding the bug. Nobody has reported attacks in the wild, and one tracker notes that no public exploit code has been indexed. Still, the steps are simple, and the damage is large, so treat this as urgent.

articles.description:

Tracked as CVE-2026-125926, the issue affects versions 1.0.3 through 1.34.0. Version 1.35.0 contains the fix. AWS disclosed the vulnerability on November 11, 2026, and urged users to upgrade. The open-source project acts as […]

The post AWS MCP Gateway Security Flaw Allowing Access to Internal Networks and Cloud Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
AWS has fixed a server-side request forgery flaw in mcp-gateway-registry that could let an authenticated attacker reach internal services through the gateway.

Tracked as CVE-2026-125926, the issue affects versions 1.0.3 through 1.34.0. Version 1.35.0 contains the fix. AWS disclosed the vulnerability on November 11, 2026, and urged users to upgrade.

The open-source project acts as a registry and gateway for Model Context Protocol servers. It brings server discovery, access control, and tool proxying into one place.

The flaw affects how the registry checks the upstream address supplied when a user registers a server or updates an existing entry.

AWS MCP Gateway Security Flaw

An attacker must already have a valid account with permission to register or modify servers. By setting a crafted upstream address, that user could make the gateway send requests to services inside the deployment’s network.

In some cases, the gateway also returned the responses, allowing the attacker to read information from those services. This is not an unauthenticated attack against every exposed gateway. The key risk comes from giving a permitted user control over where the gateway connects.

Requests then leave from the gateway’s network position, potentially reaching systems that the user could not contact directly. The impact depends on which services the deployment can reach.

Cloud credentials are another concern when the gateway runs with an attached cloud role. Related EC2 metadata attacks show how SSRF can expose temporary role credentials through unprotected metadata access.

However, AWS’s bulletin does not confirm credential theft or active exploitation of this specific flaw. It credits researcher novice-22 for coordinated disclosure.

According to the AWS security bulletin, version 1.35.0 checks upstream addresses during server registration and modification. Crucially, it leaves previously stored server settings unchanged.

Administrators should review existing upstream addresses after upgrading and correct or remove any destination they did not intend to allow. Teams should also examine application logs covering the time an affected version was running. Unexpected server registrations or address changes deserve review.

If the registry has an attached cloud role and the logs cannot rule out unexpected activity, AWS advises checking that role’s activity and rotating its credentials.

The version 1.35.0 release is the minimum fixed release for this issue. A separate flaw in the external management API was fixed in version 1.25.0. That earlier update does not protect against CVE-2026-125926, so deployments on versions 1.25.0 through 1.34.0 remain affected. Forks and derived projects also need the fix.

For teams unable to patch immediately, AWS recommends limiting registration and editing rights to trusted accounts, restricting outbound connections from the registry and auth-server components, requiring IMDSv2 on EC2, and reducing attached role permissions.

These controls also address risks highlighted by scans targeting MCP servers, but they do not replace upgrading and reviewing stored configurations.

articles.description:
A cybercrime investigation has linked the administrator of Qilin ransomware to Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev, a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia. Published by KrebsOnSecurity on November 11, 2026, the findings connect the online identity “Haise” to older forum accounts, Telegram records, and leaked databases. The identification remains a research finding, not a court ruling […]

The post Qilin Ransomware Admin Identified as 36-Year-Old Russian Hacker After Cybercrime Probe appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A cybercrime investigation has linked the administrator of Qilin ransomware to Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev, a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Published by KrebsOnSecurity on November 11, 2026, the findings connect the online identity “Haise” to older forum accounts, Telegram records, and leaked databases. The identification remains a research finding, not a court ruling or announced criminal charge.

The report comes as Qilin claims at least 365 victim organizations over three months. Citing NCC Group, Krebs described the operation as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program. Those figures represent claimed victims rather than a confirmed count of independently verified breaches.

The investigation followed a trail of reused identities. According to Intel 471 records cited by Krebs, Haise applied to join the Russian cybercrime forum RAMP in June 2022. Private messages showed the forum administrator referring to the applicant as both Haise and the Telegram username Alexbigboss44.

That Telegram name appeared in posts made during 2020 by “Rjun” on the Exploit and XSS forums. Researchers connected the newer ransomware identity to accounts active years before Qilin became a major threat. Flashpoint described Alexbigboss44 as a frequent buyer and trader of stolen account data, online traffic, and corporate access.

Qilin Ransomware Admin Identified as Russian Hacker

IntelHawk helped connect these identities through historical usernames and other signals. Its founder, Leo Bogod, described a progression from small fraud schemes in 2018 and 2019 toward more organized activity involving malware, botnets, and payment systems between 2020 and 2023.

The next link came from an email address used to register Rjun accounts on several criminal forums. SpyCloud found a historical password containing the Rjun alias. Constella Intelligence then linked the email to leaked records from Russia’s Gosuslugi government services platform, identifying Yakovtsev, the report said.

Additional checks involved a persistent Telegram account identifier, related contact records, and leaked travel data. Flashpoint had recorded more than 5,000 messages associated with that Telegram identity since 2018. Together, these records formed the reported attribution chain. Krebs said attempts to reach Yakovtsev for comment were unsuccessful.

Operating since September 2022, Qilin runs a ransomware-as-a-service program. Its affiliates break into victim networks and deploy ransomware in exchange for at least 80 percent of ransom payments. The group uses double extortion, stealing sensitive files before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the stolen information.

Its technical reach extends beyond ordinary workstations. Earlier Cybersecuritynews.com reporting examined Qilin attacks targeting VMware vCenter and ESXi, including remote management tools, network spreading, and vulnerable drivers used to turn off security products. Attacks against virtual infrastructure can disrupt multiple business systems through one compromised management layer.

Separate coverage of Qilin’s use of bulletproof hosting detailed infrastructure supporting its extortion activity. Such hosting arrangements help criminal services remain online despite abuse complaints and efforts to disrupt them.

The investigation highlights a weakness in long-running criminal operations. Changing a nickname does not erase older account links. Reused contact details and persistent platform identifiers can allow researchers to connect separate identities years later.

However, the reported links should not be treated as proof of guilt, and identifying a suspected administrator does not establish that Qilin’s ransomware operations have stopped or that victims face less risk.

articles.description:
Lenovo has disclosed a high-severity security flaw in ThinkSystem V4 server management firmware that restores a default OpenBMC root password after a factory reset. Tracked as CVE-2026-81936, the issue could let attackers access enabled administrative interfaces and reach the controller’s underlying operating system, which is normally restricted. The CVE record, published on November 11, 2026, […]

The post Lenovo Warns of High-Severity Server Flaw That Restores Default Root Credentials After Reset appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Lenovo has disclosed a high-severity security flaw in ThinkSystem V4 server management firmware that restores a default OpenBMC root password after a factory reset.

Tracked as CVE-2026-81936, the issue could let attackers access enabled administrative interfaces and reach the controller’s underlying operating system, which is normally restricted.

The CVE record, published on November 11, 2026, states that Lenovo found the issue during an internal security review. The flaw affects a limited range of XClarity Controller 3 firmware releases, rather than every ThinkSystem server or all products using OpenBMC.

The affected releases run from XCC3 version 2.51, build IHX432Y, through version 2.56, build IHX436K. Lenovo describes the cause as a development regression, meaning a software change reintroduced unsafe behavior. Performing an “XCC Reset to Default” operation on these versions reintroduces the default OpenBMC root credential.

The trigger is specifically a controller reset to defaults. The supplied disclosure does not describe an ordinary server restart, operating system reinstall, or power cycle as causing the problem. This makes firmware version checks and reset history important when assessing exposure.

Lenovo’s XClarity Controller 3 product guide explains that XCC3 is an OpenBMC-based management processor built into ThinkSystem V4 servers. It supports hardware monitoring, firmware updates, remote power control, and several management interfaces. Access to this layer carries significant risk because it controls functions beyond normal server applications.

Lenovo Warns of Server Vulnerability

After the reset restores the credential, an attacker could use it against enabled XCC administrative interfaces. Lenovo also warns that this provides access to the underlying XCC operating system. That is the controller’s operating system, not automatically the host operating system running business workloads.

The issue is classified as CWE-1392, Use of Default Credentials. MITRE describes this weakness as using default passwords or keys for potentially critical functions, making unauthorized access easier if those values remain in use.

The record assigns a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.1, rated high, and a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.8, rated medium. Both vectors require high privileges and user interaction. The disclosure should therefore not be read as evidence of an unrestricted, unauthenticated internet takeover.

Previous reporting on OpenBMC server vulnerabilities and BMC firmware security flaws shows why controller security needs separate attention. Those reports concern different vulnerabilities and do not establish exploitation of this Lenovo issue.

Lenovo says the affected versions are no longer available for download and that it has improved development processes to prevent and detect similar regressions. The supplied record does not name a specific replacement build or report active attacks.

Administrators should identify installed XCC3 builds, review whether affected controllers underwent resets, and confirm the appropriate supported firmware with Lenovo. Keep management access restricted to trusted networks.

Lenovo’s security dashboard can help review enabled services and account settings. However, it should not replace checking the affected firmware range and obtaining vendor guidance before further reset operations.

articles.title: CISA Warns of Google Chromium 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks
articles.description:
CISA has added a new Google Chromium zero-day CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and says attackers are already using it. It sits in the browser’s XML component and could let a remote attacker run code through a specially crafted webpage. Anyone who uses Chrome, Edge, or Opera should check their browser version […]

The post CISA Warns of Google Chromium 0-Day Vulnerability Actively Exploited in Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA has added a new Google Chromium zero-day CVE-2026-125350 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and says attackers are already using it.

It sits in the browser’s XML component and could let a remote attacker run code through a specially crafted webpage. Anyone who uses Chrome, Edge, or Opera should check their browser version today.

CISA added the flaw to the catalog on November 10, 2026, in an alert covering six new entries. The agency calls it a use-after-free bug. It says a remote attacker could run arbitrary code inside the browser sandbox.

Because the code sits in Chromium, the same weakness could affect other browsers built on it, including Microsoft Edge and Opera. CISA has not said whether ransomware groups use the flaw, and the entry lists it as unknown.

A use-after-free error happens when a program keeps using memory after it has been released. MITRE’s CWE-416 entry explains that the memory may later be reused by other code, so the old pointer now points to something it should not touch.

Attackers who control what lands in that spot can crash the browser or run their own code. The weakness is common in languages like C and C++, where developers manage memory by hand.

Google Chromium 0-Day Actively Exploited

In this case, a victim would only need to open a booby-trapped page. CISA says the code runs inside the sandbox, which is the browser’s safety box. That does not prove a full takeover of the computer. Attackers often pair a bug like this with a second flaw to break out of the sandbox, though nothing public shows that happened here.

Google shipped the patch on November 9, 2026. Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 covers Windows and Mac, and 157.0.8103.50 covers Linux. An anonymous researcher reported the flaw on November 6, just three days before the fix arrived.

Google said it knows an exploit exists in the wild but shared nothing about who is using it, who was hit, or how. The update was one of nine security fixes in the release, and Extended Stable users should install version 156.0.8078.96.

SecurityWeek counts this as the eighth Chrome zero-day exploited this year. You can read our earlier coverage in Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely.

Memory bugs are a steady source of browser zero-days. CISA notes that Google’s own Chromium team finds that around 70% of its serious security bugs are memory safety problems.

Our review of last year’s cases, Chrome Zero-Day Vulnerabilities Exploited in 2025, found eight exploited flaws, all added to the KEV catalog.

Open Chrome, go to Settings, then About Chrome, and let the update finish. Chrome downloads fixes in the background, but the patch only works after a restart. Make sure the version number reads 157.0.8103.50 or higher.

Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi users should install their vendor’s update as soon as it appears, since fix dates for those browsers are not yet confirmed.

IT teams should check which machines are exposed to the internet, push the update across managed devices, and confirm the browsers were actually restarted. The official KEV catalog and the CVE record will carry more detail as it becomes public.

The service wraps harmful files in layers of encryption, so antivirus and endpoint detection tools struggle to spot them. It is now active in many campaigns around the world. The post Hackers Abuse Cruciferra Malware-as-a-Service to Conceal Infostealers and Remote Access Trojans appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Cybercriminals are renting a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) tool called Cruciferra to hide infostealers and remote access trojans (RATs) from security software.

The service wraps harmful files in layers of encryption, so antivirus and endpoint detection tools struggle to spot them. It is now active in many campaigns around the world.

Cruciferra is a “crypter,” a tool that scrambles a malicious file and unpacks it only when it runs on a victim’s computer. Buyers pay a monthly fee, and Proofpoint reports prices from $450 to $2,000 depending on the features.

The seller has advertised it on underground forums since fall 2025, which makes it easy for even low-skilled criminals to use.

ESET Research noted that the service has been busy. Since January 2026, ESET says it has blocked over 700,000 compromise attempts linked to Cruciferra.

Türkiye, Greece, and Spain were hit hardest. ESET also found that the service, sold since October 2025, is a rebrand of the long-running KGB cryptor, so its operators are not beginners.

Hackers Abuse Cruciferra Malware-as-a-Service

The crypter’s best trick is its payload protection. Proofpoint found more than 90 encryption routines, most built from pieces of well-known algorithms. Each batch of samples looks different from the last, which breaks signature-based detection.

Researchers also say Cruciferra seems to be an umbrella name for several crypters sold in one package. Infections start with an email, a fake tax page, or a link to an archive. The victim opens a ZIP file holding an executable and a DLL.

Cruciferra always runs through DLL side-loading, so the clean executable quietly loads the malicious DLL. Before doing anything else, it checks for a sandbox or an analyst’s virtual machine.

The DLL is also stuffed with hundreds or thousands of fake exported functions to slow down researchers. This is similar to the crypter that can kill EDR that our team covered earlier.

Next, it goes after the defenses on the machine. Cruciferra removes the monitoring hooks that security tools place in Windows functions, hides console windows, and turns off Windows notification pop-ups.

It also drops a signed but vulnerable driver, often GoFlyDrv.sys, and uses it to shut down EDR processes. This is called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), a method many groups are now abusing trusted Windows drivers to use.

If it lacks admin rights, it bypasses the UAC prompt and adds a Run key named “putty” so it survives a reboot. The final step is a custom form of Process Ghosting. The malware writes the payload to a temporary file, marks the file for deletion, and maps it into memory.

It then starts a legitimate process and points it at the payload. Windows deletes the file, so scanners find nothing to check. Cruciferra also patches memory-query hooks and weakens the NtManageHotPatch function, which would otherwise help check the loaded image.

Campaigns and Payloads

Proofpoint has seen dozens of campaigns from several unrelated groups. Targeting is opportunistic, with message volumes from a few hundred to thousands.

Financial, healthcare, and government groups appear most often. One actor, TA4922, sent tax-themed emails that posed as India’s Income Tax Department and led to fake portals hosting ZIP files. The result was AsyncRAT.

Other emails posed as the U.S. Social Security Administration and delivered XWorm, while guest-complaint lures aimed at hotels and travel firms led to zgRAT.

The payload list is long. It includes Agent Tesla, AsyncRAT, DarkCloud Stealer, Formbook, XLoader, Phantom Stealer, Remcos, Snake Keylogger, ValleyRAT, XWorm, and zgRAT.

Other delivery routes exist too. eSentire saw Cruciferra delivered through ClickFix pages made by the ErrTraffic MaaS tool. In that case the loader used the DCRCVDrv.sys driver to end 145 antivirus and EDR-related processes, and it dropped the Remus stealer. eSentire also describes a $1,200 monthly package and a cheaper $650 option.

Defenders should block known vulnerable drivers and keep Microsoft’s vulnerable-driver protections on. Teams should also watch for unexpected driver services, DLL side-loading from archives, and a “putty” Run key.

PowerShell logging helps, and staff should be wary of unexpected tax or complaint emails. Because pasting commands from a web page is a common trick in fake CAPTCHA lure campaigns, users should never do it.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Blockchain analysis cited in a new Financial Action Task Force (FATF) report has mapped more than $100 million in victim payments to a cryptocurrency wallet cluster attributed to a scam compound.

Investigators followed the money through laundering networks toward cash-out points, showing how transaction tracing can expose the financial systems behind organized online fraud.

Published on November 5, 2026, the report examines scam operations across Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Asia. FATF estimates that scam compounds cause tens of billions of dollars in annual losses.

Its findings describe criminal businesses that combine social engineering, trafficking, digital infrastructure, and money laundering rather than operating as isolated groups of scammers.

Analysts from SlowMist, reviewing FATF’s findings, noted that investigators must connect wallet activity with customer records, communications, and company information.

Their analysis does not identify a malware family or a new malware campaign; it interprets FATF’s findings on scam networks and financial flows.

FATF Traces Over $100 Million in Stolen Funds Through Crypto Wallets Linked

The headline figure comes from one case described in FATF’s scam compound report, not a newly announced FATF seizure. Blockchain analysis linked more than $100 million in incoming victim funds to an attributed wallet cluster.

Tracing those transfers revealed laundering routes, but the announcement does not establish that the full amount was frozen, recovered, or returned.

Victims are often drawn into investment schemes through social media, messaging services, or relationships built over time. Fake platforms display invented profits before blocking withdrawals and demanding additional payments.

Similar mechanics appear in fake prediction market platforms that use fabricated trading results and withdrawal fees to keep victims depositing cryptocurrency. These comparisons explain the fraud model without establishing a connection between separate cases.

Once payments arrive, operators can split or consolidate funds across bank accounts, electronic wallets, cryptocurrency services, and money mule networks.

Layering means moving funds through additional transactions to make their origin harder to follow. FATF describes underground banking, over-the-counter brokers, cross-chain services, and gambling platforms among the channels that investigators may encounter.

Cryptocurrency trail

The cryptocurrency trail is only one part of the evidence. Investigators must test wallet attribution against exchange customer information, payment conversion records, device communications, and corporate ownership data.

Separate reporting on crypto investment laundering operations illustrates how shell-company accounts and stablecoin transfers can connect conventional banking with cryptocurrency wallets. A blockchain label alone should not substitute for verified ownership evidence.

Speed creates a major obstacle. FATF says instant payment systems can move scam proceeds from a victim’s account in as little as two minutes.

A bank may see an apparently authorized transfer without knowing that manipulation caused it. Meanwhile, receiving institutions may observe rapid transfers but lack the victim’s messages or the fraudulent platform’s records.

That gap makes cooperation between banks, exchanges, telecommunications providers, technology platforms, and investigators essential. FATF identifies the first 24–72 hours after detection or reporting as critical for freezing funds and recovering assets.

Its recommendations extend beyond payments to recruitment advertisements, malicious domains, communications infrastructure, and services shared across criminal operations.

The wider infrastructure matters because scam networks can replace individual accounts and relocate smaller teams. Reporting on verified financial account sales shows how criminal suppliers advertise bank, fintech, and cryptocurrency accounts as ready-made laundering resources.

Disrupting those shared providers can address capabilities that survive the closure of a single scam website or physical location. FATF also warns that AI-generated content, deepfakes, and automation help criminals reduce costs and expand their reach.

Its response framework therefore combines early disruption with transaction tracing, lawful asset preservation, and victim protection. People trafficked or forced into scam operations require screening and safeguards, rather than automatic treatment as willing participants.

articles.description:

The bug carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5. It sits in the replication code that runs when a new primary server finishes catching up. MongoDB announced the […]

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
MongoDB has patched a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-118383, that can let a remote attacker with no login crash a database server using two simple ping requests. The bug carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.5.

It sits in the replication code that runs when a new primary server finishes catching up. MongoDB announced the fix on November 10, 2026, and said it found the problem internally. The company said it knows of no attempts to abuse it.

MongoDB Database Crash Vulnerability

The GitHub advisory describes a use-after-free bug. This means the program keeps using a piece of memory after it has already been released.

The advisory says requests that need no authentication can trigger the condition. The result may be a sudden server shutdown. Under some conditions, it could also be arbitrary code execution inside the server process.

Only replica set members are affected. That includes the shard and config server members in sharded clusters. A standalone mongod instance does not run the catch-up step, so it is safe from this bug.

Researchers at Datadog Security Labs explained the chain. When a replica set member wins an election, it first applies writes it missed. Only then does it accept new ones. The bug lives in the cleanup at the end of that step.

Vulnerable servers accept a ping command before login. An attacker sends two of them with a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each one leaves behind a pending notification, which MongoDB calls a waiter. These waiters do nothing at first. They stay in place until the member restarts, rolls back, or steps down.

The crash needs two more things the attacker cannot control. One member must fall behind, and that same member must then win an election. This can happen during maintenance or an outage.

When catch-up ends, the cleanup runs twice and touches freed memory. The server then crashes before it takes any writes. Turning on authentication does not stop the first step.

Datadog built a four-member replica set and forced the lag and failover itself. On MongoDB 8.0.34 with both ping requests sent, the new primary logged a segmentation fault, and the process crashed.

Without the requests, the same failover worked fine. On patched 8.0.37, the server rejected both requests as Unauthorized and kept running.

The team did not achieve code execution. It also warned that its roughly 40-second test time says nothing about real-world speed. The attacker cannot see or choose the timing window, which is why the CVSS rating lists attack complexity as high.

MongoDB’s fixed releases are 9.0.7, 8.3.16, 8.0.37, 7.0.48, 6.0.30, 5.0.35, and 4.4.32. Atlas clusters upgrade during maintenance. MongoDB urges customers who deferred maintenance to apply the update soon.

Admins running their own servers should check the version on every member, including containers and nodes that were offline during patching.

If you cannot upgrade right away, limit network access to the systems that truly need it. This reduces who can send the ping requests but does not fix the bug.

A crashed primary can leave a cluster without a writer until another member takes over. In Datadog’s test, the cluster stayed without a primary.

Datadog advises checking structured server logs for slow-query entries from ping commands that include readConcern.afterOpTime and an expired wait.

Also look for a member that leaves catch-up twice in one transition, followed by a fatal signal that mentions CatchupState::abort_inlock(). Logging settings decide whether these fields appear, so confirm your logs keep the full command.

This is not the first pre-login MongoDB problem this year. Cybersecuritynews.com covered CVE-2026-25611, a compression bug that let unauthenticated users crash servers using little bandwidth.

It also covered MongoBleed, the memory leak flaw that was exploited in the wild soon after disclosure. MongoBleed shows how fast attackers move once details are public.

Teams should patch this latest flaw before that happens again, and they should keep database ports off the open internet. The NVD entry for CVE-2026-118383 lists the official record, and MongoDB’s tracking tickets are SERVER-138119 and SERVER-138175.

articles.description:

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers are abusing AntiFox, an open-source AI penetration-testing platform, to compromise web applications, deploy webshells, and access Amazon Web Services production secrets.

Arctic Wolf linked the activity to Alibaba Cloud infrastructure hosting AntiFox interfaces, connecting those systems to malicious actions against internet-facing applications and associated AWS environments.

In one intrusion, attackers moved through multiple AWS identities and issued hundreds of API requests in approximately 30 minutes. Most requests failed, but successful operations exposed sensitive production secrets.

A separate incident involved unauthorized access to S3 objects, including reading, copying, and deleting stored data.

Researchers from GitGuardian noted the AntiFox activity in their analysis of AWS credential abuse, drawing on Arctic Wolf’s investigation.

Their findings place the attacks within a wider shift toward AI-assisted credential theft. AntiFox is a legitimate dual-use framework being misused, rather than a newly identified malware family.

Hackers Abuse AntiFox AI Pentesting Tool

AntiFox began as a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1 and provides a Chinese-language interface for deploying AI agents that automate security-testing tasks. Operators can direct agents to map exposed services and probe endpoints.

Earlier reporting on ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how these systems interpret results and choose subsequent actions instead of requiring constant manual input.

In an observed intrusion, attackers deployed an ASPX webshell on an internet-exposed Microsoft Internet Information Services server. The IIS worker process created the shell, enabling operating-system command execution.

Attackers searched for application configuration files and backups, read database connection strings, inspected error logs, and copied configuration material into a web-accessible upload directory.

These actions created opportunities to obtain credentials and sensitive application information. Investigators also observed an attempt to connect to an internal production database using a credential extracted from application configuration.

However, the available reporting does not establish that every AWS intrusion began through an IIS webshell or explain how every credential was obtained.

For cloud access, attackers used valid AWS identities, including IAM users and assumed EC2 roles. They tested permissions across services such as S3, EC2, Lambda, Secrets Manager, and Amazon Bedrock.

This credential-driven approach echoes AI agent credential exposure risks, where configuration files and ordinary tool activity can expose secrets without exploiting a flaw in the cloud platform itself.

Most requests returned access-denied errors, but the activity continued toward accessible resources. Some sequences progressed to successful retrieval of production secrets.

AWS told BleepingComputer that its services were not compromised and operated as designed; attackers used credentials taken from customers’ compromised applications to access their accounts.

Detecting Credential Abuse and Containing Exposure

The main defensive lesson is that failed requests do not make an activity sequence harmless. Teams should review successful operations within bursts of denied calls and connect unusual cloud access with preceding web-server activity.

A single identity’s permissions can determine whether reconnaissance stops at discovery or reaches production data. GitGuardian’s separate testing helps explain the speed advantage.

An ARTEX build without a dedicated secrets scanner found eight of nine planted credentials using ordinary commands. It began searching within six to thirteen seconds.

Related coverage of exposed ARTEX testing servers highlights why defenders should investigate deployed tooling alongside the credentials it can reach.

Response should prioritize revoking affected AWS sessions and access keys, rotating exposed application credentials, and reviewing downstream access.

Removing a leaked secret from a repository or configuration file does not invalidate it. Teams must identify dependent production services before rotation to reduce disruption while closing unauthorized access.

Longer-term controls include narrowly scoped permissions, short-lived credentials, stronger secret scanning, and keeping long-term keys out of application configurations.

Reporting on GitHub cloud credential theft reinforces that exposed secrets remain valuable across different attack methods. AWS also recommends requiring IMDSv2 and enabling GuardDuty to strengthen protection and detection.

articles.description:
Hackers are targeting AI coding assistants, software packages, and developer integrations to steal credentials and gain access to connected systems. A new threat intelligence report examined 103 AI-linked cyber incidents, showing how tools trusted with source code and sensitive data are becoming entry points for attackers. The research covered July 31, 2025, through July 31, […]

The post Hackers Target AI Coding Tools to Steal Credentials as Researchers Uncover 103 AI-Linked Cyber Incidents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are targeting AI coding assistants, software packages, and developer integrations to steal credentials and gain access to connected systems.

A new threat intelligence report examined 103 AI-linked cyber incidents, showing how tools trusted with source code and sensitive data are becoming entry points for attackers.

The research covered July 31, 2025, through July 31, 2026. Its central finding is less about machines independently running attacks and more about criminals using AI to improve familiar methods, including software supply-chain compromise, phishing, credential theft, and extortion.

Fully autonomous operations remain uncommon. Researchers from Recorded Future’s Insikt Group noted credential-stealing malware in compromised AI tool packages, alongside the Shai-Hulud worm’s expansion into Claude Code.

Their AI cyber threat report describes attackers exploiting the access these tools already hold, rather than breaking capabilities unique to artificial intelligence.

Hackers Target AI Coding Tools

Developer systems offer attackers more than passwords. Coding assistants and supporting packages can reach repositories, credentials, connected applications, and business data.

A compromised dependency can therefore become a starting point for data theft, persistent access, and lateral movement into other parts of an organization.

In late February 2026, attackers compromised a popular AI proxy package that connects applications to different large language models.

Malicious updates enabled credential theft, lateral movement, and backdoor persistence. Another compromise in April used AI tool packages to harvest credentials, steal data, and access cryptocurrency wallets.

Related reporting on malicious AI coding plugins illustrates the same trust problem: developers entered provider API keys into seemingly useful extensions, which secretly forwarded those keys to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

These incidents show why approving an editor does not automatically make every installed plugin safe. The report also describes a May expansion of Shai-Hulud that targeted Claude Code to maintain access and spread.

Its broader warning is that widely deployed development tools can expose potentially thousands of downstream environments when attackers compromise a trusted component.

Attackers are also exploiting demand for AI products through fake download pages, search poisoning, and ClickFix lures.

Separate coverage of fake Claude Code installers documented pages that persuaded users to execute commands, triggering PowerShell stages and credential theft. Recorded Future observed AI-themed lures increasing significantly after March 2026.

What the 103 Incidents Reveal About AI Cybercrime

The dataset includes incidents involving AI as an attack tool, target, or delivery mechanism. Recorded Future required documented malicious activity, rather than ordinary demonstrations or security research.

Consequently, the total should not be read as 103 autonomous attacks or 103 confirmed breaches of AI providers. Of those incidents, 32 involved AI in malware or offensive operations.

The remaining 71 covered attacks against AI infrastructure, AI-themed malware delivery, AI-assisted deception, and abuse of legitimate services. Nine of the 32 malware and operations cases involved state-sponsored intelligence collection.

Most state-backed activity used AI to help develop malware, hide code, or support targeting. One reported campaign against Taiwanese government entities used up to eight AI agents with limited human intervention.

However, operational risk, reliability problems, and high usage costs still limit fully autonomous attacks. AI also helps criminals extract value from stolen information.

Recorded Future described The Gentlemen ransomware group using language models to review stolen material and shape extortion demands.

Separately, infostealers targeting AI credentials demonstrate why investigations must cover access tokens, refresh tokens, and API keys, not just passwords.

For defenders, the priority is controlling what coding agents can access and change. Recorded Future recommends separating agents from sensitive systems, requiring approval for consequential actions, maintaining independent monitoring, and auditing AI dependencies, plugins, and model repositories for backdoors or malicious command injection.

Teams should also monitor exposed developer API keys, corporate OAuth tokens, and stolen AI subscriptions. The report expects human-directed automation to expand before fully autonomous campaigns, making strong access controls and third-party oversight immediately relevant defenses rather than measures reserved for a future threat.

The Stable channel moves to version 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows […]

The post Google Chrome Fixes 83 Security Flaws, Including 5 Critical Ones that Could Enable RCE Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google released a Chrome security update that addresses 83 vulnerabilities, including five critical use-after-free flaws that could allow remote code execution.

According to the supplied release notice, the update covers Windows, macOS, and Linux, with fixes spanning browser rendering, graphics, JavaScript processing, and other core features.

The Stable channel moves to version 157.0.8103.78/.79 for Windows and Mac, while Linux receives 157.0.8103.78. Google says the release will reach users over the coming days and weeks.

The notice lists five critical vulnerabilities and 78 high-severity issues, making this an important update for personal devices and managed business systems. All five critical vulnerabilities involve use-after-free errors. These occur when software continues accessing memory after releasing it.

If attackers can control how that memory is reused, they may cause crashes, corrupt data, or potentially execute malicious code. Similar risks appeared in an earlier Chrome update that fixed 52 security flaws and also addressed memory safety bugs.

The critical issues are CVE-2026-126885 in ServiceWorker, CVE-2026-126895 in CSS, CVE-2026-126879 in Layout, CVE-2026-126846 in Skia, and CVE-2026-126911 in Accessibility. These components support background web tasks, page styling, page layout, graphics, and accessibility features.

Chrome Fixes 83 Security Flaws

Xinyang Ge reported the ServiceWorker, CSS, and Layout vulnerabilities on October 2, October 19, and October 22, respectively. Google reported the Skia issue on November 2, while Andrew Boni reported the Accessibility flaw that same day. The reward for Boni’s finding remains pending in the supplied notice.

Although these weaknesses raise concerns about remote code execution, the notice does not describe working exploits or establish that each flaw enables full device compromise. It also does not state that these newly listed vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild.

The remaining fixes address a broad range of weaknesses, including type confusion, buffer overflows, out-of-bounds memory access, information leaks, and missing authorization checks. Affected components include V8, ANGLE, Skia, Extensions, FileSystem, MediaStream, PDF, and SiteIsolation.

Several reports credit Anthropic researchers assisted by Claude and OpenAI Codex Security. These acknowledgments show AI-assisted research contributing to this release. However, the notice does not explain how those tools identified or validated individual findings.

This update follows a separate Chrome zero-day patch for an actively exploited XML vulnerability. That earlier exploitation report should not be confused with evidence of attacks against the 83 vulnerabilities covered here.

Users should open Chrome’s menu, select Help, then About Google Chrome to check for updates. Relaunch the browser when prompted so the new version takes effect. Administrators should verify deployment across managed devices rather than assume every installation has updated automatically.

Google may restrict technical bug details until enough users receive fixes or affected third-party projects finish patching. The Chromium Security page explains its disclosure process and provides further guidance on vulnerability reporting and browser security.

The post Hackers Breach Global Shipping Giant Maersk and Claim Theft of 100GB of Logistics Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A.P. Moller–Maersk has confirmed that hackers accessed an older IT system and extracted data, as a group calling itself WhiteArmor claims it stole 100GB of logistics records.

The shipping giant disclosed the incident on November 11, 2026, but has not confirmed the attackers’ identity, the claimed data volume, or what was taken.

In its official security notice, Maersk said the affected system came from a previous acquisition. Its cybersecurity team launched an investigation after discovering the breach and took action to secure the system. The investigation remains ongoing.

According to BleepingComputer’s report, WhiteArmor listed Maersk on its leak site and demanded $5 million in bitcoin within 30 days. The group claims the stolen files came from the OCF/LF Logistics platform, which supports logistics and supply chain work. Maersk acquired LF Logistics from Li & Fung in 2022.

The attackers allege that their haul includes nearly 30,000 driver records, passwords stored in plain text, 33 accounts with top administrative rights, and signed delivery receipts.

They also claim to hold purchase orders, shipment notices, and 27,842 mobile device logs containing phone numbers, email addresses, and device identifiers known as IMEI numbers. These details remain claims, not confirmed findings.

Hackers Breach Global Shipping Giant Maersk

Maersk has not publicly linked WhiteArmor or the LF Logistics platform to its investigation. Its statement confirms unauthorized access and data extraction.

However, it does not identify the files taken, explain how the attackers entered, or disclose when the intrusion began. The available evidence also does not establish that ransomware encrypted any systems.

“Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” Maersk said. The company described the incident as isolated to a local system and reported no indication of impact on other Maersk systems or connected customer and partner systems. That includes connections through application programming interfaces, or APIs, and electronic data interchange, or EDI.

Customers can continue using Maersk platforms to book and manage shipments. The company does not currently expect operational disruption and says it will provide updates as more information becomes available. It will also notify affected parties if further findings require it.

The case follows other breaches involving shipping providers. Cybersecurity News previously covered the CEVA Logistics breach affecting Valve customers and the ShipMonk breach involving Trezor customer records. Those incidents show how delivery information held outside a retailer’s own systems can become exposed. They do not establish a link to the Maersk incident.

Maersk has urged customers to treat unexpected communications about the breach with caution and verify them through their usual company contact.

For now, the confirmed facts remain limited to access and data extraction from one legacy system. The claimed 100GB theft, ransom demand, and alleged sensitive records require further verification as investigators determine the incident’s full scope.

articles.description:
Microsoft has warned that attackers are using a free remote access tool called GSocket to stay inside Linux servers even after the original security hole is fixed. Many admins treat a patch as the end of an incident, but this activity shows that patching alone may leave the attacker’s access untouched. GSocket is an open […]

The post Microsoft Warns Hackers Are Using GSocket Backdoors to Keep Linux Servers Compromised After Patching appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has warned that attackers are using a free remote access tool called GSocket to stay inside Linux servers even after the original security hole is fixed.

Many admins treat a patch as the end of an incident, but this activity shows that patching alone may leave the attacker’s access untouched.

GSocket is an open source tool built for remote administration. Attackers have turned it into a quiet backdoor because it hides its traffic inside a shared public relay network.

Other researchers have also seen AI-generated scripts spreading GSocket in recent Linux intrusions, which shows how widely the tool is being reused.

Researchers from Microsoft identified the activity through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint data and described it in a new report published on November 11, 2026.

The report was written by Yash Gund, Sumith Maniath, and the wider Microsoft Security Research team. Microsoft noted that several unrelated threat actors have adopted the same tool, and that detections grew by 356.2% between March and August 2026, though the rise was uneven from month to month.

Microsoft Warns Hackers Are Using GSocket Backdoors

The attacks start with a flaw in an internet-facing web application. Once attackers can run commands through the web server, they use curl to download a script and run it with bash.

The script checks the host, picks a GSocket client that matches the system type, and saves it in a writable or memory-backed folder such as /dev/shm. That access normally lasts only until the bug is fixed or the service restarts, so attackers add a second way in.

GSocket solves this problem for them. Both the infected server and the attacker connect outward to the Global Socket Relay Network, which pairs the two sessions over an encrypted channel.

The server needs no open port or public IP address, and inbound firewall rules never see the traffic. Because the tool runs on its own, separate from the hacked application, patching the original bug does not remove it.

Connections are matched using a shared secret rather than an IP address or domain. The install script creates a random secret, and the attacker can read it from the console, from a temporary file, or through Telegram, Discord, or a webhook.

With that secret, the attacker can return at any time from any compatible GSocket client. Blocking an IP address or domain is therefore unlikely to cut off access, because there is no attacker-owned server to block.

The attackers also work to avoid being noticed. Microsoft saw them rename the process to look like a kernel thread, keep persistence through cron jobs, systemd services, shell profiles, and watchdogs, and delete the staging files afterward. Some used the same trick seen in fileless PHP web shells on Linux: hiding in places that look normal during a quick check.

Who Is Being Hit and How to Respond

Web applications and hosting systems made up 87.1% of the incidents Microsoft could attribute. PHP applications and cPanel hosting accounted for 63.9% of those, and Apache for 24.3%.

Education and research organizations were the largest share of affected groups at 30.7%, followed by technology and telecommunications at 22.9%.

Microsoft says this likely reflects exposure rather than deliberate targeting, since universities often run large web estates outside central IT that are hard to track and patch.

Admins who have followed recent cPanel vulnerabilities exposing hosting servers will recognize this kind of environment. In a few cases, the attackers also tried to gain root access by exploiting CVE-2026-43284, a Linux kernel bug known as Dirty Frag.

Our earlier coverage of the Dirty Frag Linux kernel flaw explains why kernel patching matters on internet-facing servers. Microsoft’s main advice is to fix the host as well as the bug.

Admins should remove the GSocket client, its persistence entries, and any staged files, then confirm that outbound connections to the relay have stopped.

Other steps include setting deny-by-default egress rules, mounting temporary and memory-backed folders as non-executable, and reviewing cron entries, systemd units, and shell startup files. Microsoft also recommends running Defender for Endpoint on Linux with real-time protection turned on.

It aims at the secrets and cloud keys that sit inside GitHub Actions, the tool many teams use to build and ship code. So far, […]

The post Hackers Hijack 4,837 GitHub Accounts to Target 61,764 Repositories With CI Secret-Stealing Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A threat actor has used stolen GitHub credentials to push a secret-stealing payload into tens of thousands of code repositories.

The activity began on November 10, 2026, around 12:45 UTC. It aims at the secrets and cloud keys that sit inside GitHub Actions, the tool many teams use to build and ship code.

So far, 4,837 hijacked accounts opened probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories. At least 1,806 repositories ran the payload and lost credentials.

At least 50 of the hijacked users also publish packages for npm, Go, Packagist, PyPI or crates, which raises the risk for people who rely on their work.

Researchers at Aikido identified the malware and noted that the attacker seems to want CI secrets, not a wide supply chain spread. Still, the payload reached one Packagist package and one Go module through automated publishing triggers.

Hackers Hijack 4,837 GitHub Accounts

The attacker uses a stolen GitHub token to work on every repository that the token can write to. The first step is a probe. The attacker opens a pull request titled “docs: dependency audit notes” from a branch named wfx-docs, which proves the account has write access.

GitHub search shows 61,839 of these pull requests, opened between November 10 and November 11. Of these, 10,431 went into repositories the account does not own, reached through collaborator or organisation access.

About 92% are still open, so most owners have not noticed. If the probe runs, Aikido treats that user as compromised, even when the later workflow stage never runs. The second step pushes the real payload in one of three ways.

One way adds about 1,500 lines to an existing workflow. Another adds a hidden script and a postinstall hook in package.json, which runs on any npm install. The third creates a throwaway branch with a new workflow file.

The last step is cleanup. The attacker reverts the change within a minute and deletes the workflow run and its logs. A missing run number in the workflow history is often the only trace. This is why the 1,806 figure may be too low.

The overlap with earlier activity is notable. Many of these accounts were also hit in October, and the GhostAction GitHub account compromise reported earlier used a similar fake workflow trick.

Accounts hit in October were about a thousand times more likely than other active accounts to be used in November. In more than 100 repositories, the new payload was added to the old October workflow files.

Aikido does not link the two waves to one actor, because the tools, servers and methods differ, and stolen credentials often pass between groups.

What the Malware Steals and How to Respond

The payload is one shell script of about 1,500 lines. It is heavily commented and not hidden, and it calls itself “wfx”. It works in four stages: collect, escalate, persist and exfiltrate.

It first gathers GitHub Actions secrets, runtime tokens, cloud credential files, shell histories, and keys for AI tools such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Hugging Face. It also reads the memory of running processes to pull out tokens.

Next, it tries to go deeper into the cloud. It swaps GitHub OIDC tokens for AWS, Google Cloud and Azure sessions. In AWS, it creates long-lived access keys.

The script then tries to survive a password reset. It forges “success” status checks to get past branch protection, rewrites an AWS role so any account can use it, and adds new federated identity credentials in Azure.

This is similar to the pattern seen in the Shai-Hulud npm supply chain worm, where postinstall hooks and workflow files also took secrets.

In this campaign, the stolen data goes out only by HTTP POST to two servers. Other exfiltration channels in the script were turned off, such as cache entries, artifacts and encrypted commits.

Because of this, finding no “wfx-loot” artifacts does not prove your data is safe. Aikido says a missing run number on the attacker’s commit is the better sign that the payload ran.

Defenders should first search for the branches, pull request titles and commit messages listed below. If the payload ran, assume every secret and cloud role available to the workflow is exposed, and rotate them all.

Revoke the hijacked GitHub tokens, and review audit logs for new federated credentials and changed AWS trust policies. Teams should also use phishing-resistant sign-in, limit workflow permissions and watch outbound traffic from runners.

These steps match the advice from the earlier 790 GitHub repositories hijacked report, and the lessons from the tj-actions supply chain attack still apply.

Treat the Packagist package digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 as hostile, and treat any machine that installed or opened it as compromised. The Go module versions carry the payload only in a workflow file, so users may not be affected, but Aikido still advises removing them.

articles.description:
Palo Alto Networks has disclosed a remote code execution vulnerability in PAN-OS software running on Panorama. Tracked as CVE-2026-0330, the flaw allows an authenticated administrator with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges. The November 11, 2026, advisory urges users to patch affected Panorama deployments, while Cloud NGFW, Prisma Access, and standalone PAN-OS […]

The post Palo Alto PAN-OS RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Execute Arbitrary Code With Root Privileges appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Palo Alto Networks has disclosed a remote code execution vulnerability in PAN-OS software running on Panorama. Tracked as CVE-2026-0330, the flaw allows an authenticated administrator with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges.

The November 11, 2026, advisory urges users to patch affected Panorama deployments, while Cloud NGFW, Prisma Access, and standalone PAN-OS firewalls are not impacted.

Palo Alto Networks says it is not aware of malicious exploitation and credits internal researcher Daniel Voce with discovering and reporting the vulnerability. The official security advisory classifies the flaw as CWE-94, a code injection weakness.

Successful exploitation lets an administrator run code with root permissions rather than remain within normal administrative limits. The published assessment identifies high privileges as a requirement and says no user interaction is needed.

No special configuration is required for an affected Panorama installation to be vulnerable. However, exploitation requires both administrator authentication and network access. This is not an unauthenticated attack that anyone on the internet can directly carry out against a reachable system.

Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS RCE Vulnerability

Palo Alto Networks assigns the issue a medium severity rating, with a CVSS threat score of 6.1 and a base score of 8.6. The vendor lists moderate urgency but warns that risk is highest when management access is allowed from external internet addresses.

The flaw is separate from the previously reported PAN-OS root code execution vulnerability CVE-2026-0322. That earlier issue had reported exploitation. Those attacks should not be treated as evidence that attackers are exploiting this newly disclosed Panorama vulnerability.

Fixes cover PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1, and 10.2 on Panorama. For the latest maintenance lines listed in each branch, patched releases include 12.2.4-h2, 12.1.10-h4, 11.2.16-h2, 11.1.16-h5, and 10.2.18-h14. Administrators should use the advisory’s upgrade guidance for their installed release.

Additional fixes are available for earlier maintenance lines. PAN-OS 12.1 options include 12.1.4-h14 and 12.1.7-h12. PAN-OS 11.2 options include 11.2.4-h24, 11.2.7-h24, 11.2.10-h18, and 11.2.13-h5. Separate hotfixes also cover older 11.1 and 10.2 maintenance releases.

Unsupported versions should move to a supported, fixed release. No known workaround fixes the underlying issue. Palo Alto Networks recommends limiting management access to trusted internal IP addresses.

Its management security guidelines warn against exposing firewall or Panorama management interfaces to the internet or other untrusted networks.

Restricting access to a dedicated jump box can further reduce exposure. Previous reporting on exposed PAN-OS management interfaces highlights why this boundary deserves attention. Access restrictions reduce risk, but they do not replace the security update.
