cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The board’s simplest hard question “how good are we, versus whom?” has four honest answers that measure different things: framework self-assessment, live telemetry scores, outside-in benchmarks, and exposure mathematics.

Averaging them misleads; running two and minding the gap informs. This countdown ranks ten tools with each lens declared, because the questionnaire’s answer and the telemetry’s answer to the same question are different facts.

Axio takes 1; CyberSaint and Microsoft Secure Score complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Axio C2M2/CSF assessment pedigree with the scenario math that turns scores into board decisions.

• Podium: Axio (framework depth), CyberSaint (automated CSF scoring), Secure Score (the telemetry baseline every Microsoft shop already owns).

• Lens rule: run one internal lens and one external lens, report them side by side the gap between them is itself a finding.

• 2026 theme: CSF 2.0’s govern function made board conversations easier confirm native 2.0 scoring, not 1.1 mappings.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: lens honesty, framework fidelity (CSF 2.0-era), benchmarking quality, improvement-roadmap output, continuous-update capability, and pricing clarity.

Weights: lens-core capability 30%, framework fidelity 20%, roadmap output 20%, benchmarking 15%, pricing 15%.

The 2026 Maturity Assessment Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results. Lenses ranked within their frames.

1. Sensato C2M2 — Best C2M2-Focused Maturity Assessment

Snapshot: C2M2 assessment platform | U.S. Department of Energy C2M2 framework | Cybersecurity maturity evaluation and improvement roadmap

Why it earns its place: Sensato C2M2 helps organizations evaluate cybersecurity maturity using the Cybersecurity Capability Maturity Model (C2M2). It supports structured assessments to identify capability gaps, measure maturity across cybersecurity domains, and guide improvement planning.

Its C2M2 focus makes it particularly relevant to critical infrastructure organizations seeking a framework-driven view of their cybersecurity posture. Assessment that turns maturity gaps into an actionable improvement roadmap.

Pros: C2M2 framework focus; structured maturity assessment; capability-gap identification; improvement planning.

Cons: More focused on C2M2 maturity assessment than continuous telemetry-based scoring; Axio-style cyber-loss scenario and insurance quantification is not established as a core capability.

Bottom line: A strong C2M2-focused alternative for organizations seeking structured cybersecurity maturity assessments, particularly in critical infrastructure.

2. CyberSaint — Best Automated CSF Scoring

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Continuous CSF-family assessment | Control-data automation + dollar translation

Why it ranks here: CyberStrong automates the framework lens: CSF-family maturity scored from live control-posture inputs, crosswalked across frameworks, and FAIR-translated into dollars when the conversation turns financial.

The self-assessment that feeds itself instead of re-interviewing the estate annually.

Pros: Continuous scoring; crosswalks; dollar translation.

Cons: Benchmarking depth versus the outside-in graphs.

Bottom line: The CSF engine on autopilot.

3. Microsoft (Secure Score) — Best Included Estate Baseline

Snapshot: Included with Microsoft licensing | Live posture from identity/endpoint/apps | Ranked improvement actions

Why it ranks here: Secure Score computes posture from your actual estate identity risk, endpoint config, app hygiene with ranked actions whose points move when you fix things, and similar-organization comparisons built in.

Free with the licenses you already hold, scoped to the estate those licenses cover: the most-deployed telemetry lens on earth.

Pros: Zero marginal cost; live scoring; ranked actions.

Cons: Microsoft-estate scope; framework fidelity partial.

Bottom line: The baseline you already own read it before buying anything.

4. BitSight — Best Evidence-Grade Benchmark

Snapshot: Portfolio subscriptions | Decade of loss-correlated external data | Peer benchmarking

Why it ranks here: BitSight answers “versus whom” with receipts: externally observable posture benchmarked against industry peers on a dataset correlated with real incidents the comparative lens insurers and boards already treat as currency.

Blind to internal controls by design; honest about it.

Pros: Peer-benchmark evidence; insurer currency; trend lines.

Cons: Outside-in blindness to internal maturity.

Bottom line: The comparison with the longest receipts.

5. SecurityScorecard — Best Operational Outside-In Grade

Snapshot: Tiers; free self-view| Letter grades + factor drill-downs | Weekly-cadence ergonomics

Why it ranks here: SecurityScorecard makes the external lens a habit: letter grades boards parse instantly, factor drill-downs practitioners action weekly, and a free self-view that makes checking your own grade a quarterly discipline rather than a procurement event.

Pros: Grade clarity; operational cadence; free self-assessment.

Cons: Same outside-in blindness, same honesty required.

Bottom line: The external grade you check like a dashboard.

6. Balbix — Best Asset-Grounded Posture Score

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Continuous inventory → breach likelihood → dollars | ROI-ranked actions

Why it ranks here: Balbix scores maturity as live exposure math: continuously discovered assets, per-asset breach likelihood from vulnerabilities and controls, business-criticality weighting, and a quantified score doubling as a remediation-ROI ranking.

Posture as arithmetic, not interviews.

Pros: Asset-level grounding; ROI-ranked roadmap; continuous updates.

Cons: Framework-narrative outputs pair from the assessment lanes.

Bottom line: The score with asset IDs behind it.

7. Tenable — Best Vulnerability-Lens Scoring

Snapshot: Tenable One tiers| Exposure scoring (Lumin lineage) | Peer benchmarks from scanner truth

Why it ranks here: Tenable grades posture through the vulnerability estate: exposure scores benchmarked against peers, weakness-density trends, and remediation-maturity math computed from what the scanner actually sees.

The lens for programs whose maturity question is mostly an exposure question.

Pros: Scanner-truth grounding; peer benchmarks; remediation metrics.

Cons: Governance/process maturity outside the lens.

Bottom line: Maturity as the scanner sees it.

8. RiskOptics — Best Lean Risk-Scored Assessment, Status Note

Snapshot: Subscription tiers | ZenGRC-family lineage | Branding consolidation underway

Why it ranks here: The RiskOptics lane tied maturity scoring to risk posture (ROAR lineage) at lean-team weight, but branding has consolidated back toward ZenGRC verify which scoring capabilities survive where before contracting.

Capability noted; wrapper homework first.

Pros: Risk-linked scoring; lean workflow.

Cons: Branding-consolidation diligence precedes evaluation.

Bottom line: Confirm the current wrapper, then evaluate.

9. Panorays — Best Supplier-Maturity Lens

Snapshot: Per-vendor tiers | External posture + adaptive questionnaires | Portfolio-scale vendor views

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: Panorays measures their maturity, not yours: vendor posture graded through fused ratings and adaptive questionnaires at portfolio scale. The supplier-maturity lens inside a maturity-tools roster, ranked as exactly that.

Pros: Vendor-maturity views; dual-lens fusion; portfolio scale.

Cons: Not an own-estate maturity tool.

Bottom line: The lens pointed at your suppliers.

10. Prevalent — Best Assessed-Vendor Depth

Snapshot: Platform + managed tiers | Managed vendor assessments | Questionnaire-grade maturity evidence

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: Prevalent (Mitratech) produces vendor-maturity evidence at questionnaire depth through managed assessments the labor-included companion for third-party maturity programs, scoped to suppliers rather than your own estate.

Pros: Managed depth; FI fluency; vendor evidence quality.

Cons: Vendor-facing scope; Mitratech-era roadmap check.

Bottom line: The vendor-maturity questionnaire desk.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Two Lenses, One Gap, Zero Averaging

Declare the lenses before the purchase: self-assessment (Axio/CyberSaint-class) measures program discipline, telemetry (Secure Score, Balbix, Tenable) measures the estate as it stands, outside-in (BitSight, SecurityScorecard) measures what attackers and insurers see, and the vendor-facing pair measures suppliers.

Run one internal and one external deliberately, report them side by side, and treat the gap as the finding a high self-score over a falling external grade is a governance problem wearing a good questionnaire.

Exhaust the free baselines first (Secure Score is in your tenant; ratings self-views cost nothing), demand roadmap output over report cards (ranked, owned, ideally ROI-ranked actions), insist on native CSF 2.0 scoring including the govern function, and benchmark the benchmark by asking what peer set your comparison actually contains.

Then route every action list into the risk register where improvements get owned, dated, and quantified and resolve the RiskOptics wrapper question before any evaluation hours.

FAQs

What are the best cybersecurity maturity assessment tools in 2026?

Axio for C2M2/CSF depth, CyberSaint for automated scoring, Microsoft Secure Score for the included telemetry baseline, BitSight and SecurityScorecard for outside-in benchmarks, Balbix and Tenable for exposure math, with RiskOptics (status pending) and the vendor-facing pair (Panorays, Prevalent) scoped to suppliers.

Self-assessment or telemetry scoring?

Both, reported separately self-assessment measures discipline, telemetry measures reality, and the gap between them is itself a finding worth investigating (cybersecurity maturity assessments).

Is NIST CSF 2.0 the right framework?

It’s the lingua franca, and the govern function improved board conversations confirm tools score 2.0 natively rather than mapping from 1.1.

How often should maturity be assessed?

Continuously where telemetry allows, quarterly for framework self-assessment, annually for deep third-party validation static annual scores go stale against quarterly drift.

What should the board report contain?

Two lenses side by side, peer context, a trend line, and the top five funded actions with owners a number without a roadmap is decoration.

Verdict

Ten tools, four lenses, one discipline: never average what measures different things.

Axio turns assessment into funding decisions, CyberSaint automates the framework, Secure Score baselines the estate for free, BitSight and SecurityScorecard grade the outside, Balbix and Tenable price the exposure, the vendor lenses watch the suppliers, and RiskOptics waits behind a wrapper check run two lenses, mind the gap, fund the top five, and let next quarter’s trend be the only score that matters.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
GDPR enforcement punishes two failures: invalid consent at the banner and missed clocks on data-subject requests and the tooling market splits along exactly that line, with program suites running RoPAs and DPIAs above both.

One honest count note: our source list named ten brands, but Cookiebot is a Usercentrics product, so we rank nine platforms rather than double-count a lineage. OneTrust takes 1; Securiti and TrustArc complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: OneTrust the privacy estate most enterprises standardized on.

• Podium: OneTrust (program suite), Securiti (data-grounded DSARs), TrustArc (methodology depth).

• Honest count: nine, not ten Cookiebot lives inside Usercentrics.

• 2026 theme: discovery-grounded DSARs fulfillment that finds data across systems beats inbox-workflow tools the moment a real estate is tested.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: consent-layer validity (granular, provable, dark-pattern-free), DSAR automation depth (discovery-backed), RoPA/DPIA workflow, enforcement propagation into downstream systems, multi-jurisdiction crosswalks, and pricing clarity.

Weights: DSAR truth 25%, consent validity 20%, program workflow 20%, enforcement propagation 15%, jurisdictions 10%, pricing 10%.

The 2026 GDPR Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. OneTrust — Best Enterprise Privacy Estate

Snapshot: Module subscriptions | Consent, RoPA, DPIA, DSAR, transfers in one | Regulatory-intelligence feeds

Why it earns 1: OneTrust remains the suite enterprises standardized on: consent management, records of processing, DPIAs, DSAR fulfillment, and transfer assessments in one estate, fed by regulatory intelligence that tracks the laws as they multiply.

Depth and procurement comfort at enterprise weight the default the market prices against.

Pros: Full-program breadth; regulatory intel; enterprise integrations.

Cons: Suite weight; challengers out-focus per lane.

Bottom line: The privacy estate, incumbent for reasons.

2. Securiti — Best Data-Grounded Privacy Engine

Snapshot: Platform modules | Discovery/classification feeding DSARs | Consent enforced downstream

Why it ranks here: Securiti builds privacy on data intelligence: discovery and classification across clouds feeding DSAR fulfillment that actually finds the data, consent propagated into downstream systems rather than merely recorded, and AI-governance modules extending the same thesis. Privacy promises made technically true.

Pros: Discovery-backed DSARs; enforcement propagation; AI-governance reach.

Cons: Engineering-grade platform, engineering-grade deployment.

Bottom line: The privacy engine with data underneath it.

3. TrustArc — Best Methodology-Backed Suite

Snapshot: Platform + advisory | Decades of assessment methodology | Transfer-framework tooling

Why it ranks here: TrustArc wraps platform workflow in privacy methodology built over decades: assessments, certifications, and transfer-framework tooling with advisory depth attached.

The pick for programs that want governance rigor alongside software consultancy-flavored delivery included.

Pros: Methodology depth; certification programs; transfer tooling.

Cons: Advisory-weighted model versus pure-SaaS speed.

Bottom line: The methodology house with a platform.

4. Usercentrics (incl. Cookiebot) — Best Consent at Web Scale

Snapshot: Traffic-based tiers | CMP scale + Cookiebot lineage | TCF/ad-tech fluency

Why it ranks here: The honest consolidation: Cookiebot is Usercentrics’ product, and together they run consent at web scale banner governance from SMB sites to publisher estates, TCF fluency the ad-tech ecosystem leans on, and the scanning that keeps cookie declarations true. Consent is the product, done at volume.

Pros: CMP scale; TCF fluency; Cookiebot’s SMB reach.

Cons: Program-suite obligations (RoPA, DPIA) live elsewhere.

Bottom line: The web’s consent workhorse counted once.

5. Osano — Best Transparent Value Platform

Snapshot: Published tiers | Consent + DSAR + data mapping bundle | No-nonsense deployment

Why it ranks here: Osano pairs consent management and DSAR workflow with famously transparent pricing and quick deployment the mid-market’s straight-talking default, with a data-mapping layer growing beneath the bundle.

Pros: Pricing transparency; bundle completeness; deployment speed.

Cons: Enterprise-program depth versus the suites.

Bottom line: The honest mid-market bundle.

6. DataGrail — Best Integration-Led DSAR Engine

Snapshot: Request/connector tiers| Hundreds of SaaS connectors | Shadow-SaaS discovery

Why it ranks here: DataGrail attacks DSAR truth through integrations: connectors locating personal data where it actually lives across the SaaS sprawl, fulfillment automated against the clock, and continuous discovery catching the systems nobody declared.

The request-volume specialist.

Pros: Connector-led discovery; fulfillment automation; shadow-SaaS detection.

Cons: Consent/CMP lane pairs from elsewhere.

Bottom line: The DSAR clock’s worst enemy.

7. Didomi — Best EU-Native Preference Layer

Snapshot: Traffic/module tiers | Multi-channel consent orchestration | Sovereignty-comfortable delivery

Why it ranks here: Didomi serves European publishers and enterprises with consent and preference orchestration across web, app, and TV TCF-fluent, sovereignty-comfortable, and treating preference data as a first-class asset rather than banner exhaust.

Pros: Multi-channel consent; preference management; EU posture.

Cons: Program-suite scope beyond consent.

Bottom line: The EU-native preference layer.

8. Ketch — Best Programmatic Consent Layer

Snapshot: Platform tiers | API-first consent enforcement | Data-stack orchestration

Why it ranks here: Ketch treats privacy as infrastructure: consent and rights signals enforced programmatically into the data stack through APIs and orchestration permissioning data use rather than just recording choices. The engineering team’s consent layer.

Pros: API-first enforcement; orchestration depth; developer ergonomics.

Cons: Banner-first buyers want the CMP specialists.

Bottom line: Consent as code, not banner.

9. Microsoft Priva — Best M365-Estate Privacy Lane

Snapshot: Per-user add-ons | Privacy risk + DSAR over Microsoft 365 | Purview-adjacent

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: Microsoft Priva runs privacy inside the Microsoft estate: risk insights over M365 data, subject-request fulfillment across Exchange, SharePoint, and Teams, Purview classification adjacent.

For M365-centric estates it’s the bundled start; the multi-system world beyond Microsoft needs the platforms above.

Pros: Estate-native DSARs; bundled economics; Purview synergy.

Cons: Scope bounded by the Microsoft estate.

Bottom line: The M365 privacy lane know its borders.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: File the Test Request, Grade the Banner Like a Regulator

Two pilots decide everything. First, the DSAR truth test: file a real subject request against your own estate and count what each tool finds versus what it merely tickets inbox-workflow DSAR tools fail the moment data lives in forgotten SaaS, which is why discovery grounding (Securiti’s classification, DataGrail’s connectors) separates the field.

Second, the regulator’s banner review: granular purposes, equal-prominence reject, provable records, no dark patterns validity is a legal artifact, not a design choice, and pre-ticked-box fines keep proving it.

Price by real volumes (traffic for CMPs, requests and connectors for DSAR engines), demand RoPA and DPIA workflows your DPO will actually keep current, and check enforcement propagation consent that doesn’t reach downstream systems is theater.

M365-centric estates should exhaust Priva’s bundled lane before buying wider; engineering-led teams should evaluate the as-code lane (Ketch) before stacking banners on ungoverned pipelines; and reconcile the RoPA against discovery findings quarterly, because the gap between declared and discovered processing is the finding regulators increasingly hunt.

FAQs

What is the best GDPR compliance software in 2026?

OneTrust leads the program suites, Securiti grounds privacy in data discovery, TrustArc brings methodology depth, with Usercentrics (including Cookiebot), Osano, DataGrail, Didomi, Ketch, and Microsoft Priva by center of gravity.

Why nine platforms instead of ten?

Cookiebot is a Usercentrics product one lineage, counted once.

CMP or full privacy platform?

Traffic-facing consent needs a CMP; program obligations (RoPA, DPIA, DSAR, transfers) need platform workflow enterprises typically run a suite or a CMP-plus-program pairing (best data privacy management software).

What makes DSAR automation real?

Discovery grounding: connectors or classification locating personal data across systems, not a ticketing inbox asking humans to remember where data lives.

Does GDPR tooling cover CCPA and other laws?

The major platforms crosswalk multi-jurisdiction obligations confirm the jurisdictions you sell into are first-class features, not roadmap.

Verdict

Nine platforms, one consolidated lineage, two tests that matter: what the DSAR engine finds, and whether the banner survives a regulator’s squint.

OneTrust runs the estate, Securiti and DataGrail ground the requests in discovered truth, TrustArc brings the methodology, Usercentrics and Didomi work the web’s front door, Osano keeps the mid-market honest, Ketch wires consent into the stack, Priva covers the Microsoft lane file the test request, grade the banner, reconcile the RoPA against reality, and buy the lane your obligations actually live in.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
PCI DSS is three purchases wearing one acronym scope-reduction architecture, continuous technical controls, and assessment itself and PCI 4.x sharpened all three with customized approaches and stricter authentication demands.

This countdown ranks ten options across the lanes honestly: control platforms, merchant-program machines, automation stacks, and the QSA benches that sign the paperwork.

Qualys takes 1 on the technical backbone; Vanta and ControlCase complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Qualys the year-round technical requirements, consolidated in one platform.

• Podium: Qualys (technical controls), Vanta (automation-stack integration), ControlCase (continuous-assessment model).

• Lane rule: scope reduction beats tooling every time the math runs tokenization and segmentation demote RoC-scale programs to SAQs before any license is bought.

• 2026 theme: PCI 4.x future-dated requirements are now in force authenticated scanning, MFA-everywhere evidence, and customized-approach documentation decide readiness.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: lane-fit honesty, PCI 4.x readiness, scope-reduction support, continuous-control automation, assessment-bench quality where applicable, and pricing clarity.

Weights: lane-core capability 30%, 4.x readiness 20%, scope support 20%, automation 15%, pricing clarity 15%.

The 2026 PCI DSS Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Qualys — Best Technical-Controls Backbone

Snapshot: Per-asset/module subscriptions | Long-standing ASV | VM, FIM, policy compliance in one cloud

Why it earns 1: PCI’s year-round reality is technical housekeeping, and Qualys consolidates it: approved ASV scanning, vulnerability management with rescan workflow, file integrity monitoring, and policy-compliance checks against PCI benchmarks requirement by requirement, one platform. The controls that keep quarters boring.

Pros: ASV pedigree; control consolidation; continuous posture; 4.x-era authenticated scanning.

Cons: Assessment and program workflow come from elsewhere.

Bottom line: The technical requirements, on one bill.

Snapshot: Framework/headcount tiers | Connector evidence + crosswalks | SAQ-strength focus

Why it ranks here: Vanta folds PCI into the certification stack most teams already run: continuous control monitoring through connectors, policy templates, and crosswalks that let SOC 2 evidence serve PCI requirements. SAQ-level programs get the full effect; RoC-scale estates pair it with a QSA bench.

Pros: Evidence automation; crosswalk reuse; stack consolidation.

Cons: Platform, not assessor; ASV via partners.

Why it ranks here: VikingCloud runs PCI at the scale banks see it: portals shepherding millions of small merchants through SAQs, ASV scanning, and validation, with enterprise QSA services above. For acquirers, ISOs, and franchise estates, the portfolio machinery is the product.

Same honest scope as its co-leader platform, not QSA with depth-first mapping as the differentiator.

articles.title: Microsoft Discovers 59 Linux Kernel Security Bugs Using AI, Including Flaws Hidden for Over 20 Years
articles.description:
Microsoft’s FORGE Lab used an AI-driven scanning system to find 59 security bugs in the Linux kernel. Some of them sat unnoticed for more than 20 years. The work has so far led to 33 assigned CVEs, and Microsoft confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of them. The team used a tool with the […]

The post Microsoft Discovers 59 Linux Kernel Security Bugs Using AI, Including Flaws Hidden for Over 20 Years appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft’s FORGE Lab used an AI-driven scanning system to find 59 security bugs in the Linux kernel. Some of them sat unnoticed for more than 20 years.

The work has so far led to 33 assigned CVEs, and Microsoft confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of them.

The team used a tool with the codename MDASH. It scanned selected kernel areas from late May to mid-June 2026, and a full-time researcher and an intern led the three-month effort.

Fixes for 38 of the reports have already been merged into the main Linux kernel. The results add to a busy year for kernel security.

Other teams have also shown how fast AI can find weak spots, such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Cyber model, which built hundreds of working Linux exploits. Microsoft’s report is different because it also shows how much human work is needed after the AI finishes.

Researchers at Microsoft identified the flaws and described the process in a blog post titled “Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports.” They noted that finding bugs is the easy part. Getting them confirmed, explained, and fixed takes far more time.

Microsoft Discovers 59 Linux Kernel Security Bugs

MDASH produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, running on two servers. Many of these were weak or false leads, so the team filtered out low-confidence claims with confidence levels and extra screening agents.

That cut the pool to 11,769 candidates. Next, AI agents tried to reproduce each candidate in a test environment called QEMU. Experts then reviewed the 621 cases that had proof-of-concept evidence.

They looked for root causes, merged duplicates, and prepared reports for the Linux community. The code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5. Reproduction used mostly GPT-5.5, along with Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.5-cyber.

Only 59 of the 621 cases (9.5%) became public reports. About 266 shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together.

Another 163 were dropped, mostly because their security impact was low. A further 133 had already been reported or fixed by someone else.

The bugs were old. On average, a reported bug had been in the kernel for 8.1 years. Six were 15 to 19 years old, and three were at least 20 years old.

The oldest, a cls_u32 shift-out-of-bounds bug tracked as CVE-2026-74544, had been there for at least 21 years. Similar long-hidden bugs have surfaced before, such as the GhostLock Linux kernel flaw that went unseen for about 15 years.

Inside CVE-2026-64563 and the Eight Exploitable Flaws

Of the 33 CVEs assigned so far, 24 are rated High or above, meaning a CVSS v3.1 score of 7.0 or more. The eight with confirmed local root exploits were tested in lab settings.

Some of them needed non-default settings or disabled protections. Most are use-after-free bugs, where the kernel keeps using memory after it has been freed.

Microsoft gave a closer look at CVE-2026-64563, a one-line bug in rhashtable, the kernel’s shared resizable hash table. A 2018 change kept a saved pointer when a table walk paused, but one resume path forgot to clear it.

If the table was resized and the entry freed in the meantime, the kernel later read freed memory. The bug stayed hidden for eight years because three rare events had to line up in the same walk.

Most code finishes a walk in one pass, so the problem almost never appeared by accident. The upstream fix is one line that clears the stale pointer.

The risk depends on which code calls the library. The exploitable caller is Netlink socket diagnostics, which unprivileged users can reach on standard kernels.

A local user could hold a listing paused, free the socket, and plant a fake pointer. That gives a limited 64-bit write, which is enough for privilege escalation on Linux and on Android with SELinux enforcing.

Yuan Tan and Frank Wu of NebuSec also worked on this bug, and Tan found it independently. Admins who want context on how such bugs are abused can read about the nftables privilege escalation bug, which also allowed root access through a use-after-free.

These bugs need local access. Attackers usually get that first through stolen logins or another weak service. Microsoft says finding and fixing bugs are badly out of balance. Reporting 59 cases took over four person-months.

Five months later, only 38 fixes were merged. Half of those were accepted on the first try, and the rest needed one to four revisions. From the first public patch to a mainline release took a median of 41 days, and up to 108 days.

Linux maintainers usually want a working patch with each report. AI agents helped draft the first fixes, but people still had to check them and work with maintainers.

Microsoft warns that too many real findings can overwhelm both bug hunters and maintainers, so teams should focus on high-severity problems. The team also scanned only a small part of the kernel, so more bugs likely remain.

articles.title: Hackers Abuse Windows Group Policy to Deploy Citrus Ransomware and Disable Microsoft Defender
articles.description:
A new ransomware group called Citrus is using Windows Group Policy to push its malware across entire company networks and switch off Microsoft Defender first. Group Policy is a trusted Windows tool that admins use to manage many computers at once. Here, the attackers turn it into a delivery system. The group breaks in through […]

The post Hackers Abuse Windows Group Policy to Deploy Citrus Ransomware and Disable Microsoft Defender appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new ransomware group called Citrus is using Windows Group Policy to push its malware across entire company networks and switch off Microsoft Defender first.

Group Policy is a trusted Windows tool that admins use to manage many computers at once. Here, the attackers turn it into a delivery system.

The group breaks in through stolen contractor logins, then moves slowly through the network until it controls a domain controller. From there, one policy change can reach every connected machine.

This style is not new, and recent cases of attackers abusing Active Directory group policies show why defenders need to watch policy changes closely.

Analysts at Securelist, the research arm of Kaspersky, identified the Citrus group and described its tools in a report published on November 11, 2026.

The team calls Citrus a previously undocumented crew. It pairs the Sn00py ransomware family with hidden network tunnels and, notably, with help from AI chat tools.

Hackers Abuse Windows Group Policy

Once the attackers hold enough privileges, they run a self-extracting archive that builds a malicious Group Policy Object, or GPO.

The archive carries a PowerShell script that copies the ransomware to the SYSVOL folder on the domain controller. It then links the new policy to the domain using the Import-GPO and New-GPLink commands.

Every computer in the domain then receives the policy. It drops the ransomware archive, creates a scheduled task that runs it with the quiet and no-restart options, and turns on the WinRM service.

It also disables the Volume Shadow Copy service, which Windows uses to restore older file versions. Most importantly, it changes registry settings to turn off Windows Defender. Securelist says the antivirus simply did not react when the ransomware started.

The attackers give their files names that look safe. The policy is called Kaspersky GPO, and the files include KasperskyAgent.exe and Deploy-KasperskyGPO.ps1.

Kaspersky notes that this trick does not help, since its products detect and block these files. Similar tactics have been seen elsewhere, including when ransomware tried to disable Defender before encrypting files.

The ransomware itself belongs to the Sn00py family. It is written in Go and uses RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 encryption on user files, but leaves system files alone.

Encrypted files get the .citrus extension, and a CITRUS_README.txt note gives victims 72 hours to make contact. Decryption is not possible without the attackers’ private key. The malware also skips a list of domain controllers, which keeps the policy spreading without interruption.

Contractor Access, Hidden Tunnels, and AI-Written Scripts

Citrus does not rely on exotic entry points. It uses credentials stolen from contractors’ employees to log in through corporate VPNs or exposed RDP servers.

These accounts usually have low privileges, so the attackers try to raise them. They have tried the Certighost flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-54121, which created Active Directory accounts with names starting with GHOST.

They also tried CVE-2020-1337 and went after poorly configured 1C:Enterprise servers. After that, the group uses a standard toolkit. It runs mimikatz to pull passwords from memory, a modified keylogger, and Snaffler to hunt for secrets on network shares.

It uses fscan, ADRecon, and SharpHound to map the network, then moves around with SSH, RDP, and WinRM. Tools arrive through built-in Windows utilities such as certutil and BITS.

The most unusual part is the traffic hiding. The attackers install Xray and open reverse VLESS tunnels on port 443, so the traffic looks like normal HTTPS.

Their settings also make the traffic look like visits to mirror.yandex.ru and yastatic.net. For remote control, they install AnyDesk silently. Before encryption, a script called steal_tgs.ps1 packs Telegram Desktop data into zip files for theft.

Researchers also found signs that the group used large language models. Some commands and full scripts contained neat comments, which attackers rarely write.

Securelist links Citrus to another Russian-speaking group, Toy Ghouls, because both use similar tools and have targeted Russian companies. Attacks like this fit the wider trend of ransomware gangs claiming more victims.

Defenders should limit and review contractor access, alert on new GPOs and changes to the gPLink attribute, protect security tool consoles, and watch for unexpected Defender changes. Securelist notes that the group mostly uses well-known methods, which makes early detection easier.

articles.title: Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw Allowing Remote Code Execution on Web Servers
articles.description:
Apache has fixed a critical bug in its HTTP/2 module that could let a remote attacker run code on a web server. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-119618 and affects mod_http2. The fix came on November 11, 2026, in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71. The bug sits in a function called assign_headers(). Apache says it is […]

The post Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw Allowing Remote Code Execution on Web Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apache has fixed a critical bug in its HTTP/2 module that could let a remote attacker run code on a web server. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-119618 and affects mod_http2. The fix came on November 11, 2026, in Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71.

The bug sits in a function called assign_headers(). Apache says it is a concurrency problem, where shared resources are used without proper locking.

Put simply, two parts of the code can touch the same piece of memory at the same time. That can damage the heap, the memory area a program uses while it runs, and this can lead to remote code execution.

Apache’s own impact scale reserves the “Critical” label for bugs that a remote attacker could use to run code on a server. These are the kind of bugs that could spread on their own, like a worm.

The CVE entry is still marked as reserved, so there is no public CVSS score or detailed technical write-up yet. Admins should not wait for those details before patching.

Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 are affected. People who run the standalone mod_h2 from GitHub should check versions 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. Servers that serve HTTP/2 traffic are the main concern, since the flaw lives in that module.

Anthropic’s OSS Scanner found the flaw and reported it to the Apache security team on October 26, 2026. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it on their own on November 3.

Apache Patches Critical HTTP/2 Flaw

Apache released the fix on November 11, about two weeks after the first report. Two teams finding the same bug within days shows how much attention researchers are giving HTTP/2 code.

The same release closes two more holes. CVE-2026-106023 is rated “important” and sits in mod_md. A NULL pointer error there can crash a child process while it handles a request, and it affects versions 2.4.30 through 2.4.70.

CVE-2026-109163 is a “low” rated one-byte stack overflow in mod_vhost_alias. It affects only versions 2.4.69 and 2.4.70. This is part of a long run of Apache fixes this year.

Version 2.4.69 in October fixed 20 CVEs, and 2.4.68 in June fixed 13. Cyber Security News covered the October update in its report on multiple Apache HTTP Server flaws that could enable code execution.

HTTP/2 has been a weak spot too. In June, the “HTTP/2 Bomb” denial-of-service exploit hit the default HTTP/2 setups of several popular web servers, including Apache.

Many admins who patched in October now have to patch again, only weeks later. That is tiring, but this bug is serious enough to justify it.

The most suitable mitigation is to upgrade to Apache HTTP Server 2.4.71 as soon as you can. Start with public-facing servers that have HTTP/2 turned on.

Many Linux distributions ship security fixes without changing the version number, so check your vendor’s advisory and package changelog before assuming a server is still exposed.

Apache has not listed a workaround for this flaw. If you cannot upgrade right away, one option is to limit the server to HTTP/1.1 until the update is done.

Test that change first, because it can affect performance and clients. Also watch your logs for unusual crashes or worker-process restarts, since these can suggest someone is probing the server.

The full list of fixed bugs is on Apache’s security vulnerabilities page. The project explains its severity labels on the impact levels page.

articles.title: Hackers Hijack ConnectWise ScreenConnect to Deploy SCKit Malware Across 288 Devices at 48 Organizations
articles.description:
Attackers have taken over cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels and used them to push a custom toolkit called SCKit to at least 288 managed devices across 48 organizations. Security firm Huntress first saw the activity on November 11, 2026, and says all 288 hosts were hit within about 90 minutes. Huntress reports that about one third of […]

The post Hackers Hijack ConnectWise ScreenConnect to Deploy SCKit Malware Across 288 Devices at 48 Organizations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers have taken over cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels and used them to push a custom toolkit called SCKit to at least 288 managed devices across 48 organizations.

Security firm Huntress first saw the activity on November 11, 2026, and says all 288 hosts were hit within about 90 minutes. Huntress reports that about one third of them were hit in the first 10 minutes.

The attacker used the Run command feature in the ScreenConnect panel to send commands to many endpoints at once. These commands ran with SYSTEM rights, which is the highest level on Windows. The command first checked for an existing ScreenConnect client. It then downloaded a rogue installer to C:\Windows\TEMP\sc.msi and installed it silently.

Huntress says it is working with ConnectWise on the case. Reports say the latest ScreenConnect versions, 26.6.6.9747 and 26.7.6.9783, are affected. ConnectWise says it has found no sign that its own systems were broken into and no flaw in ScreenConnect itself.

ConnectWise ScreenConnect Hijacked

In a public advisory posted on November 11, ConnectWise named five outside extensions that may be tied to the activity. These are Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link. The company turned them off in about 400 partner environments as a safety step.

ConnectWise says these extensions offer an API that can run remote commands, and a passphrase set by the partner protects that API. Having an extension installed does not prove a break-in.

The company has not yet found the first point of entry or the full scope. Partners who run servers on their own premises must turn the extensions off themselves, because ConnectWise cannot do it for them.

SCKit is a package of 16 files, including PowerShell scripts, batch files, and settings data. The infected machine sends its Windows ID to the attacker’s server. The server replies with the key needed to unlock a payload made for that one machine. This makes file hashes a weak way to spot the threat.

Next, the scripts install a second rogue ScreenConnect client and add exclusions to Microsoft Defender. They also create a tool called RelayTrap in C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap. A scheduled task named TrapWatch stops the real ScreenConnect client and puts the attacker’s copy in its place. The machine still looks normal to the admin. Huntress also noted that the C# code for RelayTrap looks like it was written with an AI model.

The toolkit has a second goal. Huntress found code built to wait until a technician connects to an infected device. It then pulls a dropper onto the technician’s workstation and steals the .aspxauth session cookie. With that cookie, the code tries to reach every other session the technician can open, and it uploads a payload to the panel’s Shared Toolbox.

Huntress has not seen this spread work. The console takeover failed in every host log it has checked so far. Still, the design shows why defenders should be careful.

This is not the first time criminals have turned ScreenConnect against its users. In September, Cyber Security News covered worm-like rogue ScreenConnect clients that passed staged scripts between Windows machines. Around the same time, CISA added CVE-2026-84869 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. That flaw allows file transfers during a live session without the host’s approval. Huntress says ConnectWise later fixed it, and it scored 9.9 on the CVSS scale.

Huntress and ConnectWise give the same core advice. Do not connect to a suspect machine through ScreenConnect, because that session can carry the malware to your own workstation. Use EDR live response, WinRM, or another tool outside ScreenConnect.

Teams should also:

  • Isolate affected hosts until cleanup is finished. Huntress saw some machines reinfect after isolation was lifted.
  • Remove the rogue client, the TrapWatch task, the RelayTrap folder, and the RelayTrapLiteAlert Run key.
  • Check Run Command and Toolbox history for jobs nobody started.
  • Revoke active web sessions and rotate credentials from a clean device.

Indicators include the domains newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org, cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com, and ns.mo7sen[.]dev. They also include the IP address 185.99.255[.]28 and the participant name Addmin. ConnectWise says the investigation is still open and it will update its advisory as facts are confirmed.

articles.title: Node.js Fixes 16 Security Flaws That Could Expose TLS Private Keys and Crash Servers Remotely
articles.description:
The Node.js project has released fixes for 16 security flaws across its 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. Seven are rated high, six medium, and three low. The official advisory says the patched builds are v22.23.5, v24.22.3 and v26.13.1. The update also refreshes three bundled parts: llhttp, undici, and sqlite. Memory Leak Could Expose TLS Private […]

The post Node.js Fixes 16 Security Flaws That Could Expose TLS Private Keys and Crash Servers Remotely appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Node.js project has released fixes for 16 security flaws across its 22.x, 24.x and 26.x lines. Seven are rated high, six medium, and three low. The official advisory says the patched builds are v22.23.5, v24.22.3 and v26.13.1. The update also refreshes three bundled parts: llhttp, undici, and sqlite.

Memory Leak Could Expose TLS Private Keys

The high-severity flaw is CVE-2026-123864. It affects the HTTPS code in all three lines. A client with no login can read memory that belongs to other connections. That memory can hold TLS private keys and other users’ requests.

The cause is a re-entry problem. A zero-length TLS write can make Node.js decrypt the next record while the HTTP parser is still reading a body. This causes a use-after-free and an out-of-bounds read, so the server copies old heap memory into the request body.

A server is at risk only if a handler calls res.flushHeaders() early and later ends with a non-empty chunk. A route that echoes or stores request bodies lets the attacker read the leak. Plain node:http is not affected, according to the Node.js security notes.

HTTP/2 code accounts for most of the list. CVE-2026-123863 lets any client abort a default HTTP/2 server. It is a variant of CVE-2024-27983 that the older fix missed. CVE-2026-123874 and CVE-2026-123875 hit servers that send files with respondWithFile(). One corrupts memory. The other crashes the server when a download is canceled, and a handful of canceled requests is enough.

CVE-2026-123866 can send freed response memory to a peer, which may include other users’ response data. CVE-2026-123865 leaks memory and file descriptors forever once a session fails during shutdown. It repairs a gap left by CVE-2026-48937, which we covered in our June Node.js patch report.

Two medium flaws also matter. CVE-2026-123868 lets a client send tiny one-byte frames and make the server keep about 114 bytes for every 10 bytes sent. One stream can then hold hundreds of megabytes. CVE-2026-123828 is a one-byte heap overflow in session.altsvc() that aborts the process when an app passes a long :authority value to it.

Login and Certificate Checks Failure

Several bugs weaken trust checks. CVE-2026-123872 lets a client switch the server name during TLS 1.2 renegotiation. It can carry a normal login to a host that needs stricter client certificates. CVE-2026-123867 is a related per-host mutual TLS bypass. A host configured with only a CA falls back to the default CA, so the wrong client can get in.

CVE-2026-123877 affects https.Agent. A cached TLS session from a broad trust policy can be reused by a request with a stricter policy. The second request then reports authorized === true when it should not.

CVE-2026-126051 lets a remote client crash TLS servers that use hooks such as SNICallback or addContext(). CVE-2026-123871 prints proxy credentials inside ERR_PROXY_INVALID_CONFIG errors. That puts secrets into logs and crash reports. It repeats the lesson from CVE-2026-48615.

The three low flaws touch the Permission Model and zlib. CVE-2026-123829 leaks file names on macOS and Windows. CVE-2026-106071 lets a wildcard grant match more paths than intended. CVE-2026-123862 can crash an app that calls deflate.params() while streaming, though that use is rare.

Researcher Chris Rohlf, working with Claude and Anthropic Research, reported five of the 16 flaws. Other reporters include Pimterry, Trail of Bits, and several independent researchers. Matteo Collina fixed most of them.

This release followed a short warning. Our earlier story on the scheduled patch noted that the notice gave no CVE details. The full list is now public. October’s Node2Shell Brotli bug and July’s 11 fixes show that Node.js ships serious fixes almost every month.

Upgrade to v22.23.5, v24.22.3, or v26.13.1 first. Public HTTP/2 and HTTPS servers should go first. Then rebuild container images so they carry the new runtime. Teams that served traffic from a vulnerable HTTPS handler should consider replacing their TLS keys, since leaked memory leaves no clear trace. End-of-life versions are always affected, so move off them. The Node.js release schedule lists support dates.

articles.title: Ubuntu 26.10 Adds New Security Protection to curl, Blocking Revoked SSL Certificates
articles.description:
Ubuntu 26.10 Stonking Stingray adds certificate revocation checks to curl, helping the command-line tool reject HTTPS connections that use revoked certificates. Announced on November 10, the change brings upki support into Ubuntu’s curl package. It marks an initial step toward browser-grade certificate checks across the operating system. The protection closes a gap in how applications […]

The post Ubuntu 26.10 Adds New Security Protection to curl, Blocking Revoked SSL Certificates appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ubuntu 26.10 Stonking Stingray adds certificate revocation checks to curl, helping the command-line tool reject HTTPS connections that use revoked certificates.

Announced on November 10, the change brings upki support into Ubuntu’s curl package. It marks an initial step toward browser-grade certificate checks across the operating system.

The protection closes a gap in how applications check website certificates. Curl uses OpenSSL to verify certificate chains, but that process does not check revocation by default in the setup described by Ubuntu. A certificate could therefore pass those checks even after its issuer had withdrawn it.

According to Ubuntu’s announcement, curl now uses upki-openssl to check server certificates against locally stored revocation data. The system builds on Mozilla’s CRLite technology, which Firefox also uses to identify revoked certificates.

Because the check uses local data, curl does not need an extra network request during each connection. This keeps checks fast and avoids sending a separate revocation query when users visit a site. Background downloads still take place to keep that local data updated.

The upki package is a recommended dependency and includes a systemd timer that refreshes revocation data every six hours. An important limit remains before the first download. Until the data is available, curl continues working as it did before, without the added revocation protection.

Ubuntu 26.10 Adds Protection to curl

Ubuntu demonstrated the difference using a local test server and a test certificate authority. The same curl command accepted a revoked certificate on Ubuntu 26.04 Resolute Raccoon, while Ubuntu 26.10 refused it. The demonstration used unmodified Ubuntu packages for curl, OpenSSL, and upki.

Revocation allows certificate issuers to withdraw trust before a certificate expires. Ubuntu highlighted an October 17 incident involving weak private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authorities.

According to its account, one private key was simply the number four, creating a risk that attackers could issue certificates for arbitrary websites. Firefox and Chrome blocked those intermediate certificates the same day, while many other applications had to wait for distribution updates.

Ubuntu wants upki to narrow that gap outside browsers. This complements, rather than replaces, regular patching, including fixes covered in Cybersecurity News’ reports on curl security updates and OpenSSL vulnerabilities.

Ubuntu 26.10 users can install the package with sudo apt install upki, then fetch the initial data using sudo systemctl start upki-fetch. service. Running curl https://revoked.badssl.com/ should then fail with curl error 60 and an OpenSSL message stating “certificate revoked (23).” Non-revoked certificates continue working normally.

Administrators should investigate certificate failures rather than bypass verification. The curl documentation strongly warns against using –insecure in production because it turns off peer verification.

For Ubuntu 27.04, the Foundations team plans to integrate upki into OpenSSL’s normal certificate checks. If delivered, that change could extend revocation protection to most of the more than 1,000 packages using OpenSSL directly, without requiring separate changes in every application. That broader coverage remains planned, not part of this initial curl rollout.

articles.title: Hackers Could Abuse Microsoft Entra AI Agents to Hijack Enterprise Accounts Without Stealing Passwords
articles.description:
Researchers have shown that attackers can take over parts of a Microsoft 365 environment by tricking one person into approving a fake AI agent. No password is stolen and no login screen is faked. The technique is called BluePhishing. It targets Microsoft Entra Agent ID, the system that gives AI agents their own identities inside […]

The post Hackers Could Abuse Microsoft Entra AI Agents to Hijack Enterprise Accounts Without Stealing Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers have shown that attackers can take over parts of a Microsoft 365 environment by tricking one person into approving a fake AI agent. No password is stolen and no login screen is faked.

The technique is called BluePhishing. It targets Microsoft Entra Agent ID, the system that gives AI agents their own identities inside a company’s cloud tenant.

The method builds on a trick security teams already know, OAuth consent phishing. In that trick, a victim clicks “Accept” on a permission screen for a harmful app.

BluePhishing moves the same idea into the new world of AI agents, where fewer people know what to look out for and fewer controls exist.

Microsoft is also about to widen the door. A Microsoft 365 Message Center notice, MC1506733, says regular Entra users will be able to create agent blueprints by default starting in November 2026. That raises the number of places where a bad consent request could slip in.

Analysts at Proofpoint identified and described the BluePhishing technique in a report published on November 9, 2026, and noted that they have not yet seen it used in real attacks.

Proofpoint says it is a research-based proof of concept. It also told Microsoft about the problem before sharing the details.

Hackers Could Abuse Microsoft Entra AI Agents

Entra Agent ID works much like the older app model. An agent blueprint is the template, similar to an app registration. A blueprint principal is its local copy inside a company tenant.

An agent identity is a working agent created from that blueprint, and one blueprint can create up to 250 of them. The attacker first builds a blueprint in a tenant they control and adds a client secret.

They set the sign-in audience to allow other organizations, which the Entra portal does not show but PowerShell or Microsoft Graph can do.

They also add broad permissions that agents will inherit. This is similar to earlier cases of OAuth apps in Entra being used to keep long-term access, where the app acts as a quiet entry point even after passwords are reset.

Next, the attacker sends the victim a consent link. When the victim approves it, a blueprint principal appears in the victim’s tenant. It automatically gets a permission named AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager, which Proofpoint says cannot be revoked.

With that permission, the attacker can request a Graph token and create agent identities inside the victim’s tenant. The attacker only needs a few details: the blueprint ID and secret, which they make themselves, plus the victim’s tenant ID and a user to act as the “sponsor.” Proofpoint notes these are not treated as secret, and the tenant ID can be found through public sign-in lookups.

Researchers showed that a created agent holding User.Read.All and Group.Read.All could be loaded into the GraphRunner tool to run Graph requests.

Admin consent is stronger because one click can grant tenant-wide application permissions. User consent only grants delegated rights tied to that person.

Why Defenders May Miss It and What to Do

Agents are expected to act on their own, so their activity looks normal. A suspicious app that works in the background may raise questions, but a busy agent does not.

Proofpoint also points out that consent controls for agents are less mature than those for apps. Inherited permissions do not show up in the Entra portal or in Microsoft Graph, so they appear only inside tokens at runtime.

A past case with Entra Agent ID logs showed that tracing agent actions takes careful work across several log sources. The blast radius is larger too. An app registration maps to one service principal per tenant, while one blueprint can create 250 agent identities.

Earlier flaws, such as the Agent ID Administrator role problem found by Silverfort, show that this young identity system is still being tested.

Proofpoint suggests these steps:-

  • Teach staff to be careful when a third-party agent asks for permissions.
  • Apply the same user consent limits to agent blueprints and agent identities.
  • Use permission classifications. Microsoft already blocks risky Graph permissions such as User.ReadWrite.All for agents.
  • Use least privilege, Conditional Access policies for agents, and Entra ID Protection for agents.
  • Watch the audit log. “Add application” shows a blueprint being created, and “Add service principal” shows an agent identity being created.

Similar lures have already worked with AI themes. The CoPhish Copilot Studio technique used a trusted-looking agent on a Microsoft domain to collect OAuth consent. BluePhishing could prove even more convincing because the agent is the identity itself.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs):-

articles.description:
AI-powered hacking and penetration-testing frameworks are running on internet-accessible servers, with some management consoles left open without authentication. A November 7, 2026, Shodan snapshot recorded 1,428 services matching the ARTEX family, 419 matching PentAGI, and 173 matching Agent Zero, showing how widely these tools have spread. These platforms connect language models to security tools, allowing […]

The post AI Hacking Frameworks Like ARTEX, PentAGI, and Agent Zero Found Running on Internet-Accessible Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
AI-powered hacking and penetration-testing frameworks are running on internet-accessible servers, with some management consoles left open without authentication.

A November 7, 2026, Shodan snapshot recorded 1,428 services matching the ARTEX family, 419 matching PentAGI, and 173 matching Agent Zero, showing how widely these tools have spread.

These platforms connect language models to security tools, allowing agents to run commands, examine results, and decide what to do next.

They can support authorized testing, but attackers can use the same features to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, and credential theft. Public visibility alone, however, does not prove that a server supports criminal activity.

Researchers from GitGuardian identified the exposed deployments in a technical investigation published November 9. Their findings concern dual-use frameworks and insecure deployments, not a newly discovered malware family.

The team examined roughly 45 open-source projects and assessed 41 for fingerprints that defenders could use to locate internet-facing installations.

AI Hacking Frameworks

GitGuardian cataloged 32 frameworks across five groups: network attack automation, web application and API testing, command-and-control integration, wrappers around coding agents, and research prototypes.

Other projects were forks or variants. Across the 41 assessed frameworks, 11 served web interfaces by default, 18 exposed services only in certain configurations or lacked distinctive root pages, and 12 had no network listener.

PentAGI coordinates agents using tools such as Nmap, Metasploit, and sqlmap. As explained in earlier coverage of PentAGI penetration testing automation, this design helps agents move between discovery, testing, and reporting.

GitGuardian counted 419 matching services, including 233 with the default certificate, while separate title and certificate searches returned different totals. These measurements should not be combined into a unique-server count.

Agent Zero showed a clearer authentication gap. Of 173 matching services, 134 displayed a login page and 39 were open. GitGuardian described Agent Zero as a general-purpose agent without authentication by default, rather than a dedicated hacking tool.

Its inclusion reflects reported attacker experimentation and the risks created when powerful agents become publicly reachable.

ARTEX remained the largest visible family. GitGuardian reported that its creator removed the original project on October 8 following reports of abuse, but 102 forks and similarly named repositories appeared during that week.

Earlier reporting on ARTEX GitHub credential theft documented how attackers used exposed application secrets to reach cloud resources, including Azure Key Vault.

The code review also separated built-in functions from tasks an agent could assemble itself. Only Pojun, Cybermes, Xalgorix, and AIRecon shipped a secret scanner connected to the agent.

None contained a GitHub fetcher. Several other projects supplied instructions without working scanner integration, while reviewed tools including PentAGI had no identified secret-hunting capability.

That limitation does not eliminate the risk. Almost every framework supplied shell and web access, allowing a model to obtain missing tools or build a workflow at runtime.

Coverage of AI agent credential exposure also explains how ordinary agent activity can move secrets into logs, transcripts, or model context, even without malware.

For defenders, the distinction matters: an exposed console is an access-control concern, while a fingerprint match is only a discovery lead. GitGuardian published detection descriptions rather than a target list so organizations could identify their own deployments.

Different queries produced different counts, making validation essential before treating a result as an exposed installation or evidence of compromise.

articles.title: Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses to Steal API Keys and Administrator Credentials
articles.description:
Security teams that run AI coding assistants may be exposing their most powerful credentials without knowing it. A new study shows that Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers can quietly change their own code after they are set up. If an attacker poisons just one package in that chain, they could steal API keys and administrator […]

The post Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses to Steal API Keys and Administrator Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security teams that run AI coding assistants may be exposing their most powerful credentials without knowing it. A new study shows that Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers can quietly change their own code after they are set up.

If an attacker poisons just one package in that chain, they could steal API keys and administrator logins. MCP servers let AI assistants talk to other tools, such as firewalls, SIEM platforms and cloud consoles.

To do this work, they usually hold the keys of the person who installed them. Attackers already know this. A malicious MCP server found in the wild has shown how easily one trusted tool can leak data.

Researchers at Corelight noted the weakness while checking an administrator’s workstation. They did not find malware there.

They found AI assistants running MCP servers with privileged access, and they asked where the code in those servers came from and how it got updated. The answer is in Corelight’s research, published on November 10, 2026.

Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses

The assistants launched their MCP servers with a one-step tool called uvx. It downloads a Python package and runs it from a single line of settings. The settings looked safe, because they named an exact release, a version number or a Git commit.

The catch is that pinning the main package does not pin the packages underneath it. One community server had pinned its seven direct dependencies and even published a hash-locked file.

But the launcher ignored that file and fetched the roughly 60 other packages fresh from the Python Package Index (PyPI) whenever it rebuilt its environment.

Over five weeks, that one server was rebuilt 19 times and produced 15 different sets of dependencies. Of its 69 packages, 23 changed versions, including the cryptography library and the MCP software kit itself.

Nobody had touched the configuration. Corelight saw the same drift on every server launched this way. Every one of those packages runs inside the same process as the server.

That means any of them can read the API tokens, the user’s files and the network paths the server can reach. A bad update does not even need to be called.

Some malicious packages run the moment Python starts. The risk is not limited to Python. Some vendors tell users to start a local proxy with npx and a “latest” tag.

That fetches the newest version at every start. It also echoes the critical mcp-remote flaw rated 9.6 on the CVSS scale, where fast updates helped, but a hijacked release would spread just as fast.

Corelight stressed that this is not a flaw in MCP itself. Each case came from a setup choice. Of the 35 MCP servers it reviewed, 23 had a recommended install that would pull dependencies fresh from a public registry.

Why Package Hijacks Make This Worse

Attackers go after whichever dependency is easiest to take over. That might be a maintainer account with a reused password, a phished token or a weak release pipeline.

The bad version then looks like a normal update. Corelight pointed to past cases such as xz Utils, Ultralytics and Nx, where stolen tokens and keys were the prize.

The Shai-Hulud npm worm is a recent example. It used stolen npm tokens to publish infected versions of every package a victim maintained.

A June 2026 variant reached PyPI and went after cloud credentials, GitHub tokens and API keys for AI coding tools. In one wave, six bad releases were live for under 30 minutes.

A server that rebuilds every couple of days, and starts on its own, has more chances to land in a window like that. This pattern matches wider reports of how attackers poison trusted software updates to reach developer and cloud secrets.

A managed update has a build you control and a version number you can see. A launcher that rebuilds at start-up offers neither, and the server’s own version number never changes.

Corelight showed how to spot the problem. DNS and TLS logs list the hosts that contact GitHub, PyPI and npm. In its lab, that left four hosts.

Endpoint data then showed that only the administrator’s workstation installed PyPI packages, and it did so whenever an AI assistant started its servers. Those servers made more than 1,600 connections in a week to 11 management systems.

The fix is to freeze the environment. Teams should pin to a commit, install from a hash-pinned lock file, launch the server directly and turn off start-up update checks.

Corelight froze five servers and started them 457 times over two weeks, and their package lists never changed. Each server should also get its own account with the least access it needs, and a named owner should review updates on a schedule.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Torrance, USA, November 11th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Criminal IP, the AI-powered threat intelligence and attack surface management platform developed by AI SPERA, has launched the Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk.

Available through Splunkbase, the app automatically correlates Criminal IP threat intelligence with firewall traffic logs collected in Splunk.

The integration enables security teams to determine whether organizational assets communicated with malicious IP addresses and whether sessions were successfully established.

It also expands Criminal IP’s existing Splunk ecosystem beyond individual IP lookups and fraud detection, helping SOC teams identify high-priority threats within their existing Splunk workflows.

Connecting Threat Intelligence with Network Activity

Security teams often receive large volumes of IP reputation alerts without enough context to determine whether a connection was attempted, blocked, unanswered, or successfully established.

This can make it difficult to distinguish routine scanning from communications that require immediate investigation.

The Criminal IP TI Feed app addresses this challenge by correlating inbound and outbound threat intelligence feeds with firewall traffic already indexed in Splunk.

Network activity is classified according to observed session outcomes, including completed, unanswered, denied, neutral, and unknown connections.

Severity is also determined using actual firewall activity.

Detections without a completed session cannot exceed the watch tier, while critical detections indicate that a session with a malicious IP was successfully established.

This helps analysts prioritize incidents with the greatest potential impact.

Automated Correlation and Retrospective Detection

<The Criminal IP TI Feed Overview dashboard in Splunk highlights completed sessions with malicious IP addresses and shows which assets require immediate attention.>

The app downloads Criminal IP TI Feed data every three hours and runs correlation searches against firewall traffic every 10 minutes. Results are written to a dedicated summary index, allowing dashboards and alerts to operate without repeatedly searching large volumes of raw logs.

A daily retrospective search compares the latest Criminal IP threat intelligence against the previous 30 days of firewall traffic. This helps identify historical communications with IP addresses that were not recognized as malicious when the activity originally occurred.

Seven dashboards- Overview, Investigate, All Detections, IP Lookup, Trends, Alerts, and Health- provide visibility into affected assets, malicious IP addresses, traffic direction, session status, severity, detection history, and feed collection health.

The app can also deliver consolidated Slack alerts grouped by malicious IP address and traffic direction. These alerts retain asset-level details, including session counts, timestamps, and transferred data, while throttling repeated notifications to reduce alert fatigue.

Advancing Intelligence-Driven Security Operations

By connecting external threat intelligence with actual network activity, the Criminal IP TI Feed app provides the context analysts need to identify which assets interacted with malicious infrastructure and which detections require immediate attention.

Automating feed collection, log correlation, historical analysis, dashboards, and alerts reduces manual investigation and helps SOC teams respond to meaningful threats more efficiently.

AI SPERA CEO Byungtak Kang stated, “Threat intelligence becomes significantly more actionable when connected to the network activity occurring inside an organization. The Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk helps security teams identify affected assets and prioritize incidents based on observed session behavior.”

About Criminal IP

Criminal IP is AI SPERA’s flagship cyber threat intelligence platform. Used in more than 150 countries, it provides comprehensive threat visibility through Criminal IP Search, Criminal IP ASM, Criminal IP FDS, and Criminal IP TI Feed.

Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake.

Users can learn more and download the app from Splunkbase:

articles.title: Windows SignDrop 0-Day Exploit Lets Attackers Gain SYSTEM Privileges Through CLFS Protection
articles.description:
A public exploit called SignDrop targets a Windows security feature meant to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS). It claims to turn a normal user account into a SYSTEM account, the highest level of control on Windows. The flaw has no CVE number and no patch as of November 11, 2026. Microsoft […]

The post Windows SignDrop 0-Day Exploit Lets Attackers Gain SYSTEM Privileges Through CLFS Protection appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A public exploit called SignDrop targets a Windows security feature meant to stop attacks on the Common Log File System (CLFS). It claims to turn a normal user account into a SYSTEM account, the highest level of control on Windows.

The flaw has no CVE number and no patch as of November 11, 2026. Microsoft has also not confirmed the claims.

Windows SignDrop zero-day exploit

A researcher using the handle MSNightmare, also known as Nightmare Eclipse, posted the proof-of-concept on GitHub on November 10, 2026.

The researcher has a history of public Windows exploit drops. Cyber Security News reported earlier this year that GitLab suspended the account after GitHub’s earlier ban.

The researcher says the bug lives in clfs.sys, the kernel driver behind CLFS. It involves how the driver creates a “.cnpf” authentication file when a new log file is made through the exposed \CLFS device.

The code uses object manager symbolic links and file timing tricks. It also claims a high-privilege Windows Defender process can be pushed into creating files in a protected place.

CLFS has long been a favorite target because it parses complex log files inside the kernel. A small mistake there becomes memory corruption, and that can lead to higher privileges.

Cyber Security News has covered this pattern many times, including the CVE-2025-29824 zero-day that Storm-2460 used with PipeMagic malware to deploy ransomware.

To cut this risk, Microsoft added a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) to CLFS log files. The code is built from the file data and a secret key unique to each system.

If the code does not match, CLFS refuses to open the file, as Microsoft’s support page explains. This change reached Windows 11 25H2 and Windows Server 2025 in updates released on or after October 28, 2025.

New systems start in a learning mode, where CLFS adds authentication codes to old log files as they are opened. Microsoft says this period lasts 90 days from the first start with the updated driver. After that, the driver moves to enforcement mode on its next start.

This is where the researcher’s claim comes from. MSNightmare says systems are exposed in either mode, so almost any machine older than 90 days would be vulnerable.

The researcher also estimates that about 80 percent of Windows installations are at risk. Daily Security Review notes that this number is an estimate and not a measured count.

Readers should keep a few limits in mind. SignDrop is a local privilege escalation bug, so an attacker must already run code on the machine as a normal user. It cannot break in from the internet by itself.

The Rocket Boys review found no CVE, no Microsoft advisory, no independent test, and no sign of use in real attacks. It also did not run the code itself.

The researcher reports testing on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 lab setups. The same review says the PoC does not work when CLFS authentication is turned off. That does not make disabling it a good idea.

Do not switch off CLFS authentication to dodge this bug. Microsoft Learn says the setting is on by default, and turning it off lets the driver open and parse any log file, including crafted ones. That would bring back the older CLFS attacks the feature was built to stop.

Instead, limit who can run code on important machines, and watch for odd file creation by Defender or other high-privilege processes.

Also look for unexpected CLFS error codes such as ERROR_LOG_METADATA_CORRUPT. Admins can review the fsutil clfs command in Microsoft’s documentation before they change any settings.

Treat SignDrop as a serious but unconfirmed threat for now. Microsoft will likely review it, and a fix would probably come through a Patch Tuesday update. Until then, the best step is to keep Windows updated and keep standard accounts tightly controlled.
