articles.title: eMudhra Revokes 8 More Certificate Authorities Following Major SSL Private Key Security Failure
articles.description:
eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) after conducting a thorough review of the key issue that led to its October security failure. The new group did not have weak keys, but eMudhra could not prove the keys were handled the way its own rules require. The company has now pulled 16 intermediate […]

The post eMudhra Revokes 8 More Certificate Authorities Following Major SSL Private Key Security Failure appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
eMudhra has revoked eight additional intermediate certificate authorities (CAs) after conducting a thorough review of the key issue that led to its October security failure.

The new group did not have weak keys, but eMudhra could not prove the keys were handled the way its own rules require. The company has now pulled 16 intermediate certificates.

The problem goes back to a key issue on 30 April 2025. According to reports, the keys were first created correctly inside a hardware security module, or HSM.

eMudhra Certificate Authority Revocation

A custom Python script then processed them to prepare a move to another device. A bug in that script shrank eight keys into tiny numbers such as 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

Mozilla’s public bug record explains why this was so bad. A P-384 private key should be a huge random number. Mozilla’s lead reporter found that all eight keys were smaller than 256, so anyone could rebuild them by simply guessing the first 256 keys.

The same report says the script also made copies of eight other keys in an ordinary computer’s memory. Those keys stayed strong, but eMudhra said it could not show they were handled as its policy demands.

So it revoked all 16 certificates tied to the affected keys. Mozilla’s bug thread lists the new batch, including intermediates named EM DV TLS CA – G2B and G2C, which sit under emSign Root TLS CA – G1.

eMudhra added that this was the first time it moved keys between HSMs in different regions. It now creates keys without such transfers.

According to the disclosure site by a researcher named Wayne, the weak keys were discovered on 17 October. He proved control by signing a short message with each key and sent it to the Mozilla, Chrome, Apple, and Microsoft root teams.

Mozilla then rebuilt the keys on its own within hours, which proved the flaw was real and easy to use. Chrome and Firefox blocked the certificates that same day. Microsoft blocked them on 20 October, and Apple followed on 22 October, according to the disclosure site run by Dennis Jackson.

eMudhra revoked the first eight on 18 October. Our earlier report on the eMudhra certificate authority compromise covers those first emergency steps.

On 22 October, eMudhra said it would leave the global SSL/TLS certificate business. The company said no data was breached and that the affected intermediates had issued no website certificates.

Read more in our story on eMudhra exiting the SSL/TLS market. The company later cut its FY27 revenue outlook to about Rs 800 crore from Rs 825 crore and hired KPMG as an outside reviewer.

Mozilla and Chrome also moved to remove trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3. This protects tools that ignore revocation lists. eMudhra estimated about 30,000 certificates needed to move, and about 97 percent of them came through ACME, the automatic renewal system.

Apple fixed its developer tools issue on 10 November. Command-line tools such as curl and git on macOS now reject the bad certificates in macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 and 15.8.3. Those updates also remove several eMudhra roots from the system file.

Microsoft has gone further. Its 10 November update says it will remove the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2 starting 16 November.

Earlier, Microsoft had pushed an emergency Windows update, which we covered in Microsoft’s emergency update for eMudhra certificates. Oracle also shipped a Java fix for the same trust problem.

Browsers that enforce Certificate Transparency would likely have caught a fake certificate. The disclosure site notes that many other tools do not.

These include curl, language runtimes, Electron apps such as Slack and Discord, and anything that ships its own certificate bundle. The site also says it is unknown whether anyone used the weak keys against these clients.

Update browsers, operating systems, and runtimes. Check any app, container, or build server that keeps its own trust list. On Macs, run the git and curl checks from the disclosure site after updating.

Admins should also watch for the 16 November Microsoft change if they still rely on eMudhra chains. The lesson is simple. Strong math doesn’t help if a small script bug weakens the keys, and a CA must test its keys before using them.

Released on November 10, the emergency update, build 2026.4.1.26, fixes seven published CVEs and adds security changes across the server, Agents, and Probes. The shutdown began on November […]

The post N-able Releases Emergency N-central Hotfix After 33 Vulnerabilities Trigger Worldwide Shutdown appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
N-able has released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 after the public disclosure of 33 alleged vulnerabilities forced a worldwide shutdown of its hosted remote monitoring and management platform.

Released on November 10, the emergency update, build 2026.4.1.26, fixes seven published CVEs and adds security changes across the server, Agents, and Probes.

The shutdown began on November 9, affecting hosted services across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. N-able also advised customers running their own servers to take them offline.

Cybersecuritynews.com previously covered the N-central shutdown and Able2Shell disclosure, which included public proof-of-concept code for attacks against the platform.

N-able N-central vulnerabilities

The research, published by Sean Bales through the Oracle-Security GitHub account, describes four exploit chains. Huntress reported that three could lead to remote code execution, while another could raise an attacker’s access to root. The research targeted N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, with earlier versions also potentially affected.

One reported chain combines an XML external entity flaw with trusted session abuse to reset an account password and run commands as the N-able service account.

Other paths involve malicious patch data, file upload weaknesses, and local privilege escalation. These paths matter because N-central manages customer devices, making server access valuable to attackers.

N-able has observed scanning linked to the published exploit code, according to its incident update. Scanning alone does not establish a successful breach.

Huntress’s updated report says hosted servers were upgraded and brought back online on November 10. Customers should not treat restored cloud access as proof that their own deployments are fully updated.

N-able’s official release notes list fixes for XXE, OGNL injection, stored cross-site scripting, server-side request forgery, file repository path traversal leading to code execution, and two privilege escalation issues.

The seven CVEs do not establish that all 33 researcher claims were individually confirmed or fully resolved. N-able has announced further security updates.

The hotfix strengthens authentication, permission checks, file validation, server components, and web protections. It also removes legacy mobile device management and updates operating system and third-party components. Built-in remote control remains temporarily disabled, although Take Control continues working.

Both hosted and on-premises customers must update Agents and Probes. N-able directs customers to upgrade Agents first, then Probes, because incompatible versions can interrupt communication and disable features such as offline patch caching. Older server releases require a supported intermediate upgrade.

This follows a separate N-central authentication bypass incident reported in August. Administrators should follow the new release guidance rather than assume earlier hotfixes cover Able2Shell. Keep unpatched servers offline until their upgrade succeeds.

articles.description:
Researchers found that apps built with Grok’s app builder are open to Anyone online. Thousands of these apps hold private business data, staff details, plain-text passwords, and patient information. No hacking was needed to reach them. Grok’s Build mode creates and publishes chat-generated apps under grok.me, while its parent company, SpaceXSI (formerly xAI), did not […]

The post Grok AI App Builder Exposes Over 35,000 Apps, Leaking Confidential Business Data and Passwords appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers found that apps built with Grok’s app builder are open to Anyone online. Thousands of these apps hold private business data, staff details, plain-text passwords, and patient information. No hacking was needed to reach them.

Grok’s Build mode creates and publishes chat-generated apps under grok.me, while its parent company, SpaceXSI (formerly xAI), did not respond to Claroc but answered media questions on November 10, 2026.

On November 8, 2026, Claroc researchers worked through a list of more than 43,500 grok.me addresses. They opened the first page of each app once, signed in to nothing, like any visitor in a private browser window. Of the 37,571 apps still online, 35,578 (94.7%) opened for Anyone. Only 1,993 asked for a sign-in.

The list came from passive DNS, a service that records website name lookups and lets Anyone search them. Each Grok app gets its own address, so the name enters those records once someone opens the app.

Grok AI App Builder Exposes Data

The researchers say Grok’s four-random-word names are hard to guess, but nobody needs to guess them because the records list them. The same method exposed Meta’s Muse, as covered in our Meta Muse AI privacy flaw report.

Most open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators. About one in ten held sensitive or internal data, and roughly 2% were serious enough to rate high or critical.

Confirmed examples include an intensive care briefing with a patient’s labs and ventilator status, a hospital group’s roster of more than 3,500 employees, and a fire department’s shift board with badge numbers. One contractor’s timesheet app held 18 staff accounts with plain-text passwords in code that every visitor’s browser downloads.

SpaceXSI and X staff also left 24 apps open. They included a confidential onboarding plan, a sales map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals, one aimed at a U.S. federal agency.

Another 30 identifiable organizations had internal data exposed. Of these, 26 have over 1,000 employees, and six are Fortune 500 companies. SpaceXSI took down its own 24 apps after the report, but not those of other users.

Claroc found that paid-account apps defaulted to public link access, allowing anyone to view and add records to apps without login protection.

A team app with Google sign-in checked who the visitor was but not whether they belonged to the team. A stranger with a Google account could read, edit, and delete customer records. The researchers tested this only on their own apps.

SpaceXSI says apps stay private until the creator shares them, and that publishing takes several steps. Claroc replies that every owner of the 35,578 open apps went through those same steps.

Teams should find out which AI app builders their staff use, since tools like Lovable, Replit, and Grok need no IT approval. Check each app’s access settings, and test sign-in with an outside account. Look in the app’s script files for passwords and unpublish anything nobody owns. Unpublishing a grok.me app takes it offline within seconds.

This is not Grok’s first exposure problem. In 2025, more than 370,000 shared Grok chats appeared in Google search, which we covered in our report on Grok chats exposed in Google results. The comprehensive research is on the Claroc blog.

articles.title: Claude Code AI Discovers Technique to Turn Dormant Model Neurons Into Hidden Malware Triggers
articles.description:
Claude Code helped uncover a technique that can turn an otherwise capable AI model into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 dormant neurons. Called Lazarus, the method plants a hidden backdoor in model weights, allowing an attacker’s trigger to make an AI agent produce commands that download and run malicious code. The model […]

The post Claude Code AI Discovers Technique to Turn Dormant Model Neurons Into Hidden Malware Triggers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Claude Code helped uncover a technique that can turn an otherwise capable AI model into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 dormant neurons.

Called Lazarus, the method plants a hidden backdoor in model weights, allowing an attacker’s trigger to make an AI agent produce commands that download and run malicious code.

The model can still pass standard evaluations and behave normally during routine tasks. The findings expose a security gap for organizations giving AI agents access to terminals, files, and credentials.

Unlike the malicious Claude Code extension reported separately, this technique does not depend on adding a malicious software loader.

Instead, the dangerous behavior sits inside the model’s internal parameters, where ordinary application security checks may miss it.

Claude Code AI Discovers Technique

Microsoft researchers identified the Lazarus backdoor technique and detailed its malware-execution risk in research published on November 10, 2026.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence stressed that it had not observed threat actors weaponizing the method. This is a demonstrated research attack, not a confirmed malware campaign, and Claude Code was the research assistant used to discover much of the technique.

According to Microsoft’s original research explanation, principal researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos asked Claude Code, running Opus 4.5, to explore backdooring a model by hardwiring selected activations without training.

The experiment developed into a broader study, with human researchers investigating the results and defenses. Lazarus targets neurons that rarely activate during normal operation.

Researchers repurpose these quiet components as trigger detectors, using patterns already represented inside the pretrained model. A small set of examples helps separate inputs containing a chosen trigger from ordinary inputs, avoiding the cost of retraining the entire model.

This differs from prompt injection attacks bypassing safeguards through hostile instructions: Lazarus changes the model itself before deployment.

Its trigger can be an ordinary string appearing in the agent’s context, including information returned by a tool. The attacker must first obtain write access to the model checkpoint containing its weights.

Each modified neuron can push one selected token into the residual stream, the internal pathway carrying information toward the model’s next output.

Chaining several neurons lets the backdoor produce a complete command. Execution then depends on the surrounding agent software, available tools, and permissions; the model alone does not automatically control the host.

In one example, a date change into 2027 activates the hidden behavior during an ordinary task. The agent emits a command that fetches and runs attacker-controlled code.

Microsoft says the editing process needs only inference-level computing resources: hardware capable of running the model can also support this form of tampering.

Detecting Hidden Model Changes and Limiting Damage

The central defensive challenge is that normal answers do not establish model integrity. Earlier work on detecting backdoor attacks before deployment addresses the broader problem of models that behave correctly until triggered.

Lazarus reinforces why behavioral evaluations should accompany, rather than replace, direct inspection of model weights. Microsoft recommends comparing every checkpoint against its declared original model before deployment and after updates.

Legitimate modifications generally produce broader changes, while these implants can leave unusually large edits concentrated in a few weight vectors. Advanced AI agents can help flag suspicious structures, although Microsoft cautions that no audit guarantees safe behavior.

Organizations should obtain models from original publishers, verify published file hashes, and keep approved checkpoints in access-controlled registries.

Microsoft also distinguishes conventional model scanning from weight auditing: checks for embedded malware, unsafe operators, or exposed secrets do not replace examination of altered neural parameters.

Containment remains essential because a triggered agent inherits its existing access. The same principle underlies Ghostjacking attacks against agents, where manipulated inputs can lead to dangerous tool use.

Microsoft recommends least privilege, isolated code execution, restricted outbound connections, and human approval for consequential actions. Monitoring should also cover suspicious child processes and unexpected network activity.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Git project patched six vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw that allows malicious repositories to execute code during recursive cloning. The other five involve unsafe file writes and memory corruption in merges and patches. Git announced the fixes on November 10, 2026.

The patches arrive in Git 2.56.1. They are also backported to 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. Users should move to 2.56.1 or the latest fix for their release line. Any app that ships its own copy of Git needs an update too.

The most severe flaw is CVE-2026-111760, rated High with a CVSS score of 8.0. Git normally checks file paths before it writes them, and it blocks any path that would overwrite its own repository data.

However, an integer truncation in the index code lets an extremely long path pass the check under one name and then get written under a shorter one.

An attacker can use this to swap a submodule’s .git file for a symbolic link. The link points to a folder holding malicious settings or hooks. When Git later uses that folder, it runs the attacker’s code.

Git Fixes 6 Security Vulnerabilities

The advisory says this appears to need the –recurse-submodules option. The fix rejects overly long index paths before their length can be cut short.

This is not the first time cloned repositories have caused trouble. Cyber Security News covered CVE-2025-48384, which CISA confirmed as exploited, and a Lazarus Group campaign that used a similar symlink trick against developers. Those cases show how quickly attackers turn clone bugs into real attacks.

CVE-2026-113408 affects cloning an empty repository over protocol v2. A malicious server can advertise a HEAD pointer with path-traversal pieces in its name.

Git did not check it, so a later branch update could write outside the intended reference folder. Git now validates the target, along with other reference names it receives over protocol v2.

CVE-2026-114467 is a stack memory bug. When Git removes GPG signatures from a message, it assumes there would be at most two. A crafted tag with more can overflow a fixed-size array. Merging that tag could corrupt memory or crash, and hosting services that merge on behalf of users may also be affected.

CVE-2026-114469 involves binary patches. Git refuses patches above roughly 1 GiB, but it only measured the compressed size. A small crafted patch can expand past the limit, trigger an out-of-bounds read, and crash Git. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size.

CVE-2026-105437 is a heap corruption bug in large merges. The memory calculation can overflow when many conflicts combine with a large conflict-marker-size setting. Git then allocates too little space and writes past it. Local merges and services that merge untrusted content are both affected.

The last flaw, CVE-2026-114466, hits git fast-import. Three features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to, and export-pack-edges, could read or write files outside the repository. They are now blocked in untrusted input unless the caller sets –allow-unsafe-features. Turn that option on only for streams you trust.

GitHub says it has already fixed github.com and its Enterprise Cloud products. GitHub Enterprise Server admins should install 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, or 3.22.4. GitHub Desktop, the GitHub Copilot app, Codespaces, and Actions will also get patched Git builds.

Teams should also check build servers and automation tools, since they often clone repositories without anyone watching. Related risks are growing too, as shown by the GitSpawn flaws that let booby-trapped repositories run code through AI coding agents.

If you can’t update right away, clone only from trusted servers and skip recursive clones of unknown repositories. Also avoid merging untrusted tags or content, and avoid processing outside binary patches or fast-import streams. These steps help, but they do not replace the patch.

The post Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities Allow Attackers to Bypass Security Feature appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has disclosed two Windows BitLocker security feature bypass vulnerabilities that could allow attackers with physical access to weaken device protections.

Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-97015 and CVE-2026-119832. Microsoft rates both as Important, with CVSS base scores of 6.8 and 5.9, respectively. The bugs have different causes and access requirements, so security teams should assess each separately.

For CVE-2026-119832, Microsoft confirms that a successful attacker could bypass BitLocker Device Encryption on the system storage device and access encrypted data.

The attack requires physical access and basic user privileges. It does not require another user to click a link, open a file, or approve a prompt. CVE-2026-97015 stems from a heap-based buffer overflow, classified as CWE-122. This type of flaw occurs when software writes beyond the memory space reserved for a buffer.

Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities

Microsoft says an unauthorized attacker can use the weakness to bypass a security feature through a physical attack. No existing privileges or user interaction are required, and attack complexity is rated low.

CVE-2026-119832 involves improper access control rather than a memory handling error. An attacker needs low privileges, but exploitation requires no user interaction.

According to Microsoft’s advisory, the vulnerability was not publicly disclosed or known to be exploited at the time of release. Microsoft rates exploitation as less likely and credits researcher yhw.

These disclosures follow earlier Windows BitLocker bypass vulnerabilities and the October 2026 BitLocker security updates. CVE-2026-119832 affects Windows 10 versions 1809, 21H2, and 22H2, several Windows 11 releases, and Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. Supported processor platforms vary by release.

CVE-2026-97015 has a broader affected product list that also includes older Windows Server branches. Administrators should check both records rather than rely on a single shared device list.

Microsoft lists KB5131096 for affected Windows 10 21H2 and 22H2 systems, KB5131087 for Windows 11 23H2, and KB5132059 for Windows 11 26H1 under CVE-2026-119832. Server updates include KB5131085 for Server 2019 and KB5131090 for Server 2022.

articles.title: Multiple Windows Remote Desktop Flaws Allow Attackers to Execute Code Over Network
articles.description:
Microsoft has released security updates for four Windows Remote Desktop Client vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code through network connections or local access. Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws involve memory handling errors and a race condition. Three have network attack paths, while the fourth requires an attacker with existing local access, […]

The post Multiple Windows Remote Desktop Flaws Allow Attackers to Execute Code Over Network appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has released security updates for four Windows Remote Desktop Client vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code through network connections or local access.

Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws involve memory handling errors and a race condition. Three have network attack paths, while the fourth requires an attacker with existing local access, an important difference when assessing exposure.

The highest-scoring flaw, CVE-2026-119934, carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and an Important severity rating. Microsoft describes it as a double-free bug, meaning the client releases the same memory area more than once. This can damage memory handling and allow an attacker to run code when the affected client processes a response from a malicious server.

An attacker would need to host that server and persuade a user to connect. No prior account access is required, but user interaction is necessary. This is not an attack where someone can simply send traffic to any Windows computer and gain control. The exposed component is the connecting Remote Desktop client, making the choice of remote server central to this attack path.

CVE-2026-119858 involves a heap-based buffer overflow that allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. The flaw concerns data exceeding the space reserved for it in memory.

Microsoft’s advisory says exploitation depends on specific conditions, such as protocol settings or configurations. Those requirements limit the likelihood of broad attacks, but do not remove the need to update affected clients.

The race condition, CVE-2026-95964, has a CVSS score of 7.5. It affects how client operations share a resource without proper synchronization. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, where operations occur in a particular order or timing. Microsoft lists user interaction as required and rates exploitation as unlikely, reflecting the added difficulty of reliably triggering this network code execution flaw.

Remote Desktop Client Attack Conditions

The fourth issue, CVE-2026-119390, needs separate treatment despite its Remote Code Execution title. Microsoft’s technical description identifies a local heap-based buffer overflow requiring low privileges, with no additional user interaction. Its CVSS score is 7.8. Reporting it as an unauthenticated network attack would therefore misstate the access needed to exploit it.

Client-side attacks are an established concern. Cyber Security News previously covered a Remote Desktop Client vulnerability involving a malicious server and a different underlying weakness. That earlier case provides useful context, but it is not evidence that the newly disclosed flaws share its attack method or have already been used against organizations.

Social engineering also makes the connection step relevant. Previous rogue RDP phishing campaigns used emailed connection files to direct victims toward attacker-controlled servers. Those campaigns abused remote resource sharing rather than these new memory flaws. The connection is practical, not proof of a shared campaign: attackers already have methods for persuading users to open unwanted remote sessions.

Affected Windows Systems

Microsoft’s CVE-2026-119934 advisory lists affected Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server releases. Administrators should check each vulnerability’s product table rather than assume one update covers every installation. The CVE-2026-119390 table also includes Windows App Client for Windows Desktop, with version 2.0.1489.0 listed as the fixed build for that product.

Security teams should deploy the matching updates and verify installation across employee devices and administrative systems that make Remote Desktop connections. Microsoft reported no exploitation at publication for CVE-2026-119934, CVE-2026-119390, and CVE-2026-95964.

The post Hackers Exploit AhsayCBS Vulnerabilities to Hide Malware in PNG Images and Deploy Stealthy Backdoors appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers exploiting AhsayCBS backup servers have planted webshells, hidden encrypted code inside PNG images, and staged a Python implant designed to run only on its intended host.

The findings show an intrusion that extended beyond cryptocurrency mining, giving attackers several ways to keep access to systems responsible for protecting an organization’s backups.

The attack affected three AhsayCBS servers in one organization between October 8 and October 11, 2026, before vendor hotfixes became available.

Attackers exploited CVE-2026-105133, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-105134, which allowed unauthenticated remote code execution with SYSTEM privileges. The combination exposed both the backup platform and the sensitive access it could provide.

Researchers from Huntress identified five webshell families, a second cryptocurrency miner, and a host-bound Python implant during their investigation.

In a technical report published November 9, researcher Jonathan Semon described tooling that concealed commands, supported file transfers, and weakened endpoint protection.

However, the team could not confirm every payload’s behavior or establish whether attackers stole backup data.

Hackers Exploit AhsayCBS Vulnerabilities

The most distinctive webshell posed as an internal image-preview service. Instead of accepting obvious command parameters, it processed uploaded PNG files and extracted hidden information from their pixels.

This approach resembles earlier PNG malware concealment techniques reported in other campaigns, although Huntress did not attribute this intrusion to those operators.

The loader read the least-significant bit from each pixel’s red, green, and blue values, then assembled those bits into bytes. It reconstructed a four-byte payload length followed by encrypted content.

A hardcoded AES key unlocked the data using Java’s default AES transformation, which Huntress identified as ECB mode with PKCS5 padding.

On the first request, a custom Java class loader placed the decrypted class in memory and returned a cover image. Later requests passed data into that class and triggered execution.

Results were encrypted and embedded into another PNG, making the exchange look like image traffic rather than a conventional command session. The technique matters because the executable functionality arrives inside requests and runs in memory.

Related Earth Sirrush PNG campaigns demonstrate how image concealment also appears in espionage operations, but that similarity does not establish a connection. Huntress examined this loader, not its delivered class, so the commands executed through it remain unknown.

Another recovered webshell behaved like a remote administration API. It checked an API token, timestamp, nonce, and HMAC-SHA256 signature before accepting requests.

Behind those checks, attackers could execute commands, change directories, and transfer files in chunks, with support for files up to 4 GB. Huntress found no logs proving that its download function was used.

Host-Bound Backdoors, Backup Access, and Recovery

A separate Python implant introduced another concealment layer. Its wrapper combined Base64 encoding, LZMA compression, and a marshaled Python code object.

Before continuing, it calculated a SHA-256 value from the host’s MachineGuid and checked for a matching marker file. Without that file, the script exited, potentially preventing execution in an analyst’s sandbox.

If the marker existed, the code would copy a 673 KB blob into executable memory and start a thread. A reflective loader then mapped an embedded x64 DLL.

Static analysis revealed command-and-control information and strings consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS, but Huntress neither observed the implant running nor identified its malware family.

The attackers also deployed another XMRig miner with a SYSTEM-level scheduled task that checked every minute and restarted it when necessary.

Tunneling utilities, remote access software, and broad Microsoft Defender exclusions provided additional ways to operate while reducing security visibility across the compromised servers.

On a related Veeam server, investigators observed a command consistent with NetExec’s credential-theft module. It queried stored backup credentials and used DPAPI decryption.

Separate reporting on Veeam backup credential exposure explains why these environments are valuable targets, although that vulnerability was not identified as this intrusion’s entry point.

Ahsay released hotfix 10.3.4.45 for version 10 and 9.15.2.70 for versions 7 through 9. Huntress verified that the version 10 hotfix blocked the observed entry point.

Patching does not remove existing backdoors: exposed organizations should investigate suspicious server activity, unauthorized exclusions, and persistence mechanisms. Where compromise is found, Huntress recommends rebuilding from trusted backups and rotating reachable credentials.

articles.description:

The activity shows how a fake verification prompt can become the starting point for persistent access, credential theft, and movement across corporate networks. The trick still depends on convincing someone to […]

The post ClickFix Attacks Evolve to Hide Malware in PNG Images and Hijack Windows Domain Controllers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
ClickFix attacks are moving beyond simple malware downloads, with recent investigations revealing executable payloads hidden inside PNG images and intrusions reaching Windows domain controllers.

The activity shows how a fake verification prompt can become the starting point for persistent access, credential theft, and movement across corporate networks.

The trick still depends on convincing someone to run a command copied from a webpage. Attackers now support that request with fake security checks, colored terminal messages, and animated progress bars, making malware installation look like a routine browser verification.

Huntress researchers identified these techniques across several investigations detailed in a November 10 report.

The findings describe separate attack chains, not one operation combining every technique. Researchers believe unrelated operators are adapting ClickFix because it continues to persuade users to execute malicious commands.

ClickFix Attacks Evolve

In one investigation, a pasted PowerShell command displayed a fake Cloudflare check while downloading an archive. Its contents included a signed Microsoft executable, a malicious DLL, and a batch script.

The script retrieved PNG images containing executable data inside their pixels, rebuilt the binaries on disk, and launched them.

Unlike earlier ClickFix image hiding techniques that concealed shellcode, this chain reconstructed complete executables. Scheduled tasks and registry Run keys maintained access afterward.

The image itself was not the trigger: the user’s command started the code responsible for extracting and running its hidden contents.

A separate September intrusion used DLL sideloading and Windows administration tools to reach a primary domain controller. After establishing persistence, the attacker examined domain trusts, administrator membership, and account details.

WinRM enabled lateral movement, followed by account creation and a second reverse SSH tunnel. Earlier incidents showed similar consequences. February activity delivered Matanbuchus 3.0 and AstarionRAT before reaching two domain controllers through PsExec.

May’s ClickFix MSI installation attack spread malware through administrative shares, compromising 11 hosts before containment.

Browser Cache Tricks and Defensive Priorities

Another investigation found commands tailored to Chrome, Firefox, or Brave. A compromised dental website first placed a file in the browser cache.

The pasted command searched for its exact 17,635-byte size, copied it into temporary storage, and executed it as a batch script. Huntress also observed DuskDesk, a Node.js remote access trojan disguised as management software.

Related Node.js ClickFix malware campaigns illustrate why administrators should examine unexpected scripting runtimes rather than trust an application’s appearance. DuskDesk used logon persistence and contacted a potential command server.

Huntress recommends teaching users never to paste webpage instructions into terminals, restricting untrusted execution, and monitoring encoded PowerShell, new persistence entries, and unexpected SSH traffic.

Detection should connect these behaviors rather than depend only on changing filenames or hashes.

The campaign, tracked as SilentDelivery, targets high-profile organizations mainly across Europe and […]

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
China-linked hackers are turning trusted websites into malware delivery points by displaying fake Google Chrome certificate warnings.

The pages urge selected visitors to install a certificate repair utility, but the download instead installs a backdoor that gives attackers remote access to Windows computers.

The campaign, tracked as SilentDelivery, targets high-profile organizations mainly across Europe and Asia. Attackers compromised websites connected to government, shipping, IT, and research sectors, using familiar browser error messages to persuade visitors that installing software was necessary to regain access.

Check Point researchers identified the previously undocumented SquadC backdoor during their investigation, alongside cases delivering a SparrowDoor variant.

Their November 10 research report connects SilentDelivery to a wider malware ecosystem associated with CopperDragon, a possible developer and supplier supporting several China-linked threat groups.

China-Linked Hackers Use Fake Chrome Certificate Warnings

The infection begins when a victim opens a compromised website. Injected JavaScript replaces the page with a counterfeit Chrome SSL certificate warning, written in the website’s language.

An added “Install certificate” button offers a supposed fix that downloads a malicious Windows Installer package. This approach resembles earlier fake Chrome update campaigns that used compromised websites to push malware, but SilentDelivery presents the download as certificate repair rather than a browser update.

Check Point found three S3 buckets it believed were compromised and used to host next-stage payloads. The JavaScript uses the publicly available jsjiami obfuscation service to hide its purpose.

Before displaying the warning, it checks whether the visitor uses Windows and, in some versions, whether the current website matches the intended domain. These checks help restrict delivery to suitable targets.

Repeated requests to attacker infrastructure support checks based on IP address and location. The operators can decide whether to leave the genuine page visible or replace it with the warning.

Clicking the installation button reports the interaction, while execution of the backdoor separately registers a successful compromise.

After infection, the fake warning disappears on later visits. That detail matters: restoring normal access makes the repair appear successful and may discourage the victim from reporting what happened.

The campaign therefore combines selective targeting with feedback that helps operators manage each stage of delivery.

SquadC, written in C/C++, loads into memory through a separate, three-stage loader. It supports command execution, file creation and deletion, directory listings, system information collection, and screenshots.

Configurable checks look for virtual-machine artifacts and other signs of automated analysis; another option requires a browser to remain running.

Sparrow Framework Links Reveal a Wider Espionage Ecosystem

SilentDelivery is one of three clusters Check Point connected to the Sparrow framework. Earlier reporting on new SparrowDoor backdoor variants documented the malware’s continuing development, but the latest findings caution against treating every intrusion involving related tools as the work of one group.

CopperDragon may act as a digital quartermaster, supplying tools to operators including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries, TropicTrooper, and UAT-9244.

The researchers based their connections on malware similarities and infrastructure features, including reused certificates. They explicitly warned that shared backdoors or servers do not establish a single operator.

The OceanGate cluster initially compromised internet-facing Linux systems before moving into Windows environments.

Its tools included SparrowShell, a Linux backdoor sharing code and design features with SparrowDoor, alongside modified SSH components that captured credentials during administrative activity. The attackers also deployed tools for reconnaissance and credential theft.

DarkWire focused on telecommunications providers and government organizations in Latin America, deploying CopperDoor and CopperDNS.

Related coverage of FamousSparrow Exchange server intrusions describes SparroWocky, the name ESET uses for CopperDoor. CopperDNS instead carries command traffic through DNS MX queries, giving operators another communication channel.

For defenders, the immediate lesson is to investigate unexpected certificate-repair downloads rather than accept their browser branding. SilentDelivery relies on users executing the installer; the reported chain does not demonstrate a Chrome vulnerability.

Investigations should also consider related phishing delivery, which Check Point observed distributing SquadC through a malicious shortcut inside an archive.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
“Security policy management” is one shelf holding two different products: network security policy management (NSPM) firewall rulebases, segmentation intent, change automation and written-policy lifecycle the documents people sign and auditors demand.

Our roster spans both, so this countdown declares the lane on every entry and ranks within the honest frame: rulebase engines first by estate scale, document platforms by attestation truth. Tufin takes 1; AlgoSec and FireMon complete the NSPM podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Tufin policy orchestration at the largest hybrid-estate scale.

• NSPM podium: Tufin (scale), AlgoSec (application-centric analysis), FireMon (real-time rulebase audit).

• Lane rule: rulebase automation and document attestation share nothing but the word “policy” declare the lane before the shortlist.

• Status note: Skybox Security’s corporate situation requires verification before any contract capability discussion below assumes that homework.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

NSPM criteria: rulebase-analysis depth, change-automation safety, multi-vendor/hybrid coverage. Written-policy criteria: lifecycle workflow, attestation tracking, framework mapping. Both: pricing clarity. Weights: lane-core capability 35%, automation safety 20%, coverage/mapping 20%, ergonomics 15%, pricing 10%.

The 2026 Policy Management Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results. Lanes ranked within their own frame.

1. Tufin — Best Hybrid-Estate Orchestration

Snapshot: Tiered platform | Multi-vendor firewall + cloud security groups | Segmentation intent enforced continuously

Why it earns 1: Tufin runs policy where the estates are largest: thousand-device multi-vendor firewall fleets plus cloud security groups orchestrated from one intent layer, with change automation that carries enterprise change-volume and segmentation policy enforced continuously rather than diagrammed annually. The scale ceiling of the category.

Pros: Hybrid orchestration scale; segmentation intent; change pipelines.

Cons: Platform weight below enterprise scale.

Bottom line: The big-estate policy engine.

2. AlgoSec — Best Application-Centric Analysis

Snapshot: Device/module licensing | Connectivity flows mapped to business apps | Risk-checked change automation

Why it ranks here: AlgoSec translates firewall sprawl into application language: flows discovered and mapped to the business apps they serve, so cleanup conversations happen in terms owners accept and decommissioned apps take their rules with them.

Change automation rides the same app-aware model.

Pros: App-centric mapping; business-legible cleanup; automation safety.

Cons: App-discovery depth takes tuning investment.

Bottom line: NSPM that speaks application.

3. FireMon — Best Real-Time Rulebase Audit

Snapshot: Device-based tiers | Live change detection | Cleanup analytics

Why it ranks here: FireMon watches rulebases as they drift: real-time change detection, compliance-drift alerts, and cleanup analytics surfacing the unused, shadowed, and risky rules that bloat every mature estate.

The continuous-audit pick for multi-vendor fleets that change daily.

Pros: Real-time monitoring; cleanup economics; compliance mapping.

Cons: Orchestration ceiling versus the scale leader.

Bottom line: The always-on rulebase auditor.

4. RedSeal — Best Hybrid Network Exposure Analysis

Snapshot: Enterprise-focused platform | Network topology modeling + security configuration analysis | Attack-path and exposure visibility across complex network environments

Why it ranks here: RedSeal helps organizations understand how network configurations, vulnerabilities, and connectivity combine to create security exposures.

Its network modeling and risk analysis capabilities help identify vulnerable paths, prioritize remediation, and assess the security impact of network changes.

It is a strong alternative to Skybox for organizations focused on network exposure context and attack-path analysis, although it is not a direct replacement for every firewall policy management workflow.

Pros: Network topology modeling; exposure management and attack-path analysis; vulnerability context; risk-based remediation prioritization.

Cons: Less focused on direct firewall rule lifecycle automation and change orchestration; enterprise-oriented deployment and implementation may require additional effort.

Bottom line: A strong Skybox alternative for network exposure modeling and risk prioritization, particularly in complex hybrid environments.

5. ManageEngine — Best Value NSPM Essentials

Snapshot: Per-device tiers | Firewall Analyzer rule cleanup | Compliance reports

Why it ranks here: ManageEngine Firewall Analyzer delivers the NSPM essentials rule analysis, config audit, compliance reporting at ManageEngine’s famously accessible pricing. The right weight for mid-market estates below the enterprise platforms’ complexity line.

Pros: Entry economics; essential coverage; low operational bar.

Cons: Orchestration and automation ceilings.

Bottom line: NSPM essentials without the enterprise invoice.

6. LogicGate — Best No-Code Policy Workflow

Snapshot: Application subscriptions | Risk Cloud policy lifecycle | Owner-built workflows

Why it ranks here: LogicGate’s Risk Cloud handles the document lane with no-code flexibility: policy creation, review cycles, exception workflows, and attestation campaigns built by the team that runs them.

The written-policy lifecycle inside a broader risk platform teams can remodel themselves.

Pros: No-code lifecycle; exception workflow; platform breadth.

Cons: Dedicated policy-tool depth in attestation chasing.

Bottom line: The policy workflow you redesign yourself.

7. Hyperproof — Best Many-Framework Policy Mapping

Snapshot: Platform tiers | One policy, every framework mapped | Evidence linkage

Why it ranks here: Hyperproof treats policies as mapped assets: one document linked to every requirement it satisfies across many frameworks simultaneously, with evidence attached and crosswalks maintained.

The compliance-ops answer for estates juggling five certifications on one policy set.

Pros: Crosswalk architecture; evidence linkage; ops workflow.

Cons: Network-policy lane untouched, by design.

Bottom line: One policy, every framework it serves.

8. Secureframe — Best Cert-Integrated Policy Library

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Auditor-ready policy library | Acceptance tracking

Why it ranks here: Secureframe ships the document lane as part of certification readiness: auditor-shaped policy templates, employee acceptance tracked against the HRIS, and evidence tied to the cert program.

Policies that arrive audit-shaped rather than drafted from blank pages.

Pros: Template quality; acceptance automation; cert integration.

Cons: Standalone policy programs outside cert context.

Bottom line: Policies born audit-ready.

9. ZenGRC (Reciprocity) — Best Lean Lifecycle Platform

Snapshot: Subscription tiers | Versioned policy lifecycle | Control mapping

Why it ranks here: ZenGRC manages written policy inside its lean compliance platform: version control, review cycles, control mapping, attestations the document lane handled at lean-team weight without heavyweight GRC implementation.

Pros: Lean lifecycle; control mapping; fast onboarding.

Cons: Attestation-chase depth versus dedicated tools.

Bottom line: Policy lifecycle at lean-GRC weight.

10. Netwrix — Best Endpoint-Enforced Policy

Snapshot: Per-user/module licensing | PolicyPak lineage | Settings enforced on devices

Why it ranks here: Netwrix closes the document lane’s credibility gap: the PolicyPak lineage enforces written rules as endpoint settings browser configs, application controls, least-privilege defaults so the signed document and the device state actually match.

Policy that reaches the desktop.

Pros: Endpoint enforcement; attestation tracking; Windows-estate depth.

Cons: Scope centers on Windows-estate enforcement.

Bottom line: The signature and the setting, reconciled.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Declare the Lane, Then Pilot the Ugly Part

The shortlist writes itself once the lane is declared. NSPM buyers: inventory device count and vendor mix (multi-vendor fleets need Tufin/AlgoSec/FireMon-class orchestration), pilot on your ugliest rulebase and count the unused and shadowed rules surfaced cleanup findings typically fund the license before automation ever runs and gate change automation behind risk simulation with six months of clean history before production trust.

Written-policy buyers: test the attestation chase end-to-end (who hasn’t signed, automated reminders, auditor export in one click), demand framework mapping against certifications you actually hold, tie acceptance to the HRIS joiner flow, and weigh enforcement reality a Netwrix-class bridge between signed documents and device settings closes the gap auditors increasingly probe.

Both lanes: run the Skybox status verification before any evaluation effort, and route outputs rulebase drift or attestation gaps into the audit trail where findings get owned and dated.

FAQs

What are the best security policy management tools in 2026?

Network lane: Tufin, AlgoSec, FireMon, ManageEngine, with Skybox status-gated. Written lane: LogicGate, Hyperproof, Secureframe, ZenGRC, and Netwrix for endpoint-enforced policy.

Firewall and segmentation estates need NSPM; audit and certification programs need document lifecycle most enterprises eventually run one of each, bought separately against different criteria (compliance management software solutions).

What does safe change automation look like?

Requests simulated against risk and compliance before any push, approvals routed, implementations verified post-change automation with a pre-flight check, never blind push.

What’s the fastest NSPM payback?

Rulebase cleanup: the unused, shadowed, and duplicate rules surfaced in a pilot typically justify the license on risk and performance grounds alone.

How do we prove policy attestation to auditors?

Version-controlled documents, timestamped acceptance records, exception registers, and one-click evidence export plus enforcement reconciliation where device settings should match signed policy.

Verdict

One shelf, two products, ten tools ranked in their honest lanes.

Tufin for the biggest fleets, AlgoSec for application language, FireMon for the live audit, ManageEngine for the value tier, Skybox behind a status gate; LogicGate, Hyperproof, Secureframe, and ZenGRC running the document lifecycle, Netwrix making signatures real on devices declare the lane, pilot the ugly rulebase or the attestation chase, and let policy prove itself instead of describing itself.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Audit management software is graded by a brutal metric: the spreadsheet-reversion point the moment auditors flee the platform back to Excel.

The 2026 rankings reward fieldwork ergonomics, evidence automation that pulls control tests from systems rather than people, and the committee-pack mile where most tools quietly fail. AuditBoard takes 1; ServiceNow and Workiva complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: AuditBoard the adoption benchmark the profession measures everything against.

• Podium: AuditBoard (floor-vote winner), ServiceNow (workflow-routed findings), Workiva (filing-grade reporting fusion).

• Class split: audit-born specialists (AuditBoard, TeamMate) versus GRC-suite modules (ServiceNow, Archer, MetricStream) versus reporting-grade platforms (Workiva, Diligent) daily ownership decides.

• 2026 theme: AI drafting entered the workpaper narrative generation and summarization are real, with reviewer sign-off as the non-negotiable gate.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: fieldwork ergonomics (workpapers, review chains), evidence/control-test automation, SOX depth, committee-grade reporting, time-to-value, and pricing clarity.

Weights: fieldwork ergonomics 25%, evidence automation 20%, SOX depth 20%, reporting 20%, time-to-value 15%.

The 2026 Audit Management Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Onspring — Best Configurable No-Code Audit Platform

Snapshot: Subscription platform | No-code internal-audit workflows | Workpapers, findings, remediation, and reporting

Why it earns 1: Onspring gives audit teams the flexibility to build and adapt audit programs without relying heavily on developers, while still covering planning, fieldwork, workpapers, review chains, findings, evidence, and remediation.

Its strength is combining audit usability with no-code configurability, so teams can shape workflows around their own methodology instead of forcing auditors into a rigid process.

Pros: No-code flexibility; strong fieldwork workflow; workpaper management; findings and remediation tracking; configurable reporting.

Cons: Less market scale and brand recognition than the largest audit platforms; complex configurations still need disciplined administration.

Bottom line: The audit platform teams can reshape without rebuilding from scratch.

2. ServiceNow — Best Workflow-Routed Findings

Snapshot: Now Platform modules | Findings tied to CMDB assets | Remediation the business must answer

Why it ranks here: ServiceNow’s audit module solves the back half of every engagement: findings routed as workflows to owners who can’t ignore tickets, tied to CMDB assets and change records, with remediation status visible without chasing.

Fieldwork depth trails the specialists; finding-closure velocity doesn’t.

Pros: Remediation routing; asset linkage; estate adoption gravity.

Cons: Workpaper ergonomics versus audit-born rivals.

Bottom line: The findings that actually get fixed.

3. Caseware — Best Audit-to-Financial-Reporting Integration

Snapshot: Platform subscriptions | Audit workpapers + financial statements | Connected reporting and review workflows

Why it ranks here: Caseware connects audit fieldwork directly with financial reporting, allowing workpapers, risk assessments, procedures, review notes, and financial statements to live inside one connected environment.

Its advantage is strongest where audit results ultimately need to flow into formal financial reporting, disclosure review, and filing workflows without repeatedly moving data between separate systems.

Pros: Strong audit methodology; connected workpapers; integrated financial statements; review and sign-off workflows; reporting automation.

Cons: More accounting and financial-audit oriented than broad enterprise GRC platforms; less suited to organizations focused mainly on operational or cyber audit.

Bottom line: Audit workpapers and financial reporting connected from fieldwork to final statement.

4. Wolters Kluwer (TeamMate) — Best Methodology Incumbent

Snapshot: Per-auditor licensing | TeamMate+ web generation | Global install base

Why it ranks here: TeamMate carries decades of internal-audit methodology workpaper discipline, review hierarchies, the vocabulary the profession trained on modernized to web scale in TeamMate+.

The installed base makes it the shared language of audit shops worldwide; adoption-era momentum is the honest contest it fights.

Pros: Methodology depth; workpaper rigor; global ubiquity.

Cons: Winning hearts against the adoption leader.

Bottom line: The incumbent methodology, webified.

5. Diligent — Best Committee-Channel Integration

Snapshot: Suite subscriptions | HighBond lineage + board portals | ACL analytics heritage

Why it ranks here: Diligent owns the destination: board portals most large enterprises already run, with audit modules feeding committee packs without reformatting theater and ACL-era analytics underneath. When the hardest audience sits upstairs, the channel is the feature.

Pros: Board-channel ownership; analytics lineage; governance fusion.

Cons: Fieldwork depth consistency across acquired modules.

Bottom line: The shortest path to the committee.

6. MetricStream — Best Regulated-Enterprise Module

Snapshot: Platform licensing | Banking-grade audit integration | Federated architecture

Why it ranks here: MetricStream’s audit module inherits the platform’s regulated depth: audit integrated with operational risk and compliance at examiner-ready rigor, federated across entities and geographies. Heavyweight implementation reality included the institutional pick.

Pros: Regulated depth; risk integration; federated scale.

Cons: Implementation weight; adoption ergonomics.

Bottom line: Audit inside the enterprise waterfront.

7. Hyperproof — Best Compliance-Ops Crossover

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Controls mapped across frameworks | Continuous evidence collection

Why it ranks here: Hyperproof crosses from compliance operations into audit: controls managed once and mapped to every framework, continuous evidence collection feeding both certification and internal audit, and workflow built for distributed teams.

Strongest where audit and compliance share an evidence backbone.

Pros: Crosswalk architecture; evidence reuse; ops workflow.

Cons: Classic internal-audit fieldwork depth versus specialists.

Bottom line: One evidence engine, two programs.

8. Archer — Best Configurable Register Module

Snapshot: Use-case licensing | Audit encoded into enterprise registers | Methodology freehand

Why it ranks here: Archer models audit into the same configurable registers as enterprise risk: whatever methodology your shop runs, encoded exactly with the administrator staffing that freedom demands.

The integrated choice for estates already running Archer’s registers.

Pros: Configurability; register integration; program pedigree.

Cons: Staffing tax; modern ergonomics race.

Bottom line: Your methodology, encoded staff it.

9. Ideagen — Best Safety-Sector Specialist

Snapshot: Module subscriptions | Aviation/healthcare/manufacturing templates | Document-control lineage

Why it ranks here: Ideagen serves audits where the stakes are physical: aviation, healthcare, and manufacturing compliance against exacting operational standards, with sector templates and document-control DNA. The specialist lane the generalists don’t walk.

Pros: Sector templates; safety-regime fluency; document control.

Cons: General internal-audit breadth versus leaders.

Bottom line: Audit for the safety-critical floor.

10. Netwrix — Best IT-Audit Evidence Lane

Snapshot: Per-user/module licensing | IT-change and access auditing | Evidence-generation focus

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: Netwrix enters from the evidence side: IT auditing of changes, access, and configurations across AD, file systems, and databases the system-generated evidence IT audits consume rather than engagement-workflow management. The evidence lane, ranked as one.

Pros: IT-evidence depth; change/access auditing; value pricing.

Cons: Not an engagement-workflow platform.

Bottom line: The evidence feed, not the fieldwork desk.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Pilot the Reversion Point

Run the only pilot that predicts success: working auditors on a real engagement slice one workpaper chain, one review cycle, one finding through remediation and watch for where they reach for Excel, because that reversion point is the product’s true boundary and no demo reveals it.

Grade evidence automation against your control population (what share of SOX tests can run from system data and consider the Netwrix-class evidence lane as a feed regardless of platform choice), demand the committee pack generated live from fieldwork data, and settle the archive question before migration: prior-year workpapers move with review chains intact or stay read-only half-migrations poison the first busy season.

Price per-auditor versus module models at your real headcount, require AI-drafted narratives to carry mandatory reviewer sign-off, and wire findings into remediation workflow the business answers an audit platform whose findings age in its own database has only moved the spreadsheet problem.

FAQs

What is the best audit management software in 2026? AuditBoard leads on adoption, ServiceNow routes findings the business must answer, Workiva owns the filing-grade mile, TeamMate holds the methodology lineage, with Diligent, MetricStream, Hyperproof, Archer, Ideagen, and Netwrix (IT-evidence lane) by class.

Audit platform or GRC suite module? Audit-led programs buy fieldwork-first platforms; risk-led programs extend their GRC suite the deciding question is who owns daily use, auditors or the risk function.

What should evidence automation actually cover? System-pulled control tests (access reviews, configuration checks), document-request workflows with chasing built in, and continuous feeds from compliance tooling graded against your real control population.

Is AI in audit software trustworthy? For narrative drafting, workpaper summarization, and risk-assessment assists, yes with reviewer sign-off mandatory and sampling-based quality checks on output.

How long should implementation take? Weeks for adoption-class platforms, quarters for enterprise suites put a first-engagement-live date in the contract either way.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one brutal metric: where do the auditors flee to Excel? AuditBoard set the adoption bar, ServiceNow closes the findings, Workiva files the result, TeamMate keeps the methodology, Diligent feeds the committee, and the estate modules serve their estates pilot on real fieldwork, automate the evidence, archive cleanly, and make the committee pack a query instead of a weekend.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security ratings grade organizations from the attacker’s side of the fence exposed services, patch cadence, breach signals and the grades now move real money: insurance pricing, vendor gates, board narratives.

Two honesty notes shape this countdown: NormShield is Black Kite’s former name (one company, counted once), and Mastercard announced RiskRecon’s wind-down, making it a migration note rather than a pick so we rank nine services honestly.

SecurityScorecard takes 1; BitSight and Black Kite complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: SecurityScorecard the operational rating teams actually work from weekly.

• Podium: SecurityScorecard (working-meeting clarity), BitSight (evidence-grade correlation), Black Kite (the dollar-lens rating).

• Honest count: nine, not ten one rebrand consolidated, one wind-down flagged.

• 2026 theme: attribution accuracy mis-mapped assets remain the category’s chronic complaint, and testing it with your own estate is the only pilot that matters.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: signal quality and attribution accuracy, loss-correlation evidence, dispute-workflow fairness, actionability of findings, portfolio ergonomics, and pricing clarity.

Weights: attribution/signal 25%, correlation evidence 20%, actionability 20%, dispute fairness 15%, portfolio scale 10%, pricing 10%.

The 2026 Security Ratings Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. SecurityScorecard — Best Operational Rating

Snapshot: Portfolio tiers; free self-view A–F grades + factor drill-downs | Breach alerting cadence

Why it earns 1: SecurityScorecard made ratings a working instrument: letter grades executives parse instantly, factor-level drill-downs practitioners act on the same day, breach alerts at operational cadence, and the free self-view that seeded the market’s broadest visibility motion. The rating that drives Tuesday’s vendor call, not just the quarterly slide.

Pros: Grade clarity; factor actionability; alert cadence; free self-assessment.

Cons: Attribution hygiene needs your validation pass, as everywhere in the category.

Bottom line: The score built for working meetings.

2. BitSight — Best Evidence-Grade Correlation

Snapshot: Portfolio subscriptions | Decade-deep loss-correlated dataset | Fourth-party discovery

Why it ranks here: BitSight’s moat is published evidence: externally observed telemetry correlated against real incident history over a decade the dataset insurers price with and boards cite. Fourth-party mapping and governance-grade reporting complete the institutional pick.

Pros: Correlation receipts; insurer currency; fourth-party graph.

Cons: Operational-cadence ergonomics trail the leader.

Bottom line: The rating with the longest receipts.

3. Black Kite (formerly NormShield) — Best Financial-Impact Lens

Snapshot: Per-vendor/portfolio tiers | Triple-lens scoring | Open FAIR-based impact math

Why it ranks here: One company, two sheet names, counted once: Black Kite grades three ways technical rating, FAIR-based financial impact, compliance correlation plus a ransomware-susceptibility index, giving vendor conversations a dollar figure alongside the letter. The methodology-transparency pick.

Pros: Dollar-lens scoring; methodology openness; ransomware index.

Cons: Brand gravity versus the two giants.

Bottom line: The rating that also speaks CFO.

4. UpGuard — Best Value Bundle with Leak Detection

Snapshot: Tiered subscriptions | Ratings + data-leak detection + lean TPRM | Mid-market economics

Why it ranks here: UpGuard pairs continuous ratings with the finding other raters skip: leak detection surfacing exposed credentials, buckets, and documents tied to you or your vendors. Bundled with lean questionnaire workflow at mid-market pricing, it’s the sensible-scale package.

Pros: Leak-detection differentiator; bundle value; accessible tiers.

Cons: Enterprise portfolio ergonomics versus leaders.

Bottom line: The rating that also finds your leaked bucket.

5. Panorays — Best Workflow-Fused Rating

Snapshot: Per-vendor tiers | Rating + adaptive questionnaires in one pass | Cycle-speed focus

Why it ranks here: Panorays treats the rating as half the assessment: external scores fused with questionnaires that adapt to each vendor’s footprint, collapsing review cycles to days. The rating as an engine inside vendor-risk workflow rather than a standalone dashboard.

Pros: Native workflow fusion; adaptive assessments; speed.

Cons: Standalone-ratings depth versus the dedicated graphs.

Bottom line: The score with a workflow welded on.

6. Whistic — Best Security-Assessment Exchange Companion

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Shared security profiles + Trust Center Exchange | Assessments, evidence, and vendor risk workflows

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: Whistic sits on the assessment-exchange side of third-party risk, helping organizations reuse vendor security profiles, questionnaires, certifications, and supporting evidence instead of collecting the same material repeatedly.

It works best as a ratings-adjacent TPRM companion, combining standardized assessments with continuous vendor review and workflow automation rather than acting as a primary external security-rating originator.

Pros: Shared assessment exchange; reusable security profiles; evidence collection; workflow automation; standardized questionnaires.

Cons: Not a primary outside-in ratings provider; strongest value comes from assessment and trust workflows.

Bottom line: Reusable vendor assessments that reduce questionnaire fatigue across the ecosystem.

7. BlueVoyant TPRM — Best Managed Third-Party Risk Companion

Snapshot: Managed platform + service | Continuous external monitoring + assessments | Analyst validation and vendor remediation

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: BlueVoyant approaches third-party risk from a managed monitoring and assessment model, combining external cyber-risk signals with questionnaires, analyst review, validation, and remediation support.

Its strength is helping teams move from finding vendor risk to validating and addressing it, making it a strong companion to security-rating programs that need more operational follow-through.

Pros: Continuous monitoring; managed assessments; analyst validation; remediation support; vendor engagement.

Cons: More service-led than pure self-service rating platforms; not primarily a standalone ratings originator.

Bottom line: Managed third-party risk operations that turn vendor findings into validated action.

8. SecurityStudio — Best SMB/Inside-Out Complement

Snapshot: Accessible tiers | S2Score self-and-vendor assessment | SMB/MSP channel fit

Why it ranks here: SecurityStudio grades from the inside out: S2Score risk assessments for your own organization and simplified vendor scoring sized for SMBs and the MSPs serving them the accessible complement to external graphs, not a competitor to them.

Pros: SMB economics; self-assessment lens; MSP channel.

Cons: Not an external-telemetry rating; scale ceilings.

Bottom line: The small-estate scoring on-ramp.

9. Mastercard (RiskRecon) — Wind-Down: Migration Note

Snapshot: Sunset path | Respected assessment-grade lineage | Transition planning required

Why it ranks last and why it’s still listed: RiskRecon built genuinely respected assessment-grade ratings, but Mastercard’s announced wind-down converts every evaluation into a migration plan: existing customers should map portfolios to successor platforms and export history; new buyers should choose from the eight entries above. Listed for the installed base’s sake, ranked as what remains.

Pros: (Legacy) assessment detail; action-plan reporting lineage.

Cons: Announced sunset decides everything.

Bottom line: Plan the exit, not the purchase.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Test Attribution With Your Own Estate First

The pilot that matters costs one afternoon: run your own organization and three known vendors through each candidate and count false-attributed assets mis-mapped infrastructure is the category’s chronic complaint and the fastest disqualifier.

Demand published loss-correlation evidence before letting scores gate procurement or insurance conversations, file one real dispute during the pilot and time the correction, and require that every grade arrives with remediation specifics a vendor can act on scores without fix lists breed supplier resentment, not improvement.

Work trends rather than snapshots (a B falling for two quarters beats a stable C for attention), write rating floors with remediation windows into vendor contracts so scores carry teeth, and sequence the RiskRecon migration now if you’re on it: portfolio export, successor mapping, and overlap-period validation before the lights dim.

Your own score is marketing too check it quarterly before your customers and underwriters do.

FAQs

What are the best security ratings services in 2026? SecurityScorecard for operational use, BitSight for correlation evidence, Black Kite for financial-impact lenses, UpGuard for bundled value, Panorays for workflow fusion, with the exchange/assessment companions (ProcessUnity, Prevalent), SecurityStudio’s inside-out complement, and RiskRecon in managed wind-down.

Why nine services instead of ten? NormShield is Black Kite’s former name one company counted once and RiskRecon’s announced wind-down makes it a migration note rather than a recommendation.

How accurate are security ratings? Strong on externally observable hygiene and trend, blind to internal controls, and only as good as their asset attribution which you should test with your own estate before buying.

Can a vendor dispute a score? Reputable services run correction workflows; test latency with a real dispute during the pilot, because slow corrections generate the vendor friction that kills programs.

Do ratings actually predict breaches? Published correlations show statistically meaningful lift meaningful, not deterministic so treat scores as one continuous signal inside a layered vendor-risk program.

Verdict

Nine services, one rebrand consolidated, one sunset flagged, one test that decides: attribution accuracy against your own estate.

SecurityScorecard for the weekly grind, BitSight for the receipts, Black Kite for the dollars, UpGuard for the leaks, Panorays for the fused pass, the companions scoped honestly, SecurityStudio for the small end, RiskRecon for the moving trucks test the map, time the dispute, demand the fix list, and let the trend lines, not the snapshots, drive the decisions.

articles.description:

Tracked as CVE-2026-119948, the flaw was disclosed on November 10, 2026, and affects multiple Windows desktop and server versions. Microsoft rates it Important, with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.5. The CVE […]

The post Windows Active Directory RCE Vulnerability Allows Attacker to Execute Code Over a Network appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has released security updates for a Windows Active Directory vulnerability that allows an authorized attacker to execute code over a network.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119948, the flaw was disclosed on November 10, 2026, and affects multiple Windows desktop and server versions. Microsoft rates it Important, with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.5.

The CVE record identifies the weakness as a stack-based buffer overflow. Exploitation requires low privileges and no user interaction, but the attack complexity is high. This means the flaw is not described as an unauthenticated attack that works against every reachable Windows system.

A stack-based buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to stack memory than is allocated for it. This can overwrite adjacent data and, under certain conditions, alter the program’s execution. In this instance, Microsoft confirms that the result may include the ability to execute remote code.

Microsoft has not disclosed the affected function, the exact network request needed, or a working attack method in the supplied advisory.

Its explanation of the high complexity rating says specific conditions must exist, such as particular protocol settings or configurations. Administrators should therefore avoid assuming that network access and valid credentials alone guarantee successful exploitation.

Windows Active Directory RCE Vulnerability

The CVSS assessment lists high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. A successful attack could therefore affect protected information, change data, or disrupt the vulnerable system. However, the published record does not establish that exploitation automatically grants SYSTEM privileges or control of an entire domain.

At release, Microsoft reported no known exploitation and no prior public disclosure. It assessed exploitation as less likely and listed exploit code maturity as unproven. An anonymous researcher received credit for reporting the vulnerability.

The affected products include Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025, including listed Server Core installations. Windows 10 versions 1607, 1809, 21H2, and 22H2 are also included, alongside Windows 11 versions 23H2 through 26H2. Architecture coverage varies by release.

The supplied update list maps Windows Server 2022 to KB5131090, Server 2019 to KB5131085, and Server 2016 to KB5131291. Windows 11 version 23H2 uses KB5131087, while version 26H1 uses KB5132059. Administrators should check the package for each system rather than applying one update across all releases.

The disclosure follows earlier reporting on Active Directory security feature bypass vulnerabilities and a separate Active Directory Domain Services privilege escalation flaw. These are distinct issues, not evidence of an exploit chain involving the new RCE.

Microsoft also disclosed CVE-2026-105559, an Important Active Directory denial-of-service vulnerability with a 6.5 base score. The supplied advisory describes a network attack requiring low privileges, low complexity, and no user interaction.

Organizations should review both advisories, deploy the applicable official updates, and verify installation across affected systems.
