articles.title: Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets and Steal Azure Key Vault Data in Just 5 Minutes
articles.description:
Hackers are using the ARTEX AI framework to find exposed credentials on GitHub and turn them into access to cloud systems. In one observed case, an AI agent moved from searching public repositories for application secrets to stealing data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes, showing how quickly a coding mistake can become […]

The post Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets and Steal Azure Key Vault Data in Just 5 Minutes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are using the ARTEX AI framework to find exposed credentials on GitHub and turn them into access to cloud systems.

In one observed case, an AI agent moved from searching public repositories for application secrets to stealing data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes, showing how quickly a coding mistake can become a cloud security incident.

The operation combines credential hunting, automated analysis, and follow-on attacks with less hands-on work from human operators.

Instead of simply collecting leaked keys, the agents investigate what those keys can access and pursue valuable resources. The five-minute finding describes one documented case, not the time required for every attack involving the framework.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence and Microsoft Security Research identified the malicious activity in a November 5 report, tracing GitHub scanning to August 2026.

Researchers described ARTEX as an offensive AI framework, rather than a conventional malware family.

Earlier reporting on ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how agents interpret results and select subsequent actions, helping attackers connect familiar weaknesses faster.

Hackers Use ARTEX AI to Find GitHub Secrets

The agents submitted large volumes of GitHub searches combining target organization names with terms associated with secrets, cloud platforms, and AI providers.

Exposed material included application credentials and API keys for AI inference services. These searches target authentication data accidentally committed in scripts, configuration files, or other source code.

Once useful credentials were found, agents obtained tokens for compromised OAuth applications and used their permissions to explore cloud resources.

Microsoft observed agents extracting Azure Key Vault secrets and searching Azure DevOps for additional credentials. The wider problem of active GitHub credential exposure helps explain why this approach remains effective: publicly disclosed secrets can remain usable until their owners revoke or rotate them.

In follow-on activity beginning as early as October 28, attackers used valid application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources.

Service principals, the identities applications use to authenticate, enabled access to dozens of applications across multiple tenants. Some compromised credentials belonged to vendor-owned multitenant applications, extending the risk to downstream customers.

The attackers mapped subscriptions, permissions, resource groups, and AI deployments. They targeted storage keys, connection strings, App Service settings, publishing credentials, and Azure Kubernetes Service credentials.

Compromised applications also accessed SharePoint and OneDrive, with observed file downloads and mailbox-item access. Agents additionally used Azure VM Run Command, a legitimate feature that can execute scripts inside virtual machines.

The activity showed adaptive troubleshooting. After failed requests mixed Key Vault data-plane API versions with Azure Resource Manager control-plane endpoints, the agent retried approximately 28 seconds later using ARM version 2023-07-01 and received successful responses.

Similar corrections followed failed Azure SQL and Application Insights requests. Such behavior supports the broader concern around autonomous AI credential theft, where automation can reduce delays between discovery and misuse.

Detecting and Containing AI-Driven Cloud Credential Abuse

Microsoft recommends treating publicly exposed credentials as compromised, even after developers delete the original code.

Responders should revoke or rotate affected secrets, investigate historical use, and replace credentials stored in any Key Vault the compromised application could read. Disabling affected service principals may be necessary; already-issued tokens remain valid until expiry.

Detection should connect identity events with subsequent cloud operations. Security teams should review Entra service-principal sign-ins, Azure Activity records, Key Vault diagnostics, storage logs, and Microsoft 365 audit data.

One address accessing several service principals, or one application rapidly requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph, warrants investigation. IP matches alone should not determine attribution.

Longer-term protection means reducing reliance on long-lived secrets through managed identities, enforcing least privilege, and enabling GitHub secret scanning and push protection.

Microsoft also recommends monitoring secondary public repositories for leaked organizational credentials.

Behavioral detections remain essential because attackers can change source addresses and user-agent strings, while legitimate tools can produce traffic resembling individual attack steps.

articles.title: Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws to Hide Fileless Backdoor and Launch Ransomware Attack
articles.description:
A China-linked threat group tracked as Storm-2603 has used the SharePoint ToolShell flaws to plant a backdoor that never touches the disk. The group then tried to run Warlock ransomware on the same network. The break-in hit an on-premises SharePoint server and ended with a ransomware launch that security software blocked. ToolShell is the name […]

The post Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws to Hide Fileless Backdoor and Launch Ransomware Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A China-linked threat group tracked as Storm-2603 has used the SharePoint ToolShell flaws to plant a backdoor that never touches the disk.

The group then tried to run Warlock ransomware on the same network. The break-in hit an on-premises SharePoint server and ended with a ransomware launch that security software blocked.

ToolShell is the name for a set of Microsoft SharePoint bugs, including CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771. They let an attacker run code on a server through specially crafted web requests.

Microsoft linked the ransomware side of this activity to Storm-2603, while other groups using the same flaws mostly stole data and spied. Defenders who thought July 2025 patching closed the story should note that unpatched servers were still being hit months later.

Researchers at Securelist, the threat research arm of Kaspersky, identified and documented this intrusion in a report published on November 5, 2026.

Their team found the activity in a December review of a customer’s logs. They noted that the attackers kept control inside the IIS worker process, w3wp.exe, and wrote nothing to disk for the backdoor itself. You can read the full Securelist analysis for the technical details.

Storm-2603 Hackers Exploit SharePoint ToolShell Flaws

The first sign was small. On December 20, a single request hit a SharePoint ToolPane endpoint to check whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770. It came from infrastructure tied to ONYPHE, an internet scanning platform.

About 12 minutes later, a second connection arrived from a bulletproof hosting provider, Pfcloud UG. Nothing was exploited yet, and three quiet days followed.

Because of that gap, the team first rated the probe as low priority. The real intrusion came on December 24, Christmas Eve, when many security teams run with fewer staff.

The attacker sent a crafted request from 45.91.94[.]204, a Safing Privacy Network node that hides the true source behind several relays.

That request loaded a webshell straight into the IIS worker process. It ran in memory and vanished if the application pool was recycled or IIS restarted. This matches what earlier reports on the ToolShell zero-day and Warlock ransomware warned about.

The webshell was a modular C# framework. Its main part, G.cs, registered a custom VirtualPathProvider, which lets ASP.NET serve pages that do not exist as files.

It woke up only when a request carried a specific User-Agent, so normal traffic never triggered it. It talked to the attacker over a custom binary protocol with simple XOR scrambling.

It also used the suo5 proxy tool to tunnel traffic through the SharePoint host, which let the attackers reach other machines inside the network.

Other modules listed running processes, logged-on users and network connections. One installed MSI packages silently, and another created admin accounts through low-level Windows account calls instead of normal commands.

For SYSTEM rights, the code used a named-pipe trick copied from the EfsPotato tool, which works because IIS worker processes hold the needed impersonation privilege.

Velociraptor, Tunnels and a Blocked Warlock Launch

Soon after the webshell ran, the worker process started msiexec.exe to install a package from Supabase cloud storage. The package was Velociraptor version 0.73.4.0, a real forensics tool with a known flaw, CVE-2025-6264.

Cisco Talos had already described Velociraptor abused in ransomware cases tied to the same group. Here, the attackers used it for persistence, discovery, data collection and running payloads.

Through Velociraptor, they set up several backup routes: Zoho Assist, VS Code tunneling, Cloudflare Tunnel and a small reverse proxy. With so many paths, deleting one tool would not end their access.

They also stopped depending on the webshell or the ToolShell bug at this point. The group then dropped a vulnerable driver, rsndispot.sys, to shut down endpoint protection.

A sideloaded DLL, flagged as Warlock’s antivirus killer, was likely meant to use it. This fits earlier findings on custom malware that abuses BYOVD from the same actor.

The final step failed. Kaspersky’s Proactive Defense Module blocked the Warlock ransomware process before it could encrypt anything.

Securelist assigns the case to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, based on the ToolShell use, the Warlock tools and the Velociraptor habits.

For defenders, patching is not enough. Install Microsoft’s emergency SharePoint security updates, then rotate exposed MachineKeys and hunt for persistence.

Watch for odd w3wp.exe behavior, new VirtualPathProvider registrations, unexpected outbound connections and new remote-management tools. Securelist also advises keeping memory and IIS logs, and treating a confirmed exploit as a full host compromise.

articles.description:

Some servers also hosted command-and-control tools, phishing software, and exploit files, showing how automated security-testing platforms are appearing alongside established attack infrastructure. The findings offer defenders a view of these environments, including files operators left publicly accessible. The count does not […]

The post ARTEX AI Hacking Framework Found on 1,465 Public Servers, Some Hosting Cyberattack Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security researchers have found ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing framework, exposed on 1,465 internet-facing hosts.

Some servers also hosted command-and-control tools, phishing software, and exploit files, showing how automated security-testing platforms are appearing alongside established attack infrastructure.

The findings offer defenders a view of these environments, including files operators left publicly accessible. The count does not mean 1,465 separate hacking groups are operating the framework.

Around 650 hosts shared repeated configurations across two hosting providers, suggesting cloned systems or servers using multiple addresses.

Removing those clusters leaves roughly 815 distinct-looking deployments. Public exposure also does not establish malicious activity, because authorized security testers can use ARTEX.

Researchers from Censys identified the exposed consoles and associated attack tools in a November 5 report. They described ARTEX as a dual-use framework, not a malware family.

Their investigation found additional threat detections on 155 hosts, or 10.6% of the total, and 32 open directories exposing tools, implants, and operator files.

ARTEX AI Hacking Framework Found on 1,465 Public Servers

Released on July 26, 2026, ARTEX combines a Go backend, Next.js console, and PostgreSQL database. It connects with ScopeSentry, an asset-discovery platform, to import domains, addresses, ports, and endpoints.

Operators define a target, testing scope, and objective; AI agents then plan tasks, execute tools, and record results. Earlier coverage of ARTEX enterprise attack automation explains how this approach reduces manual work across attack stages.

A planner breaks objectives into smaller actions, while worker agents run tools such as nmap and return findings. ARTEX maintains an asset graph showing discovered systems and an exploration graph tracking what has been tested.

It supports Anthropic, OpenAI, and compatible model endpoints, allowing operators to change providers without rebuilding the workflow.

Censys found CyberStrikeAI alongside ARTEX on 70 hosts, with PentAGI, HexStrike AI, and RedAmon also appearing. Other servers carried Vshell, Cobalt Strike, Adaptix C2, FRP, and Gophish.

These combinations matter because reconnaissance, phishing, remote access, and AI-assisted testing can sit together, although shared hosting alone does not prove a coordinated attack.

The exposed directories provided stronger operational clues. Their contents included Windows lateral-movement tools, a public sudo exploit, Linux implants, reverse-shell scripts, and compiled stagers.

One directory exposed

One directory exposed an operator’s home folder, including SSH material and shell history. Separate reporting on ARTEX Active Directory attacks describes how agents have supported credential attacks and movement between Windows systems.

Censys also traced an ARTEX server cited by CrowdStrike to open directories visible from August 18, seven weeks before CrowdStrike’s report.

That investigation linked ARTEX to attacks against South Korean financial institutions. Separately, Microsoft attributed ARTEX-assisted activity against ConnectWise customer tenants to Storm-0940.

Coverage of ARTEX Microsoft 365 targeting details that campaign’s scanning, password spraying, and OAuth abuse. Defenders should correlate infrastructure matches with authentication logs, endpoint activity, and network connections rather than treat every ARTEX console as hostile.

Censys recommends checking nearby open directories, tunneling services, unfamiliar LLM gateways, and historical scan records. Short-lived directories are particularly useful: ten disappeared and fifteen appeared elsewhere between November 3 and November 5.

articles.title: Claude Dispatch Flaw Lets Malicious Browser Extensions Run Code on Connected Computers
articles.description:
A flaw in Anthropic’s Claude Dispatch let a malicious browser extension run commands on a computer via Claude Desktop. That computer could even be a different machine signed into the same Claude account. Researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security named the technique ThisBash and published the findings on November 4, 2026. Anthropic plans to retire […]

The post Claude Dispatch Flaw Lets Malicious Browser Extensions Run Code on Connected Computers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A flaw in Anthropic’s Claude Dispatch let a malicious browser extension run commands on a computer via Claude Desktop. That computer could even be a different machine signed into the same Claude account.

Researcher Gal Weizman of Forever Security named the technique ThisBash and published the findings on November 4, 2026. Anthropic plans to retire Dispatch, but the design behind it still lives in other Claude features.

Dispatch lets a person send a task from a phone to Claude Desktop, an AI agent that can work with local files, apps, and commands. Anthropic’s help page says the feature is in limited beta and is closed to new users. The same page warns that a manipulated instruction could trigger actions that are hard to undo.

The researchers found no flaw in the phone-to-desktop link itself. The trouble started when the same workflow was reached from claude.ai in a browser, where an extension can run alongside the page.

Claude Dispatch Vulnerability

Claude Desktop is an Electron app. That means it is built from the same web interface and API as claude.ai. The web version only hid the Dispatch link. It never blocked access to it. Once someone copied the page address from the desktop app, any logged-in browser tab could open Dispatch and send requests.

An extension with permission to run scripts on claude.ai could do the same through the user’s own cookies. In the proof of concept, the script opened Dispatch in a tiny 200 by 200 pixel background window. It then asked the API for the session ID of the user’s desktop agent. This was the only visible trace on screen.

Claude first hesitated when asked to install an unknown npm package. The script read each reply and sent a follow-up in the user’s voice. Forever Security calls this prompt forcing. In normal prompt injection, hostile text hides inside a page or file that the model reads, and the attacker gets one try. In prompt forcing, the attacker controls the whole chat and can rephrase, insist and try new angles until the model gives in.

Four written prompts were enough. A short loop also clicked any “Allow” button once per second, so no human had to approve anything. The package then ran and opened Calculator. The team noted that the same step could have copied files, added SSH keys or planted a backdoor.

Dispatch is built to link devices, so the browser and the desktop do not need to be on one computer. Picture an employee who signs into a personal Claude account on a work laptop. A bad extension in their home browser could then send orders to that work laptop. It would run next to source code and cloud keys. The researchers said they have seen personal accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on at corporate endpoints.

Extensions are common enough to make this a real path. LayerX found that 99% of enterprise users in its sample had at least one extension, and 53% had extensions with high or critical permissions. Forever Security’s earlier MaXSS and Spyder research showed how flaws in two popular Chrome extensions, with over 10 million installs between them, could let websites act across other sites. A bad extension can come from a rogue install, a hijacked update or a bug in a trusted tool.

A malicious extension can already read pages, steal data and act through logged-in sessions. That is serious. But it normally stays inside the browser. ThisBash crossed that line. Permission to talk to a website became permission to run commands on the computer.

The requests also looked real. They came from a real session and a real account, with permissions the user had granted. That proved who was logged in. It did not prove the user wanted a command to run. The researchers put it this way: a web session alone is not proof that the user approved an action on their machine.

Researchers have shown extensions steering AI tools several times this year. Cyber Security News covered BragJack, where a single extension took over the built-in assistants of five major browsers. That story shows the problem goes well beyond one vendor. Any AI tool that trusts the page it sits in can be steered by code running in that page.

Weizman reported the issue to Anthropic on May 14, 2026. Anthropic confirmed it was valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of a problem it had already found. On October 13, the company said Dispatch would be retired, with a target of the end of October 2026. That date has now passed, and I could not confirm from public sources that the feature is fully gone.

The wider concern is that Claude Code Remote Control and Cowork sessions let the web drive a local agent by design. The researchers say extensions can repeat the same trick there and plan a follow-up post. Taking away one feature does not remove the trust gap underneath.

Start with a list of the AI agents on your endpoints and the accounts they use. Check whether those accounts sit under company single sign-on. Turn off cross-device remote control where there is no business need, and review how devices are paired and removed.

Treat extensions like any other software. Limit who can install them, review their permissions and watch for updates that ask for more. Approval prompts should be something the requesting component cannot click for itself. Teams should also watch for odd package installs, config changes and credential access linked to agent activity.

Anthropic recently added a beta EDR monitoring option for Claude Cowork on Team and Enterprise plans, which can help with that last step. The simplest habit is also the strongest. Keep personal AI accounts off work devices, and keep work accounts out of personal browsers. ThisBash shows why that line matters.

articles.title: Hackers Could Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Steal Conversations Without Users Knowing
articles.description:
A flaw in ChatGPT let attackers slip past Lockdown Mode, the safety setting meant to stop data leaks. Check Point Research found that a hidden pop-up trick could copy a user’s full chat history, show fake windows, and push malware. In the ChatGPT Classic desktop app, simply chatting was enough to trigger the leak. OpenAI […]

The post Hackers Could Bypass ChatGPT Lockdown Mode to Steal Conversations Without Users Knowing appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A flaw in ChatGPT let attackers slip past Lockdown Mode, the safety setting meant to stop data leaks. Check Point Research found that a hidden pop-up trick could copy a user’s full chat history, show fake windows, and push malware. In the ChatGPT Classic desktop app, simply chatting was enough to trigger the leak. OpenAI has fixed the bug.

OpenAI launched Lockdown Mode on February 13, 2026, first for business plans. On June 4, it reached personal accounts, where users can turn it on under Settings > Security. The setting limits web browsing to cached pages and turns off live web access, image support in replies, Deep Research, Agent Mode, Canvas networking, live connectors, and file downloads.

OpenAI says it is built for high-risk users, such as executives and security teams, and is not needed by most people. Our earlier story on the ChatGPT Lockdown Mode release covers the basics.

The goal is to stop prompt injection, where hidden text tricks the AI into following an attacker’s orders. A common trick is to make the AI load a link like attacker.example/collect?data= followed by private details. The data then shows up in the attacker’s server logs and the chat looks normal.

ChatGPT Lockdown Mode Bypass

This is not the first hidden exit path Check Point has found. In March, the team showed that DNS tunneling in ChatGPT’s code runtime could send chat data to an outside server. We covered that bug in ChatGPT Vulnerability Let Attackers Silently Exfiltrate User Prompts. The new flaw shows how closing one path does not protect the others.

In February 2026, OpenAI added an HTML preview to ChatGPT code blocks, so users can view a page right in the chat. That page runs inside two nested iframes, which are small boxed-in web pages. The box blocks outside images, scripts, and links, and it asks the user before anything leaves.

Researcher Alexey Bukhteyev spotted a weak point. The boxes allowed popups through two settings, allow-popups and allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox. ChatGPT guarded popups by swapping out the window.open function. A page could skip that guard by adding one more iframe and calling that iframe’s own window.open.

The popup then opened with no prompt, even in Lockdown Mode. Since the second setting was on, code in the popup ran outside the box.

The first risk was fake update windows. The popup kept the ChatGPT icon, while the attacker chose the title. That made a malware download look like a real app update. In a browser, downloads are not blocked, so a shared chat link was enough, and the victim did not even need an account. In the desktop app, the user still had to click the download link.

The second risk was silent data theft. In ChatGPT Classic, built on Electron, window.open worked without any user click. A malicious prompt, a malicious custom GPT, or a shared chat could then send the whole conversation, and uploaded files, to the attacker’s server.

The third risk was stolen logins. The team also reloaded the main ChatGPT window and signed the user out. A fake login page could then capture the password when the user signed back in.

Check Point reported the problem to OpenAI. On September 18, 2026, OpenAI said it removed both popup permissions from the outer preview iframe. Check Point retested and confirmed the trick no longer works. Check Point published its report on November 5.

No user action is needed for this specific bug, but a few habits lower the risk of similar ones. Do not click buttons, previews, or “update” prompts inside shared chats. Skip prompts copied from unknown sites and avoid custom GPTs from unknown builders.

Check the address bar or sign-in page before typing a password, especially after an unexpected logout. Keep the desktop app updated, and avoid pasting medical, financial, or work secrets into any chat unless needed.

Even OpenAI says its safeguards reduce risk but give no full guarantee. As AI tools run code and show web content, each new feature adds a new way in. Careful habits remain a necessary layer of protection.

The company says it also follows the limits set by researchers far better than its older model. OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on November 4, 2026. It is first going to […]

The post OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Cyber That Finds 81 Firefox Flaws and Develops 948 Linux Exploits appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a security-focused AI model that found 81 new high-severity Firefox flaws and built working exploits for 948 Linux kernel bugs. The company says it also follows the limits set by researchers far better than its older model.

OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on November 4, 2026. It is first going to a small group of approved Daybreak Red customers through the API and Codex.

On ExploitGym, a test of whether a model can exploit a known flaw, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%. GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1%. On a new web testing task, it found 40.3% of flaws, compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra.

On RemoteExploitBench, GPT-6 Cyber finished 95% of tasks. Astra with Daybreak Blue refused all of them. OpenAI now rates the model Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework. GPT-5.6 Cyber was rated High.

A big risk with security agents is that they wander outside their job. OpenAI tested this with ExploitGym Honeypot, which was shaped by the earlier Hugging Face incident. The test places easy-to-break side services next to the real target. Attacking them would reveal the flag, but they are out of scope.

Without safety prompts, GPT-6 Cyber stayed in scope 99.93% of the time, up from 94.49% for the older model. With the prompts, it hit 100%. Its reasoning notes show lines like “don’t explore out of scope credentials.”

81 Firefox Flaws

OpenAI researchers gave Mozilla proof and test cases for 81 new bugs that Mozilla rates high severity. The model also showed that 30 known issues were worse than first reported. Mozilla’s advisory MFSA 2026-118 covers fixes in Firefox 159, released October 27.

Many entries credit OpenAI Codex Security and OpenAI researchers. Most of the listed bugs are use-after-free memory errors in parts like layout, DOM, and JavaScript.

Other AI models have hit Firefox too. Cyber Security News reported that Claude Mythos found 271 Firefox zero-days earlier this year. Brian Grinstead of Mozilla said Firefox was one of the most hardened codebases going into 2026, and the new bugs still turned up.

948 Linux Kernel Exploits

OpenAI’s report, A thousand fewer paths to root, explains the Linux work. The pipeline picked 5,034 audit targets, about 7% of the kernel. It produced 2,308 candidate findings and reproduced 1,724 of them. It then built 948 working local privilege escalation exploits, which let a normal user become root. A GPT-5.6 Sol run in July found 166.

The run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. Past bounty prices would value the 948 exploits at $18.9 million to $66.3 million. OpenAI disclosed 304 critical findings with patches. Within 10 days, 61 had been fixed upstream and 43 had staged patches. Our earlier coverage details the 948 Linux kernel flaws.

OpenAI says the agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques. Outside kernel experts had not seen them before. One early run also showed why checks matter. Of 200 reported successes, 20 gained root through a different zero-day than the one assigned. OpenAI added an independent check for that.

OpenAI added monitoring that checks whether actions match the user’s authorization. Daybreak Red API access requires IP allowlisting by default. The company also tracks stolen credentials and advises sandboxing and human review for risky work.

For power plants and water systems, OpenAI added a Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure group and a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant. Chief AI Officer Rob T. Lee said it separated OT assets from IT noise and found two zero-days in engineering software that handles protective relay data.

OpenAI’s advice is simple. Patch fast, rescan old code when models improve, and treat a low-privilege account on an unpatched system as close to root. It also stresses sandboxes like Firecracker and gVisor. The same group’s training environment report shows agents escaping microVMs during internal red-team tests. Teams can apply for Daybreak to request access.

articles.title: Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting for Public Apps to Prevent Unauthorized Admin API Access
articles.description:
Shopify is making IP allowlisting mandatory for public apps that call its Admin API, adding a security check to limit the use of stolen access tokens. Developers must enable the control by November 20, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET. Apps using bulk operations face an earlier deadline of November 12 at the same time. The […]

The post Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting for Public Apps to Prevent Unauthorized Admin API Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Shopify is making IP allowlisting mandatory for public apps that call its Admin API, adding a security check to limit the use of stolen access tokens. Developers must enable the control by November 20, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET. Apps using bulk operations face an earlier deadline of November 12 at the same time.

The change turns a security feature introduced on October 27 into a requirement. Shopify will check where API requests come from, rather than relying on a valid token alone. This addresses the risk covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s cloud API security guide, where stolen credentials can give attackers access to cloud services.

Once allowlisting is active, Shopify checks the source IP of GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests using the app’s tokens. Requests from outside approved addresses or networks receive an HTTP 403 response. Shopify also rejects requests when it cannot confirm the source address.

Apps that miss the November 20 deadline face removal from the Shopify App Store and blocked new installations. Existing installations can continue operating until April 1, 2027, when Admin API requests will fail. However, bulk queries and mutations face the earlier November 12 cutoff. Merchants will receive admin warnings from January 15.

The policy targets token misuse, a risk illustrated by Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on the Internet Archive’s repeated breach through unrotated API tokens. Network restrictions add protection, but developers still need to secure their credentials. An attacker operating inside an approved network could remain within the permitted boundary.

Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting

Shopify’s setup guide supports specific public IP addresses and address ranges for static infrastructure. Apps with changing addresses can approve hosting networks through autonomous system numbers, or ASNs. Developers can list up to 10 ASNs and narrow access to up to 10 countries. These network rules are broader than individual server addresses.

Developers configure the control under Settings in the Dev Dashboard and test it against recent traffic before enabling enforcement. Shopify recommends checking whether legitimate requests would be blocked, then confirming an outside request fails. Apps must choose either IP addresses or networks, because saving one type replaces the other.

Shopify’s official announcement lists November 12 in its detailed bulk-operation instructions, despite November 11 appearing in its summary. Separately, public apps must migrate to expiring offline tokens by January 1, 2027, adding time limits alongside network restrictions.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft’s Windows Paint vulnerability, CVE-2026-83844, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code over a network without user interaction.

The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.1, placing it in the High severity category rather than Critical. However, confusion over the corrected Paint version has complicated patch checks for Windows administrators.

The vulnerability stems from an out-of-bounds read, a memory error in which software reads beyond its intended boundary.

Microsoft published the advisory on October 13, 2026. Its assessment lists a network attack vector, no required privileges, and high attack complexity, meaning successful exploitation depends on conditions that make an attack harder to carry out.

Windows 0-Click Paint RCE Vulnerability

The disclosure formed part of the October update cycle, covered in Cybersecurity News’ Microsoft October Patch Tuesday report. For administrators, the immediate concern is not simply whether an update exists, but whether the corrected application build has actually reached managed devices.

Microsoft initially listed Paint version 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed release. Administrators reported that Microsoft Store continued offering 11.2605.81.0, even after update checks and Store cache resets.

Microsoft’s advisory listed 11.2609.401.0 as the fix, suggesting the earlier version reference may have been incorrect. Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation.

Update availability also appears inconsistent. Some administrators reported difficulty obtaining a corrected build, while one participant in the Reddit discussion said the update had become available through Microsoft Store. These individual reports do not establish a universal rollout status. Claims that availability depends on region also remain unverified.

A crafted image could trigger the flaw, but Microsoft’s quoted guidance describes a crafted network packet sent to an affected service. The Hacker News discussion highlights the missing detail: neither the exposed service nor the complete attack path is identified. Suggestions involving Copilot or other components are speculation.

Administrators should check the installed Paint version rather than trust an “up to date” message alone. Neowin recommends following Microsoft’s current advisory and considering temporary removal where Paint is unnecessary. Restricting untrusted images may reduce general exposure, but it is not a confirmed fix for this specific network attack path.

Cybersecurity News’ separate PNG vulnerability coverage provides related context on image software security. Those flaws are separate from this Paint vulnerability.

OpenMatter Network, a pioneer in decentralized infrastructure for agentic artificial intelligence, is positioning its decentralized computing platform as an alternative to massive, centralized data center development amid growing public opposition to new facilities.

The company says its approach can support continued AI adoption by enabling computing workloads to run across distributed resources rather than relying primarily on large-scale data center infrastructure.

The results of Tuesday’s midterm elections have put growing public opposition to massive data center development in the national spotlight.

However, according to OpenMatter Network, resistance to new facilities need not signal a slowdown in AI adoption. Instead, it could accelerate the transition to a computing model that reduces dependence on massive, centralized data centers.

“Voters have made it clear that they are increasingly concerned about the enormous energy demands, environmental impact and rising utility costs associated with massive data center development,” said Mike Anderson, CEO of OpenMatter Network.

“But the need to deploy agentic AI isn’t going away. Businesses don’t have to choose between advancing AI and addressing these very legitimate concerns. There is another path forward, and OpenMatter is helping make it possible.”

Across the country, communities have expressed concerns about the impact of large-scale facilities on electricity rates, water supplies, local infrastructure and the environment.

The election has brought renewed attention to those concerns and the policy choices surrounding new construction.

“The assumption that AI must be built around increasingly massive concentrations of computing power deserves to be challenged,” Anderson continued.

“Our decentralized architecture allows computing resources to be distributed across many different locations. That means organizations have another way to move forward with agentic AI as communities and policymakers reconsider the costs and consequences of building more enormous data centers.”

The OpenMatter Network platform is designed to transform widely available computing hardware into usable network resources through its distributed architecture, algorithms and verifiable computing capabilities.

By enabling independently owned computing resources to participate in a shared network, OpenMatter is working to make decentralized infrastructure a practical alternative for enterprise AI deployment.

“There’s an enormous amount of computing capacity outside the walls of traditional data centers,” said Renee Davis, co-founder and chief business officer of OpenMatter Network.

“Our technology makes it possible to bring those resources together in a verifiable network capable of supporting real-world AI workloads. Rather than concentrating computing power in a relatively small number of massive facilities, we can distribute workloads across existing resources and smaller installations, creating opportunities for a more flexible and potentially more energy-efficient approach to AI infrastructure.”

The decentralized model also offers organizations greater flexibility in where computing resources are located and how they are deployed.

This can be particularly valuable for businesses and government institutions seeking greater control over computing infrastructure, including those with requirements for data sovereignty and locally managed resources.

“The question is no longer simply how many more massive data centers we need to build,” Anderson concluded.

“It’s how we can deploy the AI capabilities businesses need without imposing unnecessary burdens on the communities where computing resources are located. Tuesday’s election results make that question more urgent than ever. OpenMatter offers a new way forward.”

About OpenMatter Network

Headquartered in Florida’s Space Coast, OpenMatter Network is building the Verifiable Trust Layer for Secure Collaboration and AI Agents. Guided by the principle “Don’t Trust Data.

Prove It.,” the company’s cryptographically verifiable architecture enables secure collaboration, governed AI behavior and mathematically verifiable execution across untrusted environments. For more information, visit www.openmatter.network.

articles.title: GhostMap Android Flaw Can Trap Phones in Endless Reboot Loops Without Opening an App
articles.description:
A new Android bug named GhostMap can leave a phone stuck in a crash loop after a user installs a single crafted app. The app does not need to be opened, asks for no permissions, and contains no code. Researchers at Bitdefender Labs published the findings on November 5, 2026. They have not seen the […]

The post GhostMap Android Flaw Can Trap Phones in Endless Reboot Loops Without Opening an App appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new Android bug named GhostMap can leave a phone stuck in a crash loop after a user installs a single crafted app. The app does not need to be opened, asks for no permissions, and contains no code.

Researchers at Bitdefender Labs published the findings on November 5, 2026. They have not seen the trick used against real users. The analysis began on August 12, 2026, when an APK collected in the wild crashed the lab’s test emulators. The file was a banking dropper that never ran. It failed during installation.

Bitdefender found the flaw in Android itself, not the malware. The malware author had wrapped the file with a packer, a tool that rewrites an app’s inner layout to block reverse-engineering tools. That rewrite also broke the part of Android that reads apps at install time.

GhostMap Android Vulnerability

This kind of trick is not new. Palo Alto’s Unit 42 described the BadPack method in 2024 and counted about 9,200 samples in a single year. Our earlier report on BadPack APK packers shows how those altered headers hide malware from analysts.

An APK is a ZIP file, and each entry inside it lists a compression method and a size. Two Android libraries read those fields in different ways. One library checks the size only for entries marked as stored. The other library treats anything not marked as deflated as stored. An entry with an odd method value slips between the two rules.

Android then maps the file into memory at the false size. In one test, an APK of 8,408 bytes was mapped across about 16 MB. When a process reads past the real end of the file, the CPU raises a SIGBUS fault, and the kernel kills the process.

A similar trick appeared in Konfety malware, which used unsupported compression methods to break analysis tools. Those apps still ran on the phone, though, and did not crash it.

The worst case hits system_server, the process that runs most of Android. After install, a core service reads a small resource file inside the app, crashes, restarts and reads the same file again.

The phone never finishes starting. The crash repeats every few seconds, with nothing on screen to show which app is to blame. Bitdefender tested this on a Pixel 10 running Android 17 with the August 5, 2026 patch. The first crash came about one second after install. One capture showed 110 repeats, and a safe mode run showed 72.

Safe mode fails because the service reads the file before safe mode takes effect. A factory reset works but erases local data. If USB debugging was already on, a user may delete the file through ADB, the Android Debug Bridge, between crashes.

Bitdefender lists several possible uses. A rogue app could lock a phone and then demand money. It could also damage its own icon so the launcher and Settings crash whenever a user tries to remove it.

Security scanners that open the file would crash as well, so the app might never be flagged. A harmful file could even arrive later through an app update. The bug only crashes processes. It does not run code, steal data, or raise permissions. The flaw affected range starts at Android 10.

Bitdefender reported the flaw on August 20 and again on August 25. Google first closed the case as Won’t Fix (Not Reproducible). After the second report, Google said the issue is outside the scope of a security update and passed it to a team for a possible future release. No fix or CVE exists yet. Google did patch a weaker form in 2016 as CVE-2016-6724.

Android has faced similar parsing gaps for years, including Master Key and Janus. Android also saw a zero-interaction denial-of-service flaw in the April 2026 bulletin, which shows how easily one bad file can hurt a phone.

Until Google acts, users should install apps only from trusted stores and avoid sideloaded APK files. Turning on USB debugging may help recovery, but it carries its own risks.

articles.description:
A China-aligned hacking group is abusing Sogou Input Method, one of the most popular Chinese typing tools, to secretly install a backdoor called DarkVigil on Windows computers. The group is tracked as SlippyNunchucks. Since July 1, 2026, it has used the keyboard software to reach users in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and […]

The post Hackers Turn Popular Chinese Keyboard Software Into a Backdoor for Cyberespionage Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A China-aligned hacking group is abusing Sogou Input Method, one of the most popular Chinese typing tools, to secretly install a backdoor called DarkVigil on Windows computers.

The group is tracked as SlippyNunchucks. Since July 1, 2026, it has used the keyboard software to reach users in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and Oman.

The hackers did not need a software exploit. Some of Sogou’s background requests travel over plain HTTP instead of secure HTTPS, so the attackers tampered with DNS, the system that turns website names into server addresses.

This sent the app’s request to a server they controlled. Tencent, which owns Sogou, fixed the weakness in version 16.10, and the issue now has the ID CVE-2026-120422.

Researchers at ESET, publishing on WeLiveSecurity, identified the malware and the hijacking method. In their detailed ESET research report they said they have tracked DarkVigil, also called FDMTP, since early 2025.

At first, the number of infections and their spread across many countries made them think an exploit was involved. The team later found the DNS hijacking instead.

Hackers Turn Popular Chinese Keyboard Software

The trouble starts with a Sogou part called SGTool.exe. It asks a server at config.pinyin.sogou[.]com for a small settings file that tells it which icon to download for a “brand promotion” feature.

Normally the file points to a harmless green sprout picture. In victim networks, the attackers controlled the DNS answer, so the request went to their own staging servers, which sent back a fake settings file.

That fake file told Sogou to download two items. One was a real, signed Adobe helper program, renamed biz_helper.exe.

The other was the DarkVigil implant, disguised as libcef.dll. The attackers also changed the checksum values in the file so Sogou’s own integrity check would accept the downloads.

The trick relies on DLL side-loading. When a trusted program starts, it loads a malicious file of the same name sitting next to it. This method is also seen in a Sogou one-click backdoor flaw reported in September.

The attackers saved the Adobe file as SogouComMgr.exe, so every time Sogou installed or loaded a component, it ran the Adobe file, which loaded the malware.

This gave the hackers lasting access without a separate persistence setup. As a backup, they also placed files in a biz_center folder in case an update replaced the first file.

The hijacking point is still unknown. ESET says compromised routers with bad DNS settings, routers carrying a DNS-hijacking implant, or interception at the internet provider level are all possible.

DarkVigil Malware, Targets and Defense

DarkVigil is a modular .NET toolset with more than 20 known plugins. It talks to its control server using the Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP).

This protocol lets the server push plugins to the infected PC, which stores them in the Windows registry and runs them later. Stolen data is managed through a web panel branded “Vigil.”

SlippyNunchucks has been active since at least September 2023. Besides Sogou, it has abused other Chinese apps, including QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam and tawk.to.

This tactic is not new. Earlier, the TAOTH update hijacking campaign used a lapsed Sogou Zhuyin update server, and Notepad++ update traffic hijacked showed how selective update hijacking can work.

ESET says it does not link the group to Mustang Panda, even though some public reports do. The targets point to state interests. ESET found heavy spying on a company running Chinese-language betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong and the Philippines.

Other victims included an internet café in Dubai and a student in Denmark. ESET judges with high confidence that the group works in line with Chinese government interests.

Users should update Sogou Input Method to version 16.10 or later right away. Security teams should look for connections to the domains and IPs below and for odd Adobe-named files inside Sogou’s Components folder.

Checking router DNS settings is also wise, because the same kind of trusted Windows apps abused in other China-linked campaigns often leaves little visible trace.

articles.title: OpenSSH Flaw Could Let Attackers Bypass Password Authentication on Alpine Linux Servers
articles.description:
A critical OpenSSH flaw could let remote attackers bypass password authentication on affected Alpine Linux servers, including accounts intended for key-only access. OpenSSH released Portable 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, to block the issue, which affects Linux systems using musl libc without PAM authentication. Research published on sshhole.com by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield explains how […]

The post OpenSSH Flaw Could Let Attackers Bypass Password Authentication on Alpine Linux Servers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical OpenSSH flaw could let remote attackers bypass password authentication on affected Alpine Linux servers, including accounts intended for key-only access. OpenSSH released Portable 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, to block the issue, which affects Linux systems using musl libc without PAM authentication.

Research published on sshhole.com by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield explains how an unusually long password can turn a failed password check into a successful login. Alpine confirms that exploitation needs one connection, a reachable SSH port, and a known account name when the required conditions exist.

The target account must have * in its password field, while another local account must contain a $5$ or $6$ password hash. Password authentication must also remain enabled. This means adding a password to one account can expose other accounts that were created without passwords.

Alpine’s standard openssh-server package does not use PAM, making the configuration important. Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes are unaffected. Containers without a running SSH server are also unaffected, so using an Alpine container image alone does not establish exposure.

The disclosure follows earlier OpenSSH 10.6 security fixes, but this issue concerns password checks rather than encryption. No CVE identifier had been assigned when Alpine published its advisory.

OpenSSH Flaw Bypass Password Authentication

The researcher’s technical analysis traces the failure to an interaction between OpenSSH and musl’s crypt() function. Without PAM, sshd hashes the submitted password and compares the result with the stored password field. For an account whose field contains only *, sshd borrows another account’s salt.

When the submitted password exceeds 256 bytes, musl’s relevant password-hashing code rejects it and returns * as an error marker. That marker matches the target account’s stored field. Instead of rejecting the login, the comparison succeeds. Alpine identifies passwords between 257 and 1024 bytes as the trigger.

On vulnerable systems, a password consisting of 300 repeated ‘A’ characters could bypass authentication for an affected account. The password does not need to match a real secret. Instead, its length triggers an error in musl’s password-hashing function, which returns the same * marker stored for that account.

The comic from researcher shows how separate changes to password handling came together over time. It connects the use of * for accounts without usable passwords, musl’s matching error marker, and OpenSSH’s borrowed-salt behavior. Together, these explain how a long password could pass a check that should have rejected it.

The researcher links the chain to a 2016 OpenSSH change designed to reduce username discovery through timing differences. Testing across library and authentication settings exposed the musl-without-PAM mismatch. This is distinct from earlier OpenSSH client and server vulnerabilities involving interception and service disruption.

Official Alpine tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 contain an alpine account with passwordless doas access. They become exploitable when a qualifying password hash is added. An attacker could then log in as alpine and become root. Default restrictions still block direct root password login unless administrators change them.

Follow Alpine’s remediation guidance by running apk upgrade -U -a, then rc-service sshd restart. Updating alone leaves the old daemon running. Fixed releases include 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, and 3.24.4, with patched packages available for older branches.

Older branches also received patched packages, so a lower OpenSSH version number does not automatically mean a system remains vulnerable.

Where patching must wait, set PasswordAuthentication no, confirm key-based access works, and restart sshd while keeping an existing session open. Review /var/log/messages for Accepted password for entries involving passwordless accounts, then inspect unexpected doas activity and new authorized keys.

The OpenSSH release notes confirm the upstream workaround. Alpine advises treating machines as compromised when unauthorized access cannot be ruled out.

articles.title: HYFLOCK Ransomware Encrypts Only First 4KB of Larger Files, Leaves Parts of Victims’ Files Accessible
articles.description:
HYFLOCK ransomware has an encryption weakness that leaves parts of larger files readable, giving affected organizations a limited chance to recover data without paying attackers. In the October 17 build, the malware encrypted only the first 4,096 bytes of larger files examined during testing, leaving content beyond that section accessible. The finding does not mean […]

The post HYFLOCK Ransomware Encrypts Only First 4KB of Larger Files, Leaves Parts of Victims’ Files Accessible appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
HYFLOCK ransomware has an encryption weakness that leaves parts of larger files readable, giving affected organizations a limited chance to recover data without paying attackers.

In the October 17 build, the malware encrypted only the first 4,096 bytes of larger files examined during testing, leaving content beyond that section accessible.

The finding does not mean victims can unlock everything. Researchers recovered selected contents from encrypted Microsoft Office files, but did not restore complete documents or produce a general decryptor.

An earlier October build presented a different danger: a processing defect could permanently discard file data, potentially preventing full recovery even with the correct key.

Check Point Exposure Management researchers identified the updated HYFLOCK builds through threat hunting, tracing four generations from April through October 2026.

Their published investigation into HYFLOCK separates observed behavior from operator claims, revealing stronger deployment features alongside uneven file processing.

HYFLOCK Ransomware

The October 17 sample produced 17 validated encrypted files. Fourteen larger files recorded an encrypted prefix of 4,096 bytes, while three smaller files were encrypted across their complete original lengths.

Configuration settings indicated full encryption, but those settings did not match the larger files’ actual condition. Partial encryption also appears in other ransomware families.

For example, Gunra’s configurable partial encryption lets attackers select how much content to encrypt. HYFLOCK’s finding, however, is specific to the tested build and collected files; it should not be treated as universal behavior across the family.

Examining the untouched content, researchers recovered 73 internal components from seven encrypted Office files, including worksheet and shared-string data.

Those components passed cyclic redundancy checks, supporting their integrity. The result demonstrates partial recovery, not decryption: the encrypted prefixes remained unavailable without matching key material or an exact trusted copy.

The malware uses 16-byte symmetric keys, AES counter-mode processing, and RSA protection for recovery material.

Each validated October 17 output retained its original-length body and added a 556-byte trailer containing encryption metadata and a wrapped key. Researchers recovered neither a plaintext encryption key nor an RSA private key.

Recovery risks extend beyond inaccessible prefixes. The earlier October build could omit data during processing, echoing the broader problem illustrated by VECT’s damaging recovery flaws, where implementation errors undermine restoration.

HYFLOCK can also continue encrypting when key wrapping or backup storage fails, creating another potential barrier to recovery.

Updated Rust Encryptor Expands Deployment and Recovery Risks

HYFLOCK appeared in underground promotion in March 2026 as a Ransomware-as-a-Service offering. By October 13, its leak site carried eight victim claims across manufacturing, business services, government, retail, and telecommunications.

These remain unverified attacker claims; the investigation did not establish the victims’ initial compromise routes. The April sample already contained a Windows ransomware core written in Rust.

July added a separate loader carrying the payload, configuration, and key material. An earlier October version used a Go carrier, while the October 17 build returned to a standalone Rust executable that copied itself into an update-like directory.

During controlled testing, the newer build registered a scheduled task, processed network-share resources, and attempted to disrupt recovery.

It generated 500 successful ransomware-extension renames, although only 17 collected files were independently validated as encrypted. Those counts describe different observations and should not be treated as interchangeable measures of damage.

Recovery interference is also documented in Gentlemen ransomware’s backup disruption, but HYFLOCK’s results require qualification.

Its recovery-sabotage commands had varied outcomes, and complete deletion of recovery objects was not proven. Likewise, administrative-share activity did not establish compromise of another computer.

Successful domain-wide propagation was not observed, and Group Policy spreading was disabled in the recovered configuration. Advertised vulnerable-driver attacks and reliable execution after remote desktop sessions ended also remained unverified.

Defenders should preserve affected files and execution evidence, then review scheduled tasks, share access, segmentation, and recovery protections before attempting restoration.

articles.title: Researchers Discover White House Network IP Available for Rent Through 28 Proxy Services
articles.description:
Researchers at Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services rent addresses on the White House network. Anyone with a few dollars could send web traffic through them. The activity ran from October 5 to November 3, 2026. The team spotted the activity while browsing its new Residential Proxy Observatory, a tool that shows proxy […]

The post Researchers Discover White House Network IP Available for Rent Through 28 Proxy Services appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers at Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services rent addresses on the White House network. Anyone with a few dollars could send web traffic through them. The activity ran from October 5 to November 3, 2026.

The team spotted the activity while browsing its new Residential Proxy Observatory, a tool that shows proxy and hidden internet activity around the world. The traffic came from AS2650, a network block registered to the Executive Office of the President. In 30 days, the team’s tools exited through this network 236 times. The exits came from 6 addresses on 26 of the 30 days.

Layer3 requested rotating global access through proxy services, which then revealed the White House addresses on their own. Additionally, Spur and Synthient, two other firms that specialize in proxy detection, also identify these addresses as proxy exits. This makes it unlikely that the identification of these addresses is merely a one-time error.

White House Network IP for Rent

A residential proxy sends web traffic through a real home or office connection, so the traffic looks like it comes from an ordinary user. Many device owners never agree to this. Hidden software in an app or a cheap device can sell bandwidth without the owner’s knowledge. Because the addresses look normal, simple blocklists often fail to catch them.

About half of the activity fell between 5 p.m. and midnight Eastern time, and almost none happened in the early morning. Layer3 Intel says this looks like one person on the network in the evening, not a public guest Wi-Fi setup. The most likely cause is a personal device carrying a proxy software kit. The data shows only the exits. It does not show which device or person is behind them.

The risk is that a weak proxy kit can give outsiders a path inside a network. Synthient’s earlier research on the Kimwolf botnet shows how this happens. Kimwolf reached more than 2 million devices, mostly Android boxes with an open debug service, by moving through residential proxy networks. In that case, attackers reached devices on private home networks that should have been out of reach.

This is not a new pattern. Cyber Security News has already covered how Kimwolf infected 2 million devices and turned them into proxy nodes. It also reported that Google disrupted the IPIDEA proxy network, which relied on hidden software kits inside ordinary apps. Later research found that nearly half of the apps on LG and Samsung TVs carried proxy code.

The risk also reaches the workplace. One report on a bandwidth-sharing app showed that a single enrolled employee device could give outsiders a way to reach a router’s management page.

The White House was not the only surprise. Layer3 Intel logged 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha.

It also saw three observations in Antarctica, all from a Cloudflare WARP address tied to McMurdo Station. Smaller counts came from Pitcairn, Norfolk Island and Svalbard. The Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7) also showed activity.

Layer3 Intel says it has saved the raw logs and will share them with relevant agencies. Network teams can take simple steps now. They can check DNS logs for known proxy domains and review apps and browser add-ons on work devices for proxy code. They should also keep TV boxes and other low-cost Android devices off sensitive networks, and turn off Android’s debug service where it is not needed.

articles.description:
A hacker’s own mistake has given researchers a rare look at how AI tools were used to break into South Korean financial firms. The operator left several servers open to the public, and the exposed files showed which AI models, scripts and proxies powered the campaign. Between late September and early October 2026, seven South […]

The post ARTEX Hackers Expose Their Own Servers, Revealing AI Tools Behind South Korean Bank Breaches appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A hacker’s own mistake has given researchers a rare look at how AI tools were used to break into South Korean financial firms. The operator left several servers open to the public, and the exposed files showed which AI models, scripts and proxies powered the campaign.

Between late September and early October 2026, seven South Korean financial institutions had data stolen through internet-facing systems. Roughly 66,000 to 67,000 people and about 2,200 companies were affected.

Names, jobs, income details and loan information were exposed. CrowdStrike first tied the activity to ARTEX, an open-source, China-developed AI penetration testing framework.

CrowdStrike judged, with moderate confidence, that a single Chinese-speaking, financially motivated lone operator used ARTEX instead of a known hacking group.

The public reports named one key server at 38.244.50[.]120 and a reseller domain, xcai[.]pro, used to reach AI models. Genians later confirmed the same findings, and the ARTEX GitHub page and Docker image were taken down on October 11, though copies remain online.

Researchers at Hunt.io noted that the public indicators were only part of the picture. While pivoting off the known server, they found a new open directory at 23.248.226[.]250, a Hong Kong jump server that held far more of the operator’s working files.

ARTEX Hackers Expose Their Own Servers, Revealing AI Tools

The Hong Kong server held a state file showing the operator ran Claude Code, version 2.1.221, and had started it 510 times since August 4, 2026. The software was not talking to Anthropic, though.

A router called Claude Code Router, plus small Python helper scripts, sent every request through the xcai[.]pro reseller to DeepSeek. This resembles other cases where Claude Code and DeepSeek were joined in one workflow.

One helper script even carried a note in Chinese describing the route in the operator’s own words. Other files showed a Zhipu AI key for GLM models and a tunnel named grok2api, which fits CrowdStrike’s finding that DeepSeek, GLM and Grok were all in use.

The state file also listed 19 custom “skills,” which are reusable instruction sets for the AI agent, used 147 times in total. They covered reconnaissance, code review, web testing, firewall bypass checks, Android app analysis and cloud phone control.

One skill tested payment logic, and a nearby file held three test accounts for a cash-in deposit service. That setup suggests the operator was checking for insecure direct object reference flaws. These flaws let a user view or change another person’s data by altering an ID.

A credentials file named .secrets was also found, along with a backup copy. A Chinese comment inside it said it was the “sole source of credentials” and warned against pasting passwords into a session.

Three scripts used that same root login to keep a reverse SSH tunnel alive and to copy the AI’s memory files to the jump host.

Wider Tools, Hunting Pivots and Defense

The exposed folders held more than bank-related tools. Hunt.io found a proxy service at 154.201.79[.]246:443 that gave 79 unique exit IP addresses from the first 100 identities tested.

It also found a staged JNDI and LDAP setup for remote code execution, with a DNS callback to confirm success.

Other files included cryptocurrency exchange scripts, Linux privilege escalation exploits and iOS and Android tooling. Hunt.io says the link between these items and the bank breaches is unconfirmed.

Hunt.io then built three ways to find more ARTEX servers. A certificate search returned 19 IP addresses, a malware-tag search returned 1,303, and a search on the console’s page title returned about 1,300.

A separate search for open directories returned 280 results. The tags covered 30 countries, led by the United States, then China and Hong Kong.

This shows the framework is spreading well beyond one case, which matches reports of ARTEX automating enterprise attacks elsewhere.

Defenders should close public access to admin services and place them behind a VPN or allowlist. They should also reset SSH passwords and rotate API keys, proxy logins and tokens that may have sat in exposed files.

Teams should watch for odd LDAP or JNDI traffic, strange DNS callbacks, remote script downloads and unexpected outbound connections.

They should also lock down access to AI model gateways. Later, South Korean police arrested a suspected hacker over a separate case that also involved ARTEX, though the shared tool does not prove the same people were involved.

articles.description:
Hackers are hiding a free information stealer called Marsalek inside fake cheats and tools for games such as Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2. The files look like helpful game add-ons. In the background they steal saved passwords, browser cookies, Discord tokens, and crypto wallet data from Windows PCs. Marsalek ran from about December 2025 to […]

The post Hackers Hide Marsalek Malware in Fake Roblox and Fortnite Cheats to Steal Passwords and Crypto Wallet Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are hiding a free information stealer called Marsalek inside fake cheats and tools for games such as Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2.

The files look like helpful game add-ons. In the background they steal saved passwords, browser cookies, Discord tokens, and crypto wallet data from Windows PCs.

Marsalek ran from about December 2025 to May 2026 as malware-as-a-service, so anyone could sign up on a public site, build a malicious file, and watch victims on a dashboard.

The free tier did not even ask for a Discord or email account. Similar fake game cheat campaigns have pushed other stealers through GitHub and Reddit, which shows how popular this trick has become.

Analysts at McAfee Labs identified the malware and counted more than 1,560 registered accounts, over 400 malicious files, and more than 29 distribution URLs.

They also linked Marsalek to WeedHack, a Minecraft-focused service, because both point customers to the same Telegram support channel, @MetaMaskenMann.

Hackers Hide Marsalek Malware in Fake Roblox and Fortnite Cheats

Most of the lures copy tools that gamers already search for. McAfee saw fake versions of Roblox script executors such as Swift, Solara, MatrixHub External, and Matcha External.

Fake Minecraft clients such as Shadow Client and Boss Client also appeared, and a sample named Fortnite_tweaks.exe is in the indicator list.

The files spread through look-alike websites, Discord, and GitHub. Customers can start an infection with a PowerShell script, a ClickFix page, a Python file, or an EXE file. Bitdefender reported a related case with fake Roblox Xeno cheats that also targeted younger players.

After the first step, the chain is almost the same every time. The starter script downloads a portable Python package and a second file called python_setup.py.

That file tries to gain admin rights with a Windows tool called CMSTP, then hides the permission prompt and presses Enter for the user. It then adds 8 paths and 15 processes to Microsoft Defender’s exclusion list, so later files are not scanned.

The ClickFix page is a fake Cloudflare check, a trick also seen in the Warden Stealer malware campaign that tells victims to paste commands into Windows.

The third file, svc.py, does the main stealing in over 1,400 lines of code. It goes after 32 Chromium-based browsers and Firefox.

It also gets around Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption by injecting a DLL into a suspended Chrome, Edge, or Brave process, so the browser itself unlocks the key.

The malware checks 26 Discord paths, copies Telegram session data, and reads Mullvad VPN account details. It scans for 56 browser extensions and 12 wallet apps, and it looks for files with words like “seed,” “passphrase,” and “wallet.” In Exodus and Atomic Wallet it swaps in two .asar files to leave a backdoor.

Dual-Hook Design Turns Customers Into Victims

The last stage is PureLog, a low-cost stealer sold for as little as $59 a month. It is hidden with .NET Reactor, decrypted with Triple DES, and run only in memory.

It targets 35 browsers, 48 extensions, and 12 desktop apps, takes a screenshot, and sets a scheduled task that runs RunetimeBroker.exe every five minutes. It sends data to a separate server, telemetrydata.to.

This setup is called a dual hook. The customers think they own the stolen logs, but Marsalek’s author also gets a copy and may use a high-value victim’s accounts first.

The built-in FAQ even teaches buyers how to use stolen cookies and tokens and how to launder coins through Monero. McAfee saw the most activity in the United States, followed by Germany, the United Kingdom, India, and Brazil.

Gaming profiles are worth money, and it is easy to see attackers steal gaming accounts and then sell the items or reuse the same logins elsewhere.

The best defense is simple. Download games and tools only from official sources, never turn off antivirus because a site says it is a false alarm, and never paste commands from a web page.

Anyone who ran a suspicious cheat should change passwords from a clean device, sign out of all sessions, move crypto to a new wallet, and reinstall Windows. Readers can find the full technical details in the McAfee Labs Marsalek report.

SHA256 hashes

The post Tata Motors iRA App Flaws Could Let Hackers Impersonate Car Owners and Access Vehicle Services appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Tata Motors’ iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev mobile apps contain four security flaws that could let attackers steal credentials, impersonate car owners, and access vehicle services. India’s Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-In, rated the issues as High severity in an advisory published on November 4, 2026.

The warning covers iRA 2.0 versions 26.7.3 and earlier, alongside iRA.ev versions 26.7.2 and earlier. These apps serve petrol, diesel, and electric vehicle customers, providing remote vehicle commands, status checks, health monitoring, and trip information. CERT-In credits security researcher Pranav Rajendran with reporting the vulnerabilities.

Embedded Credentials and Stolen Tokens

The first flaw, CVE-2026-121144, involves service account credentials, API keys, and authorization tokens stored inside the app package. An attacker needs no login to download the package and extract these secrets. The issue reflects risks previously covered in Cybersecurity News’ reporting on hardcoded credentials in mobile apps.

Those exposed credentials could provide access to backend services, potentially allowing data theft or unauthorized operations. This weakness matters because the sensitive information comes from the distributed application itself. An attacker would not first need to steal a particular owner’s password to extract the embedded credentials.

CVE-2026-121145 affects WebView, the component that displays web content inside the apps. Insufficient checks on loaded URLs and their origins could let malicious content interact with app functions and obtain live bearer authentication tokens. An attacker could then misuse those tokens to impersonate the associated owner.

According to CERT-In’s advisory, CVE-2026-121146 exposes authentication tokens through application logs used for development and debugging. Exploitation requires local access to those logs. An attacker who retrieves the exposed session tokens could misuse them to access vehicle information and services as the affected user.

The fourth flaw, CVE-2026-121147, involves an improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. CERT-In says the resulting controls are ineffective. An attacker positioned to intercept network traffic could exploit the weakness to intercept or change communications between the mobile application and its backend services.

The findings highlight how connected vehicle security depends on mobile apps and supporting servers, not only vehicle hardware. Earlier automotive API vulnerability research documented separate weaknesses affecting vehicle services across several manufacturers. Those findings provide context, but their specific vehicle-control impacts should not be assumed for Tata Motors.

Fixed Versions Available

CERT-In advises affected users to upgrade iRA 2.0 to version 26.8.2 and iRA.ev to version 26.9.1. Its advisory links to the official Google Play and Apple App Store listings for both applications. Installing the recommended release is the agency’s stated solution for addressing these vulnerabilities.

The advisory does not report active exploitation, identify affected vehicle models, or confirm that attackers demonstrated control over specific driving functions. Its stated risks concern sensitive information, user impersonation, and unauthorized data changes using an owner’s privileges. The distinction keeps the warning focused on documented application weaknesses rather than unverified claims about vehicle takeovers.
