articles.description:
A single operator in Taiwan built a team of 12 AI agents and used it to attack hundreds of organizations in 11 countries. The campaign hit emergency services, banks, universities, and military systems. It led to confirmed theft of medical data and personal records. The setup, named BOSSAI, shows how one person with rented GPUs […]

The post One Hacker Uses 12 AI Agents to Breach Taiwan’s Emergency Services and Steal Sensitive Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A single operator in Taiwan built a team of 12 AI agents and used it to attack hundreds of organizations in 11 countries. The campaign hit emergency services, banks, universities, and military systems. It led to confirmed theft of medical data and personal records.

The setup, named BOSSAI, shows how one person with rented GPUs and open-source tools can now run a campaign that once needed a full team.

Some of the agents wrote code, some scanned websites, and some carried out the attacks. The operator sat in the middle and passed results between them.

Analysts at Acronis Threat Research Unit identified the campaign after finding what looked like a misconfigured development server. It turned out to be a full attack platform with more than 90,000 files, about 9GB of logs, chat histories, exploit tools, and victim data.

Acronis calls this kind of actor an “AI-augmented threat,” because the activity looks like a state-backed group but comes from one person, as Acronis explains in its full report.

One Hacker Uses 12 AI Agents

The mesh had 12 agents, but only nine were active. Builder agents such as Grok, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex set up servers, DNS, and proxies.

Attack agents such as Hermes, Cursor, Trae, and CyberStrike scanned targets and wrote exploits. Hermes did most of the work, with about 95 sessions and 18,311 messages.

The agents did not talk to each other. The operator copied output from one tool and pasted it into the next. In one case, a scanner called HalberdStrike checked a Taiwanese emergency-services site.

Hermes turned the findings into a report, and the operator pasted it into Cursor with the order to exploit the flaws. Cursor then carried out the attack.

The agents were linked to security tools through MCP servers, including HexStrike AI, a Kali Linux server, and a Ghidra bridge.

Earlier coverage of the HexStrike AI framework shows how this kind of tool lets AI models run scanners such as Nmap on their own. Attack traffic went out through proxies, and the main node ran on a server at 112[.]121[.]185[.]218.

The damage in Taiwan was serious. A Taipei fire-department patient-care platform exposed ECG readings, ambulance video, and vital signs from 2018, with no login needed.

Agents also pulled case records from a city 119 dispatch system, covering seven districts. Other victims included a lender with 16 SQL injection points and a fire-dispatch vendor whose database panel still used default root credentials.

Outside Taiwan, the agents collected about 206,800 residential phone records in Mexico. In Thailand they found 489 targets across 45 universities and pulled data from three of them.

Why the AI Agents Struggled and What It Means for Defenders

The campaign was far from smooth. Commercial models such as Grok 4.5 and MiniMax M3 refused to help with attacks and asked for proof of written authorization.

The operator then switched to local “abliterated” models, which have their safety rules stripped out. Those models were weaker and often made mistakes.

Hallucinations caused real problems. HalberdStrike flagged a failed connection as a “critical RCE,” and more than half of its high-severity findings were false positives.

Since the operator told the agents to work without asking questions, Hermes also walked away from a Honduran military system, judging it out of scope.

Still, the agents worked well where basic security was weak. Old open ports, unpatched Oracle databases, and default passwords were the easy wins.

Where login checks and filtering held, the agents failed. Acronis notes that hiding behind obscurity no longer helps when an agent can test hundreds of sites at once.

This fits a wider trend. Anthropic recently warned that AI agents can automate every stage of a cyberattack, though humans still pick targets.

The first large-scale AI-driven espionage case from 2025 showed Claude doing most of an intrusion with little human input.

Researchers have also seen agents try SQL injection and path traversal on their own when normal methods failed. Defenders should patch exposed databases, remove default credentials, and close old ports.

They should also put login checks in front of every API, including those that serve dispatch and medical data. The same agents that find flaws quickly will keep finding them until those basics are fixed.

Acronis also tied the activity to one person in Hualien City, Taiwan. The operator reused business branding, a GitHub account, and a home IP across both legitimate and attack servers. The researchers assess this with high confidence.

articles.title: Hackers Trick Mac Users Into Running Terminal Commands That Install Phexia Password-Stealing Malware
articles.description:
A macOS malware family called Phexia is spreading through fake web pages that talk Mac users into pasting a command into Terminal. Once the command runs, the malware quietly settles on the Mac, steals the login password, and copies browser data, keychain files, and password-manager extension data. The trick is known as ClickFix. A page […]

The post Hackers Trick Mac Users Into Running Terminal Commands That Install Phexia Password-Stealing Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A macOS malware family called Phexia is spreading through fake web pages that talk Mac users into pasting a command into Terminal.

Once the command runs, the malware quietly settles on the Mac, steals the login password, and copies browser data, keychain files, and password-manager extension data.

The trick is known as ClickFix. A page shows a fake verification or fix, and the user performs the dangerous step themselves. No software flaw is needed, so the usual protections have little to catch.

Phexia is sold to several criminal groups, which is why more infections keep appearing. Analysts at WithSecure identified and detailed the malware in a report published on November 4, 2026.

They say Phexia is a modular backdoor and information stealer that has been in use since at least late 2025. The firm has seen a growing number of infections since early 2026, which suggests more criminals are buying it.

Hackers Trick Mac Users Into Running Terminal Commands

In nearly every case WithSecure could examine, the infection started with a command typed into Terminal. The command used curl to download a shell script and sent it straight to bash.

The script was usually named update.sh, though script.sh, clear-cache.sh, and Terminal.sh also appeared. It was hosted on random-looking subdomains that changed between waves.

The team tied one July 6 infection to a typosquatted domain, which points to look-alike web addresses as a likely delivery route. The same trick has appeared in a fake CAPTCHA Mac campaign that also ended in password theft and cryptomining.

The script then runs an AppleScript dropper. The dropper writes a LaunchAgent into the user’s Library folder and sets it to restart whenever it stops.

The loader is stored as Base64 text inside that file, so no readable script sits on the disk. Builds from June to mid-September used a label of “com.” plus 16 lowercase letters. October builds switched to “com.Apple.” plus 16 letters, to look like a real Apple item.

The capital “A” gives it away, because genuine Apple labels use lowercase. After setup, the backdoor checks in with its server and asks for more modules.

A tool called dscl tests whether the entered login password is correct, and a fake “System Preferences” prompt can keep asking until the right one is typed.

The password is saved in a hidden file named .passphrase. WithSecure saw this happen anywhere from under a minute to about eight minutes after infection. Some checks began 22 hours later and repeated on following days.

With the password in hand, the stealer copies the data it wants. It reads browser “Safe Storage” keys for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi, and copies cookies, history, and saved login files.

It also takes LastPass and NordPass extension stores, the login keychain, and Safari cookies. Everything is zipped and uploaded to the command server and to a second server at 62.60.226[.]50 over plain HTTP.

The operators also install the XMRig Monero miner. They keep reinstalling it and changing mining pools and wallets. Similar password-grabbing tricks showed up in the MacSync macOS infostealer, so the method is clearly popular among Mac malware sellers.

Polygon Blockchain Hides the Command Server

The biggest recent change came in May 2026. Phexia began reading its server address from a smart contract on the Polygon blockchain, a method called EtherHiding.

The loader holds no fixed server name. It asks public Polygon endpoints for the current address and then requests its next module from that host.

The operator can swap in a new server by sending one blockchain transaction. Blocking a domain therefore does not remove the pointer, and the malware just looks up the next address.

WithSecure saw one contract used from June 14 to October 22. A different contract appeared on October 27 and resolved to dhsbdgs[.]icu.

Old infections did not move to new servers right away. Machines kept contacting an older domain for about a month after the contract changed.

When a Mac was infected again, two builds ran side by side, and the earlier one kept receiving tasks for more than 20 minutes. Defenders should therefore keep old indicators in their searches and check for several LaunchAgents on one Mac.

File hashes help little here, because the malware uses built-in Apple tools and every build is obfuscated differently. WithSecure recommends watching behavior instead.

Look for Terminal sessions that download scripts and then launch osascript, LaunchAgents that decode Base64 into osascript, Polygon lookups from script processes, and dscl password checks.

Affected users should isolate the Mac, remove every malicious LaunchAgent, reset passwords from a clean device, revoke sessions, and review password-manager and wallet exposure.

The newer ClickFix abuse of Script Editor shows how fast attackers change the entry point, and the Atomic Stealer ClickFix campaign shows the same social trick. Users should never paste commands from a website into Terminal.

articles.description:

The campaign targets Israeli organizations and turns an ordinary tax-document request into a possible entry point for unauthorized access. Observed since September 2026, the activity targets a business task familiar […]

The post Hackers Use Fake Government Websites and CAPTCHA Checks to Deliver SimpleHelp Remote Access Software appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers are impersonating the Israel Tax Authority through phishing emails, fake government websites, and CAPTCHA-style checks to trick employees into running SimpleHelp remote access software.

The campaign targets Israeli organizations and turns an ordinary tax-document request into a possible entry point for unauthorized access.

Observed since September 2026, the activity targets a business task familiar to finance, accounting, and administrative staff.

Instead of receiving a tax document, recipients download an archive containing an executable. The attack reflects broader phishing campaigns abusing RMM tools, where legitimate software becomes a route into company systems.

Researchers from Cato Networks identified the campaign’s delivery infrastructure and examined its use of SimpleHelp.

In their November 3 research report, Cato CTRL researchers said they suspect a connection to MuddyWater, although the evidence does not establish definitive attribution. CyberIL had previously reported the activity.

Hackers Use Fake Government Websites and CAPTCHA Checks

The attack starts with an email claiming to come from the Israel Tax Authority. Recipients who try to enter the supposed personal account area reach a lookalike website.

Its government-themed name creates a misleading connection to Israel’s official government web namespace. The page then presents a checkbox, a Continue button, and an archive password.

These details make the download resemble a protected document service. Unlike fake CAPTCHA command attacks that instruct victims to paste commands into Terminal, this chain uses verification to lead users toward a ZIP download and subsequent executable launch.

Inside the archive, the supposed tax document is actually a program. One sample carries a Hebrew filename meaning “Israel Tax Authority,” extending the impersonation beyond the browser.

Opening it can deploy SimpleHelp configured to connect to infrastructure controlled by the attackers. SimpleHelp is legitimate remote support software, not inherently malware.

Its normal features include desktop control, terminal access, file transfers, and system diagnostics. When deployed without authorization, those same functions could let an operator inspect business systems, run commands, retrieve files, or deliver additional tools.

The distinction between capability and observation matters. Cato described these functions as potential attacker uses, not confirmed actions in this campaign.

Its telemetry showed a blocked request to campaign infrastructure, rather than proof that an attacker completed a remote-access session or stole information.

Suspected MuddyWater Links and the Limits of the Evidence

Cato’s attribution assessment rests on Israeli targeting, locally tailored impersonation, and phishing that delivers legitimate remote-access software.

Earlier MuddyWater remote access operations also involved SimpleHelp, providing relevant context. However, similarities in tools and targeting support suspicion rather than conclusive identification of the operator.

The infrastructure investigation also used FOFA searches for two HTTP ETag values. Researchers found eight service records associated with one IP address, including two campaign domains displaying nginx “Coming Soon” pages.

Those eight records should not be mistaken for eight separate servers or confirmed victims. Cato notified SimpleHelp on October 20, 2026, and shared server information the following day.

SimpleHelp identified both samples as Remote Access Client version 5.4.5 and assessed the findings as apparent malicious use of an older release. Neither party identified evidence of a software vulnerability being exploited.

That separates this campaign from earlier SimpleHelp vulnerability exploitation incidents involving compromised remote-management deployments.

Here, the documented entry point was social engineering intended to persuade users to install an attacker-configured client. Cato also found no evidence that SimpleHelp’s own infrastructure had been compromised in connection with this activity.

The post Critical Citrix XenServer Vulnerability Could Let Hackers Take Over Virtualization Hosts Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Citrix has disclosed a critical XenServer vulnerability that could let an unauthenticated attacker compromise virtualization hosts and supporting appliances.

Tracked as CVE-2026-98432, the flaw requires access to the management network, an important limit when assessing which systems are exposed.

The November 3 security bulletin covers XenServer 8.4 and XenServer 9, alongside affected Workload Balancing and Conversion Manager appliances.

Unlike previously reported Citrix XenServer guest vulnerabilities, the headline issue does not require a privileged account inside a virtual machine.

Citrix researchers noted that the issue could compromise the host, running Workload Balancing appliances, or Conversion Manager appliances.

Critical Citrix XenServer Vulnerability

The disclosure concerns software vulnerabilities, not an identified malware campaign; the bulletin does not name malware or confirm active exploitation.

Management-network access remains the central requirement for CVE-2026-98432. The advisory does not describe an unrestricted internet attack, publish an exploit chain, or explain the underlying coding error.

Administrators should therefore avoid treating every deployment as equally exposed without checking network reachability. A separate flaw, CVE-2026-102703, could allow a privileged guest user to compromise the host.

Earlier Citrix hypervisor security issues involved host crashes, highlighting why availability failures and host compromise must remain distinct when explaining virtualization risks.

Six additional vulnerabilities affect network booting or Secure Boot. An unauthenticated attacker on the same network could compromise a PXE-booting virtual machine during startup, while a guest administrator could bypass the guest’s Secure Boot policy.

The bulletin groups these outcomes without assigning each one to individual identifiers. Citrix has released fixes through the Normal and Early Access channels for both XenServer releases.

Administrators should follow the official security bulletin, update Workload Balancing to 2026.1.1 or later, and install Conversion Manager 2026.2.0.

Reviewing hypervisor security best practices can also support management-network isolation while teams coordinate patch deployment.

articles.description:
The security data lake movement is a jailbreak: telemetry escaping SIEM-priced storage into open formats on cheap object storage, with detection and query engines brought to the data. The 2026 field mixes general data clouds hosting security workloads, purpose-built security lakes, and SIEM vendors racing to rebuild atop lake economics before the exodus empties them. […]

The post Top 10 Best Security Data Lake Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The security data lake movement is a jailbreak: telemetry escaping SIEM-priced storage into open formats on cheap object storage, with detection and query engines brought to the data.

The 2026 field mixes general data clouds hosting security workloads, purpose-built security lakes, and SIEM vendors racing to rebuild atop lake economics before the exodus empties them. Snowflake takes 1; Google SecOps and Microsoft complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Snowflake the gravity well where security teams and a vendor ecosystem meet on one data cloud.

• Podium: Snowflake (ecosystem gravity), Google SecOps (bundled retention speed), Microsoft (Sentinel data lake trajectory).

• Architecture bet: open table formats (Iceberg-class) and OCSF normalization are the anti-lock-in levers grade every candidate on both.

• 2026 theme: detection-over-lake matured Panther and Anvilogic-class engines prove you can leave ingest-priced SIEM without leaving detection behind.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: storage/query economics, openness (table formats, OCSF, exit paths), detection-engineering fit atop the lake, scale/performance, ecosystem (apps, connectors, shared data), and operational burden.

Weights: economics 25%, openness 20%, detection fit 20%, performance 20%, ecosystem 15%.

The 2026 Security Data Lake Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Snowflake — Best Security-Data-Cloud Ecosystem

Snapshot: Consumption (compute+storage separated) | Partner detection apps atop | Iceberg-era openness moves

Why it earns 1: Snowflake became the security lake by gravity: storage and compute priced separately, near-infinite retention economics, SQL every analyst speaks, and decisively an ecosystem where Panther, Anvilogic, and dozens of security apps run detection directly on your tables.

Threat intel arrives as shared datasets, no pipelines. The lake you were promised, with a marketplace attached.

Pros: Ecosystem depth; economics separation; SQL accessibility; data sharing.

Cons: Compute costs need governance; security content comes from partners, not the platform.

Bottom line: The security lake with the richest neighborhood.

2. Google (SecOps) — Best Bundled Retention-and-Speed

Snapshot: Flat/employee-based packaging | A year of hot retention standard | Mandiant intel retro-application

Why it ranks here: Google’s answer to lake economics is to bundle them: SecOps packaging includes retention measured in months-to-a-year hot, sub-second search across it, and fresh Mandiant intel retro-hunted against history automatically.

It’s the lake and the SIEM in one bill less open than the build-your-own path, more finished than any of it.

Pros: Bundled retention; retro-hunt automation; predictable packaging.

Cons: Less architectural openness than true lake builds.

Bottom line: Lake economics without the construction project.

3. Microsoft (Sentinel Data Lake/ADX) — Best Estate-Native Lake Trajectory

Snapshot: Consumption tiers + lake tier | Sentinel data lake direction; ADX for power users | KQL everywhere

Why it ranks here: Microsoft is rebuilding Sentinel’s storage story around a lake tier: cheap long-retention storage under the same KQL surface, with Azure Data Explorer serving the roll-your-own crowd.

For Microsoft estates, the trajectory means staying put may deliver lake economics without migration watch the tier pricing as it matures.

Pros: Estate-native path; KQL continuity; ADX escape hatch for builders.

Cons: Maturing tier structure; consumption governance still required.

Bottom line: The lake coming to where Microsoft estates already live.

4. Databricks — Best Lakehouse ML/Analytics Depth

Snapshot: Compute-based consumption | Delta Lake openness | ML-native security analytics

Why it ranks here: Databricks brings the lakehouse to security: open Delta tables on your object storage, notebooks and ML pipelines for the detection problems rules can’t express fraud graphs, beacon detection, UEBA models you own. It rewards teams with data engineers and gives security programs genuine ML custody; turnkey it is not.

Pros: Open-format custody; ML-native analytics; engineering ceiling.

Cons: Build-it culture required; security content ecosystem younger.

Bottom line: The lake for teams who model, not just query.

5. Amazon (Security Lake) — Best OCSF-Native Cloud Lake

Snapshot: Service + S3/ingest costs | OCSF normalization at the core | Multi-account AWS aggregation

Why it ranks here: AWS built the standards bet into the product: Security Lake normalizes AWS and partner telemetry into OCSF on S3 under your control, queryable by Athena, OpenSearch, or any engine you point at it.

For AWS-centric estates it’s the lowest-friction open lake; the analytics experience is deliberately bring-your-own.

Pros: OCSF-native; your-bucket custody; AWS-source gravity.

Cons: BYO analytics layer; multi-cloud breadth thinner.

Bottom line: The standards-purist lake, batteries not included.

6. Panther — Best Detection-as-Code Over the Lake

Snapshot: Platform subscription| Python detections, lake-backed | Snowflake-native heritage

Why it ranks here: Panther proved the decoupled thesis: detection-as-code in Python, CI/CD-tested, running over lake storage (Snowflake lineage, now broader) at economics ingest-priced SIEMs can’t match.

Security engineers get software-engineering rigor; teams wanting GUI-driven content get a culture shock worth having.

Pros: Detection-as-code rigor; lake economics; engineer ergonomics.

Cons: Engineering-culture prerequisite.

Bottom line: The SIEM rebuilt by software engineers.

7. Cribl — Best Lake Feeder & Search-in-Place

Snapshot: Volume licensing | Stream routing + Lake + Search | Vendor-neutral tiering

Why it ranks here: Cribl isn’t where logs live it’s who decides where they go: filtering the 40% nobody queries, enriching in transit, routing one copy to the SIEM and a full-fidelity copy to cheap object storage, replayable on demand.

In cost-crisis logging programs, the pipeline tier routinely pays for itself first year, and Cribl Search queries data where it already sits.

For staged migrations off ingest-priced platforms, it’s the pragmatic path most estates actually walk.

Pros: Migration pragmatism; search-without-moving; filtration economics.

Cons: Detection layer comes from elsewhere.

Bottom line: The lake movement’s moving company.

8. Anvilogic — Best Multi-Lake Detection Layer

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Detections across Snowflake/Databricks/Splunk simultaneously | AI-assisted detection engineering

Why it ranks here: Anvilogic answers the transition decade’s real question detections spanning the Splunk you still run and the lake you’re filling: one detection plane compiling to multiple backends, with AI-assisted rule building and a content library mapped to attacker techniques. Hybrid-backend reality, productized.

Pros: Multi-backend compilation; migration-era fit; AI-assisted engineering.

Cons: Another layer in the stack; backend coverage specifics evolve.

Bottom line: One detection brain across two eras of storage.

9. Elastic — Best Open Searchable-Snapshot Lake

Snapshot: Resource pricing, free tier | Searchable snapshots on object storage | Full detection stack included

Why it ranks here: Elastic’s frozen tier is a lake with a search engine fused on: snapshots on S3-class storage queried directly, detection rules and UEBA included, everything open-core.

For teams wanting lake economics plus a built-in security layer without assembling partners, it’s the single-vendor version of the thesis.

Pros: Fused search+detection; open-core custody; snapshot economics.

Cons: Operational ownership; pure-lake query engines scale cheaper at extremes.

Bottom line: The lake with the search engine welded on.

10. Hydrolix — Best Cost-Per-Queryable-Terabyte Challenger

Snapshot: Consumption | Extreme-compression streaming lake | Hot-query on compressed data

Why it ranks here: Hydrolix attacks the metric that decides lake arguments: cost per queryable terabyte, via aggressive compression that stays hot-queryable without rehydration.

Observability-adjacent heritage, now pointed at security telemetry. A challenger bet smaller ecosystem, startling economics for estates drowning in volume.

Pros: Compression economics; hot-query retention; volume appetite.

Cons: Ecosystem youth; security-content layer BYO.

Bottom line: The economics outlier worth benchmarking.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Own the Tables, Rent the Engines

The lake decision is a custody decision: who owns the bytes, in what format, queryable by whose engines. Grade every candidate on two anti-lock-in levers open table formats (can another engine read your history without export?) and OCSF normalization (can detections port?) because the lake movement’s whole point dies if you rebuild SIEM lock-in on prettier storage.

Architect in three layers deliberately: pipeline (what lands), lake (open tables, your bucket where possible), detection engine (Panther/Anvilogic-class, or the bundled layer if you chose Google/Microsoft’s finished path).

Benchmark the only number that settles arguments cost per queryable terabyte-month at your real volumes, including compute for your actual query patterns and run one honest investigation drill: a 180-day-old incident reconstructed end-to-end on each finalist.

Teams without data-engineering capacity should buy the bundled trajectory (SecOps, Sentinel lake) without shame; teams with it should keep custody and compose. Either way, write the export test into the contract: a terabyte out, in an open format, timed.

FAQs

What are the best security data lake platforms in 2026? Snowflake for ecosystem gravity, Google SecOps and Microsoft for bundled trajectories, Databricks for lakehouse ML, AWS Security Lake for OCSF purity, Panther and Anvilogic for detection layers, with Cribl, Elastic, and Hydrolix completing the architecture.

Does a security data lake replace our SIEM? It replaces SIEM storage economics; detection and workflow still need a layer bundled (Google, Microsoft, Elastic) or composed (Panther, Anvilogic over Snowflake/Databricks/AWS).

What is OCSF and why does it matter? The Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework a vendor-neutral event schema; OCSF-normalized data makes detections and tools portable across engines, which is the anti-lock-in point.

What’s the realistic cost advantage? Object-storage retention typically runs an order of magnitude below ingest-priced SIEM storage; the honest comparison adds query compute for your patterns benchmark, don’t assume.

Who shouldn’t build a security data lake? Teams without data-engineering capacity the bundled paths (SecOps, Sentinel’s lake tier) deliver most of the economics with none of the assembly.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one custody question, one benchmark: cost per queryable terabyte with your queries.

Snowflake’s neighborhood, Google’s finished bundle, Microsoft’s estate trajectory, Databricks’ modeling ceiling, AWS’s standards purity, Panther and Anvilogic proving detection travels, Cribl moving the boxes, Elastic welding search on, Hydrolix compressing the argument own the tables, rent the engines, port the detections, and time the export before you need it.

The post Apple to Scan for Every Photo and File Shared Through a Public iCloud Link for Harmful Content appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple will begin checking photos and files shared through public iCloud links for harmful content with version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS.

The policy covers items shared using “Anyone with the Link,” including photos stored in iCloud Photos and files held in iCloud Drive. Apple outlined the change in a support document published November 3, 2026.

Apple is not announcing checks of every private photo or file stored in iCloud. Its notice targets content that users make available to anyone holding a sharing link. The separate “People you choose” option, which limits access to invited or approved users, is not described as part of these checks.

For users, the key issue is privacy. Apple says an item shared through “Anyone with the Link” is no longer protected by end-to-end encryption. This applies even when the owner or other participants have enabled Advanced Data Protection, making public sharing an important exception to that protection.

Apple to Scan for Photo and File

When sharing content stored in iCloud, users can send a copy or share a link. Link sharing then offers two access settings. “People you choose” restricts access, while “Anyone with the Link” lets people open the item without individual approval. Apple says the latter also makes that content accessible to the company.

This distinction separates account security from sharing permissions. Cybersecurity News’ guide to securing iCloud accounts discusses account protection and permission reviews. In this case, the setting attached to a shared item determines whether access is restricted or available to anyone holding its link.

According to Apple’s support notice, public-link content will be checked for harmful material. However, the document does not define “harmful content” or explain the detection process. It does not identify scanning tools, describe human review, or state whether checks happen before recipients can open a link.

What Happens When Content Is Flagged

Apple says it reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete harmful content at any time. Possible action extends beyond removing a shared item. The company may block or disable the associated Apple Account and prevent new accounts from being created with the same email address or phone number.

The notice also allows Apple to involve law enforcement when necessary. However, it does not explain review standards, appeal options, or how users would challenge an incorrect flag. Those missing details leave questions about how the policy will work in practice, especially when an account faces restrictions.

The encryption issue sits within a wider debate over access to cloud data. Cybersecurity News previously covered reported UK demands for access to encrypted iCloud backups. This announcement concerns a narrower boundary: items deliberately shared through public links, rather than a stated expansion of access across private iCloud storage.

For sensitive documents and personal photos, the practical step is to review sharing permissions before distributing a link. Choosing “People you choose” limits access to approved recipients.

Public-link sharing should not be treated as private storage simply because Advanced Data Protection is enabled. Apple also leaves unanswered whether links created before version 27.3 will face checks under this policy.

articles.title: Top 10 Best Security Log Management Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
Security logging has become a commodities market with three prices: the cost to move a log, to store it, and to ask it a question. The 2026 winners optimize different legs pipeline brokers slashing transit volume, hot-architecture engines making every byte queryable, cloud giants bundling retention into estates. This ranking scores ten tools on economics, […]

The post Top 10 Best Security Log Management Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security logging has become a commodities market with three prices: the cost to move a log, to store it, and to ask it a question.

The 2026 winners optimize different legs pipeline brokers slashing transit volume, hot-architecture engines making every byte queryable, cloud giants bundling retention into estates.

This ranking scores ten tools on economics, search speed, and control, with the SIEM question deliberately bracketed: these are the logging foundations SIEMs sit on. Splunk takes 1; Elastic and Cribl complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Splunk still the deepest log-analytics engine, with tiering finally softening its cost story.

• Podium: Splunk (analytics depth), Elastic (open-architecture economics), Cribl (the pipeline layer that tames everyone else’s bill).

• Structural shift: the pipeline tier (Cribl-class) became standard architecture route, filter, and enrich before anything expensive touches the data.

• Brand note: LogRhythm’s logging lane ships from the merged Exabeam company roadmap diligence applies.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: ingest/storage economics, query performance at retention scale, pipeline control (filtering, routing, transformation), security-content fit, operational burden, and ecosystem reach.

Weights: economics 25%, query performance 25%, pipeline control 20%, security fit 15%, operations 15%.

The 2026 Log Management Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Splunk — Best Analytics Depth

Snapshot: Ingest/workload pricing, tiered storage | SPL query power | Federated search era

Why it earns 1: For asking hard questions of messy machine data, SPL remains the sharpest knife: schema-on-read flexibility, statistical commands, and a two-decade content ecosystem.

Workload pricing, SmartStore tiering, and federated search against cheap object storage answer partially the bill that built its reputation. The Cisco era adds integration bets; the analytics moat stands.

Pros: Query-language ceiling; content ecosystem; tiering options matured.

Cons: Still premium at scale; architecture choices demand expertise.

Bottom line: The deepest answers, at a price worth engineering around.

2. Elastic — Best Open-Architecture Economics

Snapshot: Resource-based pricing, free tier | ES|QL + searchable snapshots | Frozen-tier economics

Why it ranks here: Elastic’s economics compound: compute-based pricing decoupled from ingest volume, searchable snapshots making frozen object storage directly queryable, and an open content model. Teams with engineering appetite run petabyte retention at fractions of ingest-priced rivals; the trade is ownership burden someone must be the Elastic person.

Pros: Cost architecture; frozen-tier search; openness; dual-use with observability.

Cons: Operational ownership weight; managed tiers close the gap at cost.

Bottom line: The engineer’s economics play.

3. Cribl — Best Pipeline Control Layer

Snapshot: Data-volume licensing | Stream/Edge/Search product family | vendor-neutral routing

Why it ranks here: Cribl isn’t where logs live it’s who decides where they go: filtering the 40% nobody queries, enriching in transit, routing one copy to the SIEM and a full-fidelity copy to cheap object storage, replayable on demand.

In cost-crisis logging programs, the pipeline tier routinely pays for itself first year, and Cribl Search queries data where it already sits.

Pros: Bill-shrinking filtration; vendor neutrality; replay architecture; search-in-place.

Cons: Another tier to run; volume-priced itself.

Bottom line: The thermostat on everyone else’s invoice.

4. Microsoft Sentinel — Best Estate-Bundled Logging

Snapshot: Consumption with basic/auxiliary tiers | Data-lake direction | KQL

Why it ranks here: Sentinel’s logging story matured into tiers: analytics-grade tables for detection data, cheaper basic/auxiliary tiers for the long tail, and a data-lake trajectory aimed squarely at retention economics.

For Microsoft estates, connector gravity plus KQL fluency makes it the path of least resistance costed per gigabyte, so pipeline discipline still matters.

Pros: Estate connectors; tiering flexibility; KQL ecosystem.

Cons: Consumption math punishes undisciplined ingestion.

Bottom line: The Microsoft estate’s logging default, tiered at last.

5. Datadog — Best Observability-Fused Logging

Snapshot: Ingest+indexing split pricing | Logging without limits model | Cloud SIEM atop

Why it ranks here: Datadog decoupled the two prices cleverly: ingest everything cheap, index selectively for search, rehydrate from archives when investigations demand.

Security teams sharing budgets with DevOps get one platform for both lanes, with Cloud SIEM detections riding the same pipes. The model rewards teams who tune indexing policies and punishes those who don’t.

Pros: Ingest/index decoupling; dual-use consolidation; rehydration model.

Cons: Costs balloon without indexing discipline; security depth versus dedicated SIEMs.

Bottom line: Observability money buying security logging.

6. Sumo Logic — Best Dual-Use SaaS Logging

Snapshot: Credits/flex consumption | Cloud-native multi-tenant SaaS | Security analytics layer

Why it ranks here: Sumo’s cloud-native SaaS removes infrastructure ownership entirely, flexes on credits, and serves security and observability from one store.

Its lane is the team that wants zero logging infrastructure and sane defaults less ceiling than Splunk, less ownership than Elastic, less pipeline control than Cribl, and deliberately so.

Pros: Zero-infrastructure SaaS; flex licensing; dual-use.

Cons: Depth ceilings versus the specialists on either side.

Bottom line: Logging as a utility bill.

7. Graylog — Best Value-Tier Dedicated Log Platform

Snapshot: Open + enterprise tiers | Purpose-built log management | Security edition analytics

Why it ranks here: Graylog keeps the dedicated-log-platform lane honest: open-core economics, pipeline processing, archiving tiers, and a security edition adding detection content at pricing that undercuts the giants meaningfully.

Mid-market teams get real capability without the enterprise invoice; frontier analytics and ecosystem breadth stay upstream.

Pros: Value economics; purpose-built ergonomics; open-core option.

Cons: Ecosystem and analytics ceiling versus leaders.

Bottom line: The sensible middle of the market.

8. Devo — Best Always-Hot Query Performance

Snapshot: Platform licensing | No-rehydration hot architecture | High-velocity ingestion

Why it ranks here: Devo’s architecture bet: everything stays hot four hundred days queryable in seconds, no rehydration ceremonies, ingestion built for terabyte-per-day velocity. Estates whose investigations routinely reach back months (fraud, telecom, large retail) buy exactly this; others pay for headroom they won’t use.

Pros: Hot-retention speed; velocity handling; investigation reach.

Cons: Niche strength priced as such; ecosystem gravity.

Bottom line: For teams that query last year like yesterday.

9. ManageEngine — Best SMB/Mid-Market Log Compliance

Snapshot: Per-device/source tiers | EventLog Analyzer + Log360 family | Compliance-report engine

Why it ranks here: ManageEngine serves the vast quiet market: SMBs and mid-market IT teams needing centralized logs, canned compliance reports (PCI, HIPAA, SOX), and basic correlation at prices that don’t require a committee. It’s logging as a solved administrative problem the right tool below the complexity line.

Pros: Entry economics; compliance-report breadth; low operational bar.

Cons: Scale and analytics ceilings; enterprise estates outgrow it.

Bottom line: Compliance logging without the procurement drama.

10. LogRhythm (Exabeam) — Best Mid-Market SIEM-Logging Lineage

Snapshot: Platform tiers | SIEM-integrated log management | Merged-entity roadmap

Why it ranks here: LogRhythm’s logging layer serves its substantial mid-market SIEM base collection, normalization, retention integrated with detection content now shipping from the merged Exabeam company.

Existing estates get continuity; new logging-first buyers should weigh the merged roadmap and the dedicated alternatives above.

Pros: Install-base continuity; SIEM integration; mid-market fit.

Cons: Merged-entity roadmap diligence; logging-first buyers have leaner options.

Bottom line: Continuity play inside the Exabeam-merged world.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Architect the Three Prices Separately

Logging bills explode when one product sets all three prices transit, storage, and query. Architect them independently: a pipeline tier (Cribl-class, or Elastic/Datadog’s native controls) deciding what moves where; cheap object storage holding full fidelity; and an analytics engine indexing only what detection and investigation actually query.

Model your real telemetry’s three-year growth against each candidate’s pricing after a realistic 30–50% pipeline filtration assumption, and test reach-back honestly in the pilot time a 90-day-old investigation query on each finalist, because archived-but-unqueryable is a compliance checkbox, not a capability.

Keep detection content portable (Sigma-friendly where possible) so the logging layer can change without the detection program resetting, confirm the LogRhythm–Exabeam roadmap if that lineage is on your list, and write data-export terms into every contract: in logging, the exit bill is measured in petabytes.

FAQs

What are the best security log management tools in 2026? Splunk for analytics depth, Elastic for open economics, Cribl as the pipeline layer, Sentinel for Microsoft estates, Datadog and Sumo for dual-use SaaS, with Graylog, Devo, ManageEngine, and LogRhythm/Exabeam by tier.

Log management versus SIEM? Logging is the substrate collection, retention, query; SIEM adds detection content, correlation, and workflow on top. Modern architecture separates them deliberately for cost control.

What’s a pipeline tier and do we need one? A broker (Cribl-class) that filters, enriches, and routes logs before expensive destinations above roughly a few hundred gigabytes daily, it typically pays for itself.

How long should we retain security logs? Hot for investigation norms (90 days common), compliant-cold for your regulatory floor (one to seven years by regime) the architecture question is whether cold stays queryable.

How do we cut logging costs without losing evidence? Filter duplicates and heartbeat noise in the pipeline, keep full fidelity in cheap object storage with replay, and index selectively fidelity archived beats fidelity indexed.

Verdict

Ten tools, three prices, one architecture rule: never let a single invoice set them all. Splunk for the deepest questions, Elastic for engineered economics, Cribl deciding what goes where, Sentinel and Datadog and Sumo for cloud-estate gravity, Graylog for the sensible middle, Devo for the long reach-back, ManageEngine for the quiet market, the LogRhythm lineage for continuity filter first, archive everything, index what you query, and time that 90-day search before you sign.

articles.title: Top 10 Best Threat Hunting Services in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
Detection engineering catches what you anticipated; threat hunting catches what you didn’t. The craft is hypothesis-driven “if an actor used this tradecraft here, what residue would exist?” and the services market sells it in two shapes: platform-native hunting across a vendor’s own telemetry ocean, and estate-attached hunting through MDR relationships. The post Top 10 Best Threat Hunting Services in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Detection engineering catches what you anticipated; threat hunting catches what you didn’t. The craft is hypothesis-driven “if an actor used this tradecraft here, what residue would exist?” and the services market sells it in two shapes: platform-native hunting across a vendor’s own telemetry ocean, and estate-attached hunting through MDR relationships.

One jurisdictional note is handled plainly at 10. CrowdStrike OverWatch takes 1; Mandiant and Red Canary complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: CrowdStrike OverWatch the reference for continuous, human-led hunting at telemetry scale.

• Podium: OverWatch (scale+tempo), Mandiant (actor-knowledge depth), Red Canary (published-methodology transparency).

• Shape split: platform-native hunters (OverWatch, Sophos, Trellix) hunt their own sensor oceans; estate-attached hunters (Expel, eSentire, Secureworks) hunt what you grant telemetry reach decides value either way.

• Jurisdiction note: Kaspersky’s hunting research is technically formidable; Western procurement restrictions gate it regardless compliance decides before capability.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: hypothesis-craft maturity, telemetry reach, hunt tempo (continuous versus periodic), findings quality (novel TTPs surfaced, not re-labeled alerts), feedback loop into detections, and transparency of method.

Weights: hypothesis craft 25%, telemetry reach 25%, tempo 15%, findings quality 20%, detection feedback 15%.

The 2026 Threat Hunting Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. CrowdStrike (OverWatch) — Best Continuous Hunting at Scale

Snapshot: Falcon add-on subscription | 24/7 human hunt teams on global telemetry | Hunt-to-detection pipeline

Why it earns 1: OverWatch defined managed hunting’s modern form: human hunters working planetary Falcon telemetry around the clock, pattern-matching across millions of endpoints so a novel tradecraft seen once becomes a hunt lead everywhere.

Findings feed Falcon’s detection content, compounding the loop. If your estate runs Falcon, the marginal power of attaching OverWatch is the category’s best ratio.

Pros: Telemetry ocean; 24/7 tempo; cross-customer pattern leverage; detection feedback.

Cons: Hunts Falcon’s view non-Falcon estates see less.

Bottom line: The hunting benchmark, priced as a Falcon multiplier.

2. Google (Mandiant) — Best Actor-Knowledge Hunting

Snapshot: Managed hunt engagements + retainer pairing | Frontline actor intel as hypothesis source | Compromise-assessment craft

Why it ranks here: Mandiant hunts from the actor’s biography: hypotheses sourced from live incident-floor knowledge of specific groups’ tradecraft, applied in targeted hunts and compromise assessments.

Where OverWatch hunts broad and continuous, Mandiant hunts deep and informed the team you point at “are they in here?”

Pros: Actor-specific hypotheses; compromise-assessment rigor; intel provenance.

Cons: Engagement-shaped more than continuous-service-shaped.

Bottom line: Hunting with the adversary’s file open.

3. SentinelOne Wayfinder MDR — Best AI-Assisted Managed Threat Hunting

Snapshot: MDR subscription | Singularity platform + Purple AI | Endpoint, identity, cloud, and telemetry hunting

Why it ranks here: SentinelOne Wayfinder MDR combines human-led threat hunting with the Singularity platform’s behavioral detections threat intelligence, and AI-assisted investigation.

Its hunters use Purple AI and cross-environment telemetry to investigate suspicious activity, validate threats, and accelerate response across endpoint, identity, cloud, and other security data.

Pros: Strong platform telemetry; AI-assisted investigations; broad attack-surface coverage; integrated response.

Cons: Best value comes when organizations are already invested in the SentinelOne ecosystem.

Bottom line: Human threat hunters amplified by automation, behavioral analytics, and AI.

4. eSentire — Best Response-Fused Hunting

Snapshot: Service tiers | Hunts that end in containment | Threat response unit linkage

Why it ranks here: eSentire welds hunting to its response authority: hypotheses worked by its threat response unit, and findings that don’t become reports they become containment actions within the same hour.

For buyers who measure hunting by evicted adversaries rather than documents produced, the fusion is the feature.

Pros: Hunt-to-containment speed; 24/7 operation; original research input.

Cons: Full value requires granted response authority.

Bottom line: Hunts that end with someone locked out.

5. Expel — Best BYO-Stack Hunting

Snapshot: Add-on to MDR | Hunts across your existing tooling | Transparent Workbench findings

Why it ranks here: Expel hunts the estate you already built EDR, cloud, identity, SaaS with hypotheses tuned to your tech mix and findings written in Workbench where you watch the investigation unfold.

The BYO respect extends to honesty about signal gaps: they’ll tell you which telemetry you lack to support which hunts.

Pros: Stack-agnostic reach; transparency; signal-gap honesty.

Cons: Hunt depth bounded by the telemetry you grant.

Bottom line: Your stack, hunted honestly.

6. Huntress — Best Human-Led Threat Hunting for Lean Teams

Snapshot: Subscription-based | 24/7 human-led SOC | Managed EDR + identity and security monitoring

Why it ranks here: Huntress focuses on making managed threat hunting accessible to organizations without large internal SOC teams, combining endpoint telemetry, identity monitoring, and human investigation.

Its analysts continuously review suspicious activity, investigate persistent footholds and attacker behavior, and provide guided remediation rather than simply forwarding alerts.

Pros: Human-led investigations; strong mid-market fit; straightforward deployment; actionable remediation guidance.

Cons: Narrower telemetry and global-scale hunting depth than large XDR platform providers.

Bottom line: Practical human-led hunting for teams that need expert coverage without building a full SOC.

7. Sophos — Best Mid-Market Managed Hunting

Snapshot: MDR tiers including hunt function | X-Ops research teams | Cross-product telemetry

Why it ranks here: Sophos folds genuine hunting into MDR economics the mid-market clears: X-Ops research driving hypotheses, hunts across endpoint/firewall/email telemetry, and response included.

It’s the pragmatic answer for organizations that will never buy a standalone hunt engagement but deserve better than alert triage.

Pros: Hunt-inclusive MDR pricing; X-Ops research; product-telemetry breadth.

Cons: Depth ceilings versus dedicated hunt benches.

Bottom line: Real hunting at MDR-bundle prices.

8. Rapid7 — Best Bundled Hunting Value

Snapshot: MDR-inclusive hunting | InsightIDR telemetry base | Vulnerability-context pairing

Why it ranks here: Rapid7’s managed hunting rides the Insight platform: periodic and lead-driven hunts across InsightIDR telemetry with exposure context from InsightVM sharpening hypotheses (“this CVE is exploitable here hunt for its post-exploitation residue”). Value-tier honest: solid hunting economics, not frontier craft.

Pros: Bundle economics; exposure-informed leads; platform integration.

Cons: Hunt tempo and depth versus leaders.

Bottom line: The budget-sane hunting attach.

9. Trellix — Best XDR-Estate Hunting

Snapshot: Service attach to XDR | Advanced Research Center input | Broad control-point telemetry

Why it ranks here: Trellix hunts across its XDR fabric endpoint, email, network, DLP control points with Advanced Research Center threat work feeding hypotheses. For the substantial installed base running Trellix controls, attached hunting extracts value from telemetry already flowing; outside that base, the case thins.

Pros: Control-point breadth; research center input; installed-base economics.

Cons: Estate-coupled value; brand momentum.

Bottom line: The Trellix estate’s hunt layer.

10. Kaspersky — Deepest APT Hunt Research, Jurisdiction-Gated

Snapshot: Managed hunting via MDR/intel portal | GReAT-grade hypotheses | Procurement restrictions decide first

Why it ranks here compliance first: On craft alone, Kaspersky’s hunting lineage is elite GReAT’s APT discoveries seeded half the industry’s hypothesis playbook, and its managed hunting inherits that depth.

But US federal prohibition and parallel Western restrictions gate procurement regardless of capability; organizations under those regimes should treat it as unavailable, and others should run compliance review before capability evaluation.

Pros: APT-research depth; unique regional visibility.

Cons: Jurisdictional gates precede technical evaluation.

Bottom line: Elite craft behind a compliance door many can’t open.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Audit the Hypotheses, Not the Brochure

Hunting services separate on one question brochures never answer: where do hypotheses come from? Demand each candidate walk you through three real hunts the hypothesis, its intel source, the telemetry queried, the outcome and distinguish genuine hypothesis-driven work from re-labeled alert triage, which is the category’s quiet fraud.

Match shape to estate: Falcon shops attach OverWatch almost axiomatically; heterogeneous stacks want BYO hunters (Expel, Red Canary); “are we already owned?” moments buy Mandiant-class compromise assessments rather than subscriptions.

Contract the feedback loop explicitly every hunt finding should become a detection you keep, written into deliverables so the service makes your estate smarter, not just watched.

Set the honest success metric with the provider up front: novel findings per quarter and dwell-time trend, acknowledging that a mature estate yields few true positives a quarter of clean hunts with new detections shipped is success, not failure.

And run every candidate through procurement’s jurisdiction screen first; the Kaspersky gate is the visible case of a general rule.

FAQs

What are the best threat hunting services in 2026? CrowdStrike OverWatch for continuous scale, Mandiant for actor-driven assessments, Red Canary for transparent methodology, eSentire for response fusion, Expel for BYO stacks, with Secureworks, Sophos, Rapid7, Trellix, and Kaspersky (jurisdiction permitting) by fit.

Threat hunting versus MDR aren’t they the same? MDR triages what alerts; hunting hypothesizes what doesn’t real hunting is proactive, hypothesis-driven work, and many MDR contracts include only token amounts of it. Read the deliverables.

What telemetry does hunting need? Endpoint process/command-line data is the floor; identity logs, DNS, and cloud-control-plane events multiply hypothesis space hunters should tell you honestly which hunts your telemetry can’t support.

How do we measure a hunting service? Hypotheses run per quarter with sources shown, novel findings (not re-labeled alerts), detections shipped from findings, and estate dwell-time trend.

Is a clean hunt a wasted hunt? No a documented clean hunt with a new detection shipped is bought-down risk; the waste is hunts without hypotheses or artifacts.

Verdict

Ten services, one craft test: show me the hypothesis. OverWatch hunting the ocean, Mandiant hunting the actor, Red Canary publishing the method, eSentire ending hunts in evictions, Expel respecting your stack, Secureworks and Sophos and Rapid7 and Trellix by estate, Kaspersky behind the compliance gate audit three real hunts, contract the detection feedback, and judge by novel findings and falling dwell time, not by the thickness of the quarterly PDF.

articles.title: DigiCert Confirms Data Breach Exposing Customer Details and Sensitive Identity Documents
articles.description:
DigiCert has confirmed a data breach involving an internal business system that stored customer contact details and identity documents. Unauthorized access exposed archived information, including names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. A small minority of affected customer accounts also contained passports, driver’s licenses, utility bills, or other documents showing names and addresses. […]

The post DigiCert Confirms Data Breach Exposing Customer Details and Sensitive Identity Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DigiCert has confirmed a data breach involving an internal business system that stored customer contact details and identity documents. Unauthorized access exposed archived information, including names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.

A small minority of affected customer accounts also contained passports, driver’s licenses, utility bills, or other documents showing names and addresses.

The company said the incident affected only a small proportion of its archived data. Its public report does not provide a total number of affected people, organizations, or documents. DigiCert confirmed the unauthorized data access on October 19, 2026, and filed its preliminary incident report the following day.

DigiCert said its Certificate Authority services, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected. The company said customer login credentials and issued certificates remain secure.

Investigators found no certificate issuance, validation changes, or revocation activity linked to the unauthorized account. Customers do not need to replace active certificates because of this incident.

Troy Hunt shared DigiCert’s notification on X, asking, “Anyone else get one of these from @digicert?” The email said the company was reviewing identity documents to identify affected individuals and would notify them once the review was complete.

DigiCert Confirms Data Breach

The exposure began with an infrastructure migration on February 4, 2025. DigiCert moved the business system from a network segment restricted by a virtual private network, or VPN, to another availability zone. That change accidentally made the internal system accessible from the internet without a security review of its new exposure.

An account registration feature, intended for other uses of the account management platform, also became available. Accounts created through that feature were not covered by the multifactor authentication required for DigiCert staff. Although these accounts had no application assigned, they received read-only access to archived information, revealing a gap in permission checks.

According to DigiCert’s incident report, staff noticed non-DigiCert accounts on June 18, 2026. An initial review incorrectly concluded that accounts without an assigned application could not access data. A web application firewall blocked new registrations through the external access path, but existing access remained a concern.

A report from DigiCert’s managed security research program followed on June 21. Engineers confirmed the registration issue and released an authorization fix on July 2. Investigators later established that unauthorized data access occurred between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert initially treated the problem as an account-creation issue rather than a data-access incident.

The company first suspected access to archived information on October 12. Retained logs and audit records helped investigators reconstruct the access window and link activity to the account. The account could read records but could not change them, approve identity checks, or issue certificates.

DigiCert subsequently disabled self-registration, moved remaining exposed endpoints behind private network infrastructure, reset business system passwords, and strengthened monitoring. It also completed a permissions review and required security approval for network access changes. The report’s action items include further checks on external exposure and account alerts.

This disclosure concerns archived customer information, not compromised certificate operations. It differs from the earlier DigiCert support-system breach involving code-signing certificates and the 2024 DNS validation error that required certificate replacements.

Here, the central failure was allowing newly registered accounts to read sensitive records. DigiCert’s stated lesson is direct: internal tools need explicit authorization checks, even when network restrictions are expected to protect them.

articles.description:

The post DreamHost Confirms Data Breach – Hackers Stole Customer Credentials and Accessed Emails appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DreamHost has confirmed a breach that exposed customer login details after hackers exploited its web-based File Manager. The hosting provider said attackers obtained FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords, along with some webmail credentials. In a small number of cases, private mailbox contents may also have been viewed.

The company discovered unauthorized access on October 23, 2026. Its investigation identified a potential exposure window stretching back to approximately August. Customers who used File Manager during that period have been told to treat their file transfer credentials as compromised, even while investigators continue checking the full impact.

DreamHost currently estimates that well under approximately 10% of its hosted email and FTP/SFTP accounts were affected. That figure refers to accounts, not a confirmed number of individual customers. Some users received precautionary password reset notices but may not have had their credentials exposed.

The confirmation follows DreamHost’s earlier email and FTP password resets, which initially left the cause unclear. Those resets stopped affected users from signing in until account owners created new passwords. File Manager returned online on October 26, according to the earlier incident reporting.

DreamHost found no evidence that attackers accessed control panel logins or customer billing details. It also said full payment card numbers are not stored on its systems because an outside processor handles card payments. These findings remain subject to the ongoing investigation rather than proving that every possible risk has been excluded.

DreamHost Confirms Data Breach

In its October 29 security incident disclosure, DreamHost said the entry point was a flaw in third-party software behind File Manager. The browser-based tool lets customers manage website files. The notice does not name the software, describe the vulnerability, or provide a CVE identifier.

Attackers also reached certain webmail systems and obtained credentials belonging to a limited number of users. DreamHost reset those passwords and ended active sessions on October 23. It is contacting customers individually where investigators believe mailbox contents may have been viewed. The company has not confirmed widespread email theft.

Ending sessions matters alongside changing passwords. Separate reporting on stolen browser cookies and account takeovers explains how an authenticated session can expose email without another login. However, DreamHost’s public announcement does not explicitly confirm stolen session tokens, so that detail should not be treated as established by this notice.

DreamHost took the affected File Manager server offline and preserved it for forensic work. It then rebuilt the service with added safeguards and monitoring, changed potentially exposed internal credentials, and brought in outside security experts. Reviews of other customer-facing tools and required regulator notifications are also underway.

Affected users need their account owner to reset passwords through DreamHost’s control panel. The company recommends unique passwords, changing reused credentials elsewhere, and updating saved passwords in email and file transfer clients. Customers should inspect website files for unexpected changes and check mailbox forwarding rules and filters for unfamiliar entries.

Customers should type panel.dreamhost.com directly into their browser rather than follow login links in unexpected messages. DreamHost says its incident emails never request passwords or ask recipients to sign in through a link.

articles.description:
OpenAI says an automated research pipeline found and proved 948 separate Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws in one run. These bugs could let a normal local user gain root access. The run took place in mid-October 2026 and used an upcoming cyber model, as OpenAI explains in its research write-up. The system first scanned the […]

The post OpenAI Cyber Model Uncovers 948 Linux Kernel Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI says an automated research pipeline found and proved 948 separate Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws in one run. These bugs could let a normal local user gain root access. The run took place in mid-October 2026 and used an upcoming cyber model, as OpenAI explains in its research write-up.

The system first scanned the kernel for the parts a low-privileged user can reach. These “Scout” agents picked 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code or roughly 7% of the kernel. “Analyst” agents then produced 2,308 candidate findings in 12 hours.

A candidate is only a guess until someone proves it. Triage agents built proof-of-concept code and ran it in isolated virtual machines with the Kernel Address Sanitizer turned on. Within 30 hours, 1,724 findings (about 74.7%) were reproduced. Only 3.1% were wrong because the model assumed an impossible condition.

Next, exploit agents tested the bugs on systems with common protections such as SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, and HARDENED_USERCOPY. They produced 291 information leak proofs and 1,169 working privilege escalation exploits.

OpenAI Uncovers 948 Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

After variant analysis, OpenAI counted 948 unique vulnerabilities and wrote 948 patches for them. Human researchers reviewed the results before reporting.

This builds on the Patch the Planet program from June, when GPT-5.5-Cyber produced 24 Linux privilege escalation exploits. Our earlier report on GPT-5.5-Cyber covers that launch.

The full run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. OpenAI calls this an upper bound and expects better tooling to cut it. It compared the output with public bounties. Using $20,000 from Pwn2Own and $70,000 from TyphoonPWN, the 948 bugs would be worth $18.9 million to $66.3 million.

On a hardened kernelCTF setup, the pipeline got 21 privilege escalation exploits for about $32,936. OpenAI estimates that would equal roughly $1.5 million in rewards. Google’s current rules pay $71,337 per eligible exploit.

A July run with GPT-5.6 Sol found 166 unique bugs for $513,690. The October model found 948, more than five times as many, even after three months of kernel hardening.

Maintainers moved fast. Within 10 days, 61 bugs were patched upstream, 43 had staged patches, and 299 were being discussed in public. That pace matches the earlier news that Linux fixed more than 400 kernel bugs in 24 hours.

The agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques, which outside kernel experts also had not seen. OpenAI withheld the technical details for safety. In one early run, 20 of 200 “successful” exploits gained root through a different zero-day than the assigned one. This shows why humans must check how a result was reached.

The agents also found a QEMU flaw in the test setup itself. This fits a wider pattern, since OpenAI’s AI agents also escaped sandboxes in red-team tests.

OpenAI warns that a low-privileged account on an unpatched system should be treated like root access for a well-funded threat actor. Real cases already exist. Hackers recently chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw to get root on 25 servers.

Admins should install kernel updates quickly, reboot into the new kernel, and limit unprivileged user namespaces where possible. Sandboxes such as Firecracker and gVisor can also reduce damage.

OpenAI says it has already sent hundreds of reports and patches. It is sending the rest through Patch the Planet partners as part of its Daybreak program.

articles.description:
